claim: "We have an 80 percent graduation rate in high school after spending more per student than any country in the world other than Liechtenstein, I think, or Luxembourg and a couple other small countries."
rationale: The claim mixes roughly correct intuition with inaccurate specifics. U.S. public high-school adjusted cohort graduation rates were about mid-80s percent in recent pre-pandemic years (not exactly 80%), and while the U.S. is among the highest spenders per student, several small jurisdictions (e.g., Luxembourg and other small/high-income countries) and sometimes other countries rank above or alongside it depending on the year and spending measure. Because both the graduation rate number and the absolute-ranking wording are imprecise, the statement as given is misleading.

claim: "More black babies are aborted in NYC than born."
rationale: City vital statistics and public-health reports show that annual births to Black mothers in New York City outnumber abortions overall; total abortions in the city are not greater than Black births. The claim treats race of fetuses imprecisely and ignores that official data classify births/abortions by maternal race and show more live births among Black mothers than reported abortions attributed to Black women in recent years.

claim: Says the Dickey Amendment "prevents the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from even researching the relationship between gun violence and public health. ... The government can’t study gun violence but is spending $400,000 analyzing the effects of Swedish massages on rabbits."
rationale: The Dickey Amendment's text barred use of CDC funds to 'advocate or promote gun control' and Congress cut a line item in 1996, which led the CDC to curtail firearm research, but it did not legally prohibit all research; the effect was chiefly a chilling of funding for two decades rather than an explicit ban. The anecdote about a $400,000 study of Swedish massages on rabbits is a mischaracterized or unverified example often cited to imply arbitrary spending and does not demonstrate that the government is wholly unable to study gun violence—other agencies and researchers have conducted such studies and Congress later clarified that federal agencies may research gun violence.

claim: "If the Republicans were the majority, (Rep. Barton) would have actually the gavel and the chairmanship."
rationale: The claim asserts as certain that Rep. Barton would hold the gavel and chair if Republicans were the majority. While majority-party members (often the ranking member) are the usual pool for committee chairs, chairs are chosen by the majority caucus and are not automatic—factors like internal elections, seniority rules, or disqualifying events can prevent a specific member from becoming chair. Without identifying which Barton or committee and ignoring caucus selection processes, the categorical claim is not reliably true.

claim: Says unlike Tim Kaine, who "invested" in education, Indiana Gov. Mike Pence "slashed education funding."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Tim Kaine as Virginia governor did increase education spending in several areas, but Mike Pence did not wholesale "slash" education funding across the board as a settled fact—his early budgets proposed and enacted some reductions and shifts (and he pursued voucher expansion), but many K–12 line items were restored by the legislature and overall state education funding did not reflect a simple, across‑the‑board slashing. The truth depends on time period and whether one counts proposed cuts, reductions in higher education, or policy changes like vouchers.

claim: "There comes a point in the last year of the president, especially in their second term, where you stop nominating" both Supreme Court justices and Court of Appeals judges.
rationale: This is not a fixed rule but an informal, politically contingent practice. There is a longstanding but variable Senate norm (often called the 'Thurmond rule' or election-year slowdown) that can lead to fewer confirmations in a president's final election-year, especially for the Supreme Court, but presidents typically continue to nominate and the Senate may still confirm (e.g., Garland 2016 was blocked while Barrett was confirmed in 2020). Circuit court nominations also sometimes proceed in election years, so it is not true that nominations categorically stop.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said, "When gays stayed hidden we had no mass shootings; we had no public nudity. Society was polite. Now anything and everything goes and I blame them."
rationale: There is no credible evidence, video, transcript, or contemporary news reporting that Ted Cruz ever made this statement. Such an inflammatory quote would have been widely reported and documented by major outlets and fact-checkers, but it appears only in social-media memes and misattributions or satire. Therefore the claim is not supported.

claim: "Lindsey Graham threatens to convert to Democrat if Republicans don’t Dump Trump."
rationale: There is no reliable record that Senator Lindsey Graham publicly threatened to switch parties to Democrat if Republicans didn’t abandon Donald Trump. Graham has at times criticized Trump but has consistently remained a Republican and in recent cycles has endorsed or supported Trump’s agendas rather than announcing a party conversion. The claim appears to misrepresent or fabricate a dramatic ultimatum he has not made.

claim: Says Ted Cruz said: "While there may have been an age difference, Josh Duggar’s transgressions are far less an affront to God than what gays do to each other."
rationale: There is no reliable record or contemporaneous news report of Ted Cruz making this exact statement comparing Josh Duggar’s offenses to consensual same-sex activity. While Cruz has publicly described homosexuality as sinful in other contexts and separately reacted to the Duggar revelations, credible sources do not support this quoted phrasing and no primary source (transcript, video, or verified tweet) has been found attributing it to him. Because the quote is inflammatory and specific, absence of evidence in major coverage makes the claim implausible.

claim: Says U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement "will be at every polling station" on Nov. 3, 2020.
rationale: The claim is false. ICE and DHS did not announce or implement a plan to be posted at every polling station on Nov 3, 2020, and such a blanket deployment would be logistically impractical given the large number of polling locations and would raise legal concerns about voter intimidation. Public statements and contemporaneous fact-checking found no evidence supporting the absolute claim that ICE would be at every polling place.

claim: Says Mitt Romney was clear that he "would not provide government assistance to the U.S. auto companies, even if they went through bankruptcy."
rationale: During the 2008 presidential campaign Romney repeatedly stated he opposed government bailouts of the U.S. auto industry and said he would not provide federal assistance even if the companies went through bankruptcy. Contemporary news coverage and his campaign remarks reflect that position, though exact wording varied across interviews and events.

claim: "Obama secretly gave citizenship to 2,500 Iranians as part of nuke deal."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Obama administration granted U.S. citizenship to 2,500 Iranians as part of the Iran nuclear agreement (JCPOA). Naturalization is a legal process requiring individual applications and adjudication; presidents cannot lawfully bestow large numbers of citizenships secretly through an international agreement. Major news outlets, government records, and fact-checkers found no support for this claim and it appears to be a baseless rumor or conflation with other Iran-related policies.

claim: "Actually, on some procedures, you're more likely to die if you're on Medicaid than if you're uninsured."
rationale: Multiple peer-reviewed observational studies have found that for certain high-risk surgeries and trauma care, patients insured by Medicaid experience higher perioperative or in-hospital mortality than uninsured patients. Differences are generally attributed to heavier comorbidity burden among Medicaid enrollees, delayed care, and concentration of Medicaid patients in lower-resourced hospitals rather than any direct protective effect of being uninsured.

claim: Says he didn't cancel a political rally because after Sept. 11, "the New York Stock Exchange was open the following day."
rationale: This is false. The New York Stock Exchange suspended trading after the Sept. 11, 2001 attacks and did not reopen until Monday, Sept. 17, 2001, so it was not open the following day (Sept. 12). Using the NYSE being "open the following day" as a justification is therefore inaccurate.

claim: A video shows "the COVID-19 vaccine when it hits your blood."
rationale: The claim is false because a consumer video cannot directly show the COVID-19 vaccine 'hitting your blood.' COVID-19 vaccines are administered intramuscularly and their components (mRNA and lipid nanoparticles) are far too small to be seen with standard video/optical microscopy; documented blood-video clips are typically misinterpreted, out of context, or show unrelated artifacts or blood behavior rather than vaccine particles entering circulation.

claim: Wisconsin’s middle class is the "most diminished" in the United States.
rationale: There is no clear, authoritative evidence that Wisconsin’s middle class has been reduced more than every other state. Multiple academic and think‑tank analyses show the middle class has shrunk across the country, but state rankings vary by time period and by how “middle class” is measured (share of households, real income, mobility). Wisconsin is not consistently identified as the single most diminished state in those studies, so the blanket claim overstates the case.

claim: "Maxine Waters Is Getting Criminally Charged!"
rationale: As of my latest knowledge (June 2024), there are no credible reports, indictments, arrests, or court filings showing that Representative Maxine Waters has been criminally charged. Social-media posts have circulated claims of charges, but no major news organizations or public court records substantiated them. Because criminal charges would involve formal filings and widespread reporting, the claim is not supported by available evidence.

claim: "(Pete) Sessions has held at least two fundraisers at adult-themed clubs and made no apologies."
rationale: Available reporting and my knowledge do not support the specific claim that Pete Sessions held at least two fundraisers at adult‑themed clubs and issued no apologies. While there is limited reporting associating Sessions with a fundraiser at an adult‑entertainment venue, I cannot corroborate two separate events nor a clear pattern of refusing to apologize. Because the claim asserts a specific count and a categorical lack of apology, it is not supported by verifiable sources in my knowledge base.

claim: Says the Security Against Foreign Enemies Act of 2015 would not "pause" the resettlement of Syrian refugees in the United States.
rationale: The Security Against Foreign Enemies (SAFE) Act of 2015 would have effectively halted the resettlement of Syrian (and Iraqi) refugees until federal agencies completed additional security checks and certified that adequate vetting existed. Contemporary summaries and the bill text imposed a moratorium/ban on admitting refugees from those conflict zones until specified intelligence and screening conditions were met, so it would function as a pause rather than not pausing resettlement.

claim: Says Marco Rubio tweeted a verse from the New Testament to shame "his own constituents for flocking to Trump rally."
rationale: There is no clear evidence or contemporaneous reporting that Senator Marco Rubio tweeted a New Testament verse specifically to shame his own constituents for attending a Trump rally. While Rubio has occasionally quoted Scripture and criticized Trump on policy and temperament, I could not find a documented tweet matching this precise claim. Given the lack of verifiable source, the claim appears to be a misattribution or exaggeration.

claim: Says the National Labor Relations Board told Boeing that it couldn’t build a factory in South Carolina because South Carolina is a right-to-work state.
rationale: This is inaccurate. In 2011 the NLRB filed a complaint alleging Boeing unlawfully shifted 787 production to South Carolina to avoid bargaining with unionized workers, but the Board did not tell Boeing it could not build a factory there because South Carolina is a right-to-work state. The NLRB’s action challenged the motive and sought remedies under federal labor law, not a categorical prohibition based on state right-to-work status.

claim: Trump supporters are heading to the border as the migrant caravan approaches.
rationale: The claim is too general and in present tense without a specific time or caravan to verify. While media reporting from prior migrant caravans (notably 2018–2019) documented some Trump supporters, militia members, and volunteers traveling to border areas, there is no broad, current evidence that "Trump supporters are heading to the border" en masse as a general ongoing fact. The statement overgeneralizes isolated, time‑bound events into a universal present claim.

claim: "We're the only system of federalism in the world."
rationale: The United States is not the only country with a federal system; many countries constitutionally divide sovereignty between national and subnational governments. Well-known federal states include Germany, Canada, Australia, India, Switzerland, Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, Nigeria and others. Thus the blanket claim is incorrect.

claim: The Banking Committee voted a 1,336-page bill "out of committee in 21 minutes with no amendments, with the understanding that before the bill came to the floor, we would reach this bipartisan agreement."
rationale: I cannot verify the precise quoted description as stated — no specific committee, date, or bill is identified and I have no independent evidence that a 1,336‑page bill was voted out in exactly 21 minutes with no amendments under that exact understanding. While congressional committees sometimes move legislation quickly or use unanimous-consent agreements, the specific numeric details and quoted wording are unverified and unlikely without corroborating records. Because the claim hinges on precise facts that are not documented here, I rate it as false pending evidence.

claim: "Our economy created over 6.5 million new jobs just last year, more jobs in one year than ever before in the history of the United States of America."
rationale: BLS payroll data show nonfarm payroll employment rose by about 6.6 million in 2021, which is more than 6.5 million and is the largest annual increase in the BLS monthly payroll series. Thus the claim accurately reflects official job-growth data for that year. The assertion that it was the most in history is correct when referencing the BLS series going back to 1939.

claim: Under his leadership, more people in Wisconsin "have access to health care."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because it does not identify who “his” refers to, the time period, or the metric used to define “access to health care.” Without those specifics one cannot confirm an increase in coverage, services, or provider availability in Wisconsin attributable to a particular leader. Absent supporting data (e.g., changes in uninsured rates, Medicaid/BadgerCare enrollment, or service capacity tied to that leader), the statement cannot be treated as factual.

claim: "Gina Haspel, CIA head is dead!"
rationale: The claim asserts that Gina Haspel (former CIA Director) is dead. There have been no credible news reports or official announcements indicating her death, and public records identify her as a living former CIA director who served 2018–2021. Given the lack of reliable confirmation, the claim is false.

claim: "I never was in favor of shutting down the government. … (I) voted to fund the government fully."
rationale: The statement as given is unverifiable and likely false because it lacks a named speaker and timeframe; whether someone “never” favored a shutdown and “voted to fund the government fully” requires checking specific public statements and roll-call votes. Many politicians who make similar blanket claims have voting records or public comments that contradict them, so without a concrete identity and bill details the claim cannot be accepted as true.

claim: "This kind of snowstorm happens every 10 or 15 years."
rationale: The statement is overly general and cannot be verified as universally true. Recurrence intervals for snowstorms depend on the geographic region, the specific type/intensity of storm being described, and climate variability and trends, so a blanket "every 10 or 15 years" claim is unsupported without more context.

claim: "Here's a man who brags about how he made the city safe. It was the Biden crime bill that became the Clinton crime bill that allowed him to do that."
rationale: The 1994 Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act is widely attributed to President Clinton as it was his administration that signed it, but Joe Biden, as chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee, was a principal architect and sponsor of the bill. People often refer to it both as the "Biden crime bill" (because of his authorship/role in drafting and negotiating it) and the "Clinton crime bill" (because Clinton championed and signed it into law). The claim that the bill “became the Clinton crime bill” is therefore accurate in describing its authorship and enactment, though the causal link to someone ‘making the city safe’ is vague.

claim: Barack Obama is the "first president to file lawsuits against the states he swore an oath to protect."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. The U.S. Department of Justice under many earlier presidents brought lawsuits against states to enforce federal law — notably during the New Deal and the civil-rights era when administrations sued states over segregation and voting-rights violations. Also, presidents act through the executive branch and do not personally 'file' suits, so Obama was not the first.

claim: "We’ve got 600-plus police and fire pensions Downstate that are on the cusp of insolvency because they don’t have the revenues that they need to be able to keep those pensions going."
rationale: State fiscal analyses and reporting on Illinois pensions document that there are well over 600 separate downstate police and fire pension funds and that a large share are severely underfunded and at risk of insolvency absent new revenue or reforms. The claim that 600+ downstate police and fire pensions lack sufficient revenues and are facing insolvency is consistent with those widely reported assessments.

claim: "More suicide deaths than coronavirus death past two months."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as written because it omits the geographic scope and exact two-month period; without that context it cannot be verified and is likely false for many places and times. Global and many national COVID-19 death totals over multi-month periods have often exceeded suicide totals, and suicide counts themselves vary by country and year. Because the statement is blanket and context-free, it should not be treated as fact.

claim: Gas prices during the Obama-Biden administration were $5.49 a gallon.
rationale: False. The U.S. national average retail gasoline price during the Obama–Biden administration (2009–2017) did not reach $5.49 per gallon; national averages and typical state averages were well below that level during those years. While isolated local stations in high-cost areas might have briefly charged prices that high, the claim as stated (implying typical or national prices) is inaccurate.

claim: Says President Obama has "doubled" the deficit.
rationale: The claim is misleading. Annual federal deficits spiked in FY2009 to about $1.3–1.4 trillion from roughly $450 billion in FY2008 (more than doubled), but deficits then fell substantially over the rest of Obama’s presidency and were not uniformly 'doubled' throughout his term. Without specifying the baseline year or whether one means annual deficits versus total national debt, the blanket statement that Obama 'has doubled the deficit' is incorrect.

claim: Says Scott Walker "said that forcing women facing abortion to get invasive ultrasounds was 'just a cool thing.'"
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports from 2015 documented Scott Walker telling donors at a private event that policies forcing women seeking abortions to undergo ultrasounds were “just a cool thing.” The remark was widely reported and criticized as trivializing ultrasound requirements tied to abortion restrictions.

claim: "We now consume at the federal level 25 percent of the gross domestic product. Historically we were at 20 percent. So we've taken 5 percent away from the private sector."
rationale: The statement mixes an imprecise historical baseline with a causal claim. While federal spending as a share of GDP has risen and in some recent years has been in the low-to-mid 20s percent range, the claim that a rise from 20% to 25% necessarily means the federal government has "taken" 5 percentage points directly away from the private sector is misleading. Changes in government share can be financed by taxes, borrowing, changes in private saving or investment, and shifts in GDP components, so a one-for-one transfer from private consumption or investment does not automatically occur.

claim: "A year ago we had the lowest unemployment in history without using taxpayers money."
rationale: The claim is vague and unlikely: it asserts a historical low unemployment 'a year ago' achieved 'without using taxpayers money' but gives no country or definition of terms. In the U.S., for example, unemployment hit a modern low (~3.5%) before the 2020 pandemic, but public fiscal policies (tax cuts, spending) and later relief programs involve taxpayer resources or government action; attributing a lowest-ever rate solely to no taxpayer spending is not supportable. Because 'in history' and 'without using taxpayers money' are undefined and contradicted by known public policy influences, the claim is false as stated.

claim: "Across the country, more than half of the U.S. attorney seats remain without a prosecutor chosen by Obama."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about timing and therefore misleading. There are 93 U.S. attorney offices and while many were temporarily unfilled at the start of the Obama administration due to the nomination/confirmation process, over the ensuing months a majority of seats were nominated or filled; without a specific date the blanket statement that “more than half remain without a prosecutor chosen by Obama” is not supportable. Because the statement lacks temporal context and is factually false as a standing claim, I rate it FALSE.

claim: "We have completely turned our economy around."
rationale: The claim is an absolute, broad statement that cannot be verified without specifying the country, timeframe, and which economic metrics are meant. Economic data (GDP growth, unemployment, inflation, real wages, debt, and inequality) typically show mixed results; some indicators may have improved while others remain weak, so asserting a complete turnaround is not supported. Because the claim is vague and absolutist, it is not factually verifiable as stated.

claim: The federal government "now tells us which light bulbs to buy."
rationale: This claim is misleading. The federal government has set minimum energy-efficiency standards (notably via the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 implemented by the Department of Energy) that phased out many inefficient incandescent bulbs, but it does not direct consumers to purchase specific brands or models—consumers can choose any bulbs that meet the standards (LED, CFL, etc.).

claim: "Historically," Senate ratification of arms control treaties "has been bipartisan."
rationale: While many major arms-control treaties that were ratified (e.g., ABM, SALT-era agreements, START I, New START) received cross-party support, there are notable exceptions and failures that were sharply partisan — most prominently the 1999 Senate rejection of the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty. Thus the blanket claim that Senate ratification of arms-control treaties "has been bipartisan" is an oversimplification and not uniformly true historically.

claim: "Look at what’s happening last night in Sweden. Sweden, who would believe this? Sweden. They took in large numbers. They’re having problems like they never thought possible."
rationale: The speaker asserts a specific, severe incident occurred "last night" in Sweden tied to taking in large numbers of migrants; no credible news reports or official sources documented such an event. While Sweden has accepted many refugees and faces ongoing integration and localized crime challenges, fact-checkers found the claim of a recent dramatic nationwide incident to be false and misleading as phrased.

claim: A "majority in every state favors path to citizenship for undocumented immigrants."
rationale: This is an overgeneralization. While national polls typically show a majority of Americans favoring a pathway to citizenship for undocumented immigrants, state-level results vary and multiple conservative-leaning states have shown less-than-50% support in some surveys. Therefore the claim that a majority in every single state favors a path to citizenship is incorrect.

claim: Veterans should vote Republican "because the damn Democrats blocked the VA Healthcare bill again."
rationale: The claim combines a partisan recommendation with an asserted factual claim that “the Democrats blocked the VA Healthcare bill again,” but it names no specific bill or vote. Voting records on VA-related legislation vary by bill and chamber, and many VA measures have drawn bipartisan support; without a concrete bill, date, or vote, the assertion cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false. The normative part (“Veterans should vote Republican”) is an opinion and not a factual statement.

claim: Property taxes "are now 18% higher than when (Mark Sharpe) first took office."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific numeric claim because the statement lacks the jurisdiction and timeframe tied to Mark Sharpe’s tenure; without that context there is no reliable evidence to confirm an 18% increase. Property taxes can be measured in multiple ways (aggregate collections, average bill, tax rate or assessed value) and changes will differ by measure and locality, so asserting a single 18% figure is unsupported. Given the ambiguity and absence of corroborating data, the claim is treated as unverified and therefore judged false.

claim: "Three of five detainees swapped (for Bowe Bergdahl) are now ISIS leaders."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that three of the five detainees released for Bowe Bergdahl became leaders in ISIS. Independent fact-checkers and major news outlets found that the five were Taliban-era detainees transferred to Qatar (with travel restrictions) and that subsequent reports at most allege reengagement with Taliban or other insurgent groups, not that three rose to leadership in ISIS. The claim conflates distinct militant groups and overstates documented post-release activity.

claim: After laying off 30,000 people, Carly Fiorina said that in retrospect, "I would have done them all faster."
rationale: The precise quote is not supported by reliable contemporaneous reporting. While Carly Fiorina did oversee roughly 30,000 job cuts at Hewlett‑Packard, fact‑checking and contemporary sources do not verify she said, in retrospect, “I would have done them all faster.” The line appears to be a circulated misattribution rather than a documented statement in a reputable source.

claim: Says Steph Curry decided to split with Nike because the company wouldn’t allow him to write Bible scriptures in his shoes.
rationale: This claim is false. Stephen (Steph) Curry never “split with Nike” over Bible verses — Curry signed a long-term deal with Under Armour (not Nike) in 2013 after Nike passed on him, and there is no credible reporting that any apparel company refused him the right to put Bible scriptures in his shoes as the reason for a brand change. Public accounts of Curry’s endorsement history and media reporting on his faith do not support the asserted cause-and-effect.

claim: "I was speaking out on pension reform almost 17 years ago."
rationale: The claim lacks any identifying speaker or timestamp, so it cannot be independently verified as stated. A statement that someone ‘was speaking out… almost 17 years ago’ is a temporal, person-specific claim that requires who said it and when to check; without that information it is not verifiable and therefore treated as false for fact-checking purposes. It could be true for some individuals but cannot be substantiated here.

claim: The Baucus health care bill would require taxes on medical devices such as X-ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests and surgical needles.
rationale: The claim misstates how the Baucus health-care proposal worked. The Baucus proposals discussed levying an excise-style charge on certain medical device industry sales (applied to manufacturers/importers), not a direct per-item consumer tax on things like X‑ray machines, female condoms, HIV tests or needles; many small or preventive items would likely be treated differently or excluded. The statement therefore overstates and mischaracterizes the bill’s effect.

claim: "Obamacare isn't helping anyone."
rationale: The absolute claim that "Obamacare isn't helping anyone" is false. Empirical evidence shows the Affordable Care Act (ACA) reduced the uninsured rate for tens of millions through Medicaid expansion and marketplace subsidies, and it established protections like coverage for preexisting conditions and essential health benefits. While effects vary by state and some individuals face higher premiums or narrower networks, the law has demonstrably helped large numbers of people access and afford care.

claim: The Biden administration "gifted the Taliban with $80 billion-plus" in military-grade weapons but now "wants your 9mm pistols."
rationale: The statement conflates different figures and misrepresents current U.S. policy. The often-cited ~$80–83 billion figure refers to cumulative U.S. spending on training, salaries, and equipment for Afghan forces over two decades, not a single gift of "$80 billion-plus" in weapons to the Taliban; Pentagon reporting and independent estimates put the value of equipment left behind in 2021 at far lower amounts (on the order of billions, not $80B) and not all was usable. Separately, there is no federal program ordering citizens to turn over common 9mm pistols; contemporary regulatory actions and proposals have focused on specific weapon types or features, not a blanket seizure of 9mm handguns.

claim: Rob Cornilles is a Tea Party candidate.
rationale: I found no reliable evidence that Rob Cornilles was a Tea Party candidate. Contemporary reporting and campaign materials identify him as a Republican/independent local candidate in his races, but do not show Tea Party endorsement or that he self-identified as a Tea Party candidate. Without such evidence the claim is unsupported.

claim: Obama said he would "stand with the Muslims should the political winds shift in an ugly direction."
rationale: Barack Obama did utter that sentiment in a 2008 address to the Islamic Society of Boston, saying, in effect, "I will stand with you, should the political winds shift in an ugly direction." The common paraphrase as "stand with the Muslims" reflects the speech's audience and intent, though his exact wording used "you."

claim: Quotes show Democrats supported riots "when BLM was BURNING down cities and killing people in the streets!"
rationale: This claim overstates and misrepresents the record. While some Democrats expressed understanding of protesters' anger or emphasized systemic injustice, mainstream Democratic leaders publicly condemned violence and repeatedly called for peaceful protest; there is no broad, documented evidence that Democrats supported "burning down cities" or killing people. Isolated, out-of-context quotes have been used to imply endorsement of riots, but that does not demonstrate blanket Democratic support for violent actions.

claim: Says a mall Santa beat up a child molester.
rationale: The claim is vague and unverified — it gives no time, place, or named individuals, and I found no corroborating, credible reports of a mall Santa physically assaulting a child molester. Stories like this commonly circulate as urban-legend style viral claims without independent confirmation, so it should be treated as false absent verifiable evidence.

claim: The Affordable Care Act alters the "sensible doctor-patient-relationship-centered health care program ... we see today."
rationale: The Affordable Care Act enacted broad changes to how health coverage is financed and delivered (insurance marketplaces, Medicaid expansion, essential health benefits, and new payment models), which changed incentives, administrative requirements, and access patterns that shape clinical practice. While it did not eliminate patient–physician relationships, these structural reforms have altered how care is organized and paid for and thus have affected the doctor–patient-centered system that existed previously.

claim: In Virginia, "people are going and getting marriage licenses who are 12 and 13, and 14 and 15 years old."
rationale: Current Virginia law and recent reforms do not support routine issuance of marriage licenses to children as young as 12–15, and there are no credible contemporary reports showing people aged 12–13 or 14–15 are commonly obtaining licenses. While some states historically allowed very young marriages under narrow exceptions, such extreme ages would be unlawful or extraordinarily rare in Virginia under its modern statutes and court practice.

claim: When Terry McAuliffe was governor, "Unemployment went down in every single county, including rural Virginia by nearly 50%.
rationale: The claim overstates and is misleading. While overall unemployment in Virginia fell during McAuliffe’s 2014–2018 term and many counties saw declines, independent fact-checks and labor data show declines were not uniformly nearly 50% across rural counties and the assertion that it fell in “every single county” depends on time window and whether independent cities are counted; the “nearly 50%” figure is a misleading summary that conflates percent-point and percent changes.

claim: Says Joe Biden called ANTIFA "courageous Americans."
rationale: Joe Biden did praise peaceful protesters as "courageous Americans" in remarks about 2020 demonstrations, but he did not explicitly call ANTIFA "courageous Americans." Contemporary transcripts and fact-checks show he referred to demonstrators broadly, not endorsing or naming Antifa.

claim: Says Paul Manafort "played a very limited role" in the Trump presidential campaign.
rationale: Characterizing Paul Manafort as having "played a very limited role" in the Trump 2016 campaign is misleading. Manafort served as campaign chairman from May to August 2016 and was a senior adviser involved in strategy, delegate operations and high‑level meetings; he also maintained ongoing consulting ties and contacts with outside actors. While some defenders argue his influence waned after his resignation, his formal leadership position and documented activities show more than a "very limited" role.

claim: "Paul Broun Jr. sides with sexual deviants to support sale of 'crush videos.' "
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Paul Broun publicly supported the sale of "crush videos" or allied himself with people who produce them. Federal legislation (the Animal Crush Video Prohibition Act) that criminalized creation and distribution of such videos passed with broad bipartisan support, and Broun is not documented as backing their sale. The claim appears to be an unsubstantiated personal attack using inflammatory language rather than a factual statement about his record.

claim: No one showed up for this Joe Biden and Kamala Harris joint campaign event in Arizona.
rationale: The absolute statement that “no one showed up” is not supported by available reporting and imagery from the Arizona joint Biden–Harris event. Contemporary news coverage and photos/videos show some attendees, staff, press, and security at the event even if turnout was smaller than organizers hoped. Therefore the claim that literally nobody attended is false.

claim: Rhode Island "charter schools are nationally recognized as outperforming their counterparts across the country."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. National research and reviews (e.g., large-scale CREDO analyses and other evaluations) show charter school performance is mixed and varies widely by state, network, and school; Rhode Island has some higher‑performing charter schools but is not broadly documented or widely recognized as uniformly outperforming public school counterparts across the country.

claim: Says television host Steve Harvey authored a pro-Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators.
rationale: This claim is false. The alleged pro‑Trump rant about raccoons and exterminators attributed to Steve Harvey circulated as a viral social‑media quote but credible fact‑checking and searches find no primary source (broadcast, column, or verified social post) showing Harvey authored it. The text appears to be fabricated or misattributed meme content rather than something Harvey actually said or wrote.

claim: "324,000 pregnant people experience domestic violence during their pregnancy."
rationale: The claim presents a precise count without specifying timeframe or location; prevalence estimates of domestic violence during pregnancy vary widely by study and year. While a commonly cited estimate of roughly 324,000 pregnant women abused annually in the U.S. appears in some advocacy materials, the underlying studies and methods are inconsistent and the figure cannot be verified as a definitive fact. Therefore the statement as written is not reliably supported.

claim: "Babysitter on crystal meth eats 3-month-old baby."
rationale: There is no credible reporting from law enforcement or reputable news organizations documenting a babysitter consuming a 3-month-old; such an extreme crime would draw widespread national attention. The claim appears to be a sensational rumor or mischaracterization rather than a verified incident.

claim: "#GradInsurance debacle is a DIRECT result of #ObamaCare. #MIZZOU has to break the law to do the right thing."
rationale: The claim is unsupported: there is no clear public evidence that a supposed Mizzou graduate-insurance 'debacle' is a direct result of the Affordable Care Act. University insurance problems are usually driven by institutional decisions, contracts, or state regulatory matters, and the assertion that Mizzou 'has to break the law' is speculative and unsupported — institutions must and do operate within legal frameworks. Without specific facts tying the incident to a particular ACA mandate, the causal and legal claims are not justified.

claim: Says "there have been some job gains in the McMansion State since Mr. Christie took office, but they have lagged gains both in the nation as a whole and in New York and Connecticut, the obvious points of comparison."
rationale: Chris Christie took office in January 2010 and Bureau of Labor Statistics state employment series show New Jersey experienced net job gains after that date, but the percentage growth in jobs in New Jersey was smaller than the nationwide percentage gain and was behind neighboring New York and Connecticut over the same multi‑year period. The conclusion is consistent across common measures (BLS nonfarm payroll employment and percent change comparisons) though exact percentages depend on the chosen endpoints and measure.

claim: Under my platform, "I will make no changes to the current (Medicare) system for current retirees and anyone approaching retirement."
rationale: The statement is an absolute promise that no changes will be made to Medicare for current retirees and those 'approaching retirement.' Without the exact platform text and precise definitions (e.g., how 'approaching retirement' is defined), that kind of blanket guarantee is not verifiable and is implausible because many proposals that claim to protect beneficiaries still include funding, benefit, or administrative changes that can affect them. Therefore the claim as stated cannot be confirmed and is judged false.

claim: Says Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to keep "an extreme, job-killing Internal Revenue Service paperwork mandate."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsubstantiated as stated: it cites no specific bill or roll-call showing Sen. Sherrod Brown voted to "keep" such a mandate. The IRS 1099-K reporting-threshold controversy (a proposed $600 reporting rule) generated multiple votes and later congressional fixes, but available public vote records and reporting do not support a clear, single vote by Brown described in the ad-style language. Without a specific bill/date/roll-call, the assertion that he voted to "keep an extreme, job-killing" mandate is misleading.

claim: "More people, almost twice as many, pay the penalty or take the waiver than signed up for (Obamacare)."
rationale: The claim is vague and not supported by available evidence: annual ACA marketplace and Medicaid enrollments numbered in the millions (often 8–12 million marketplace plan selections in peak years), while IRS reporting showed far fewer people paying the federal individual mandate penalty or claiming exemptions. The federal penalty was also reduced and effectively eliminated for most taxpayers beginning in 2019, making the assertion that nearly twice as many pay penalties or take waivers as enrolled incorrect for typical timeframes.

claim: "$21T in Pentagon accounting errors. Medicare for All costs ~$32T. That means 66% of Medicare for All could have been funded already by the Pentagon."
rationale: This is a misleading comparison. The "$21T" refers to cumulative accounting adjustments, unsupported journal entries and reporting deficiencies in DoD financial statements over many years—not $21 trillion in missing or available cash that could be reallocated. Medicare-for-All cost figures (often multi‑decade or gross estimates) vary by study and assumptions, and even if the headline numbers were comparable, accounting adjustments are not fungible budgetary resources that could simply fund a new program.
cited_knowledge: Based on public summaries of DoD audit findings describing large totals as accounting adjustments/unsupported transactions rather than lost cash, and on the fact that Medicare-for-All cost estimates differ by timeframe and assumptions; government budgetary law and accounting practices limit reallocation of such items.
safety_notes: Ambiguity/nuance: the two figures come from different reports/timeframes and use different definitions (accounting adjustments vs program cost estimates); precise evaluation would require the exact source documents and context.

claim: A mansion in photo is Joe Biden’s house.
rationale: No photo or provenance was provided to verify the claim, and Joe Biden's well-known private residence is a modest home in Wilmington, Delaware, while his official residence is the White House. Viral posts have frequently misattributed photos of mansions to Biden, so the assertion is unsupported without concrete evidence.

claim: Jeff Mann has an ethics complaint against him alleging he used county workers for campaign work, which is an indictable offense.
rationale: I could not verify a public ethics complaint specifically naming a person called Jeff Mann alleging he used county workers for campaign work. The claim also asserts that such conduct is an indictable offense; whether misuse of public employees is criminal varies by jurisdiction and often is handled as an ethics violation or administrative matter rather than an indictable crime. Because the statement bundles an unverified allegation about a named individual with a categorical legal conclusion, it is not supported as presented.

claim: Says as Assembly Speaker he is a "constitutional officer" of Wisconsin.
rationale: The Assembly Speaker is the presiding officer chosen by members of the Wisconsin State Assembly, not one of the statewide "constitutional officers" typically created and named by the Wisconsin Constitution (such as governor, lieutenant governor, attorney general). Calling the Speaker a "constitutional officer" misstates the usual legal/terminology distinction between legislative chamber officers and constitutionally established statewide executive offices.

claim: Says the U.S. Constitution "doesn’t say anything about (redistricting) being fair. … it’s set up to be partisan."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution does not contain an explicit requirement that congressional or legislative redistricting be 'fair' or nonpartisan. It vests the power to prescribe the ‘Times, Places and Manner’ of elections and leaves districting largely to state legislatures, which enables partisan control; constitutional limits do exist (e.g., equal-population and racial-discrimination constraints) but no general fairness mandate is specified.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Paul Ryan’s budget proposal "eliminates Medicare" in 10 years.
rationale: This is misleading. Paul Ryan's budget proposals did not immediately terminate Medicare for current beneficiaries; they proposed converting Medicare into a premium-support/voucher-like system phased in for future enrollees over time. Fact‑checkers have concluded that claims saying Ryan "eliminates Medicare in 10 years" overstate and mischaracterize the proposals' timing and mechanism.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We need to repeal Daylight Savings Time as a primary measure to decrease the rate of climate change. Less hours of sun shine equal less heat hitting Earth’s surface."
rationale: There is no credible record of Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez saying this, and the substance of the quote is scientifically incorrect. Repealing or keeping Daylight Saving Time does not change the amount of sunlight the Earth receives — it only shifts clock time — so it cannot be a primary measure to reduce global heating. The quote appears to be a misattribution or fabrication.

claim: Gina Raimondo "paid 70 million in taxpayer dollars to millionaire hedge fund managers."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Payments of roughly that scale have been discussed in critiques of Rhode Island pension investment fees, but they were investment-management fees paid out of the pension fund (authorized under prior contracts and board decisions), not sums personally paid by Gina Raimondo; she has also taken steps to reduce such fees. The precise amount, timing, and recipients are disputed and the statement omits that these were pension investment fees rather than a direct transfer of taxpayer cash from her pocket or a single decision she unilaterally made.

claim: "Just on Jan. 1 of this year, there were 40,000 new laws put on the books in one day."
rationale: There is no evidence that 40,000 new statutory laws were enacted and took effect on a single January 1. Federal and state legislatures collectively pass far fewer statutes in a year, and while many administrative rules, local ordinances, or previously enacted measures may have Jan. 1 effective dates, the specific claim of 40,000 new laws in one day is unsubstantiated and implausible.

claim: A video shows Kim Jong Un calling Joe Biden a "thug," a "coward," and "mentally unstable" in a speech.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Kim Jong Un gave a speech in which he called U.S. President Joe Biden a "thug," a "coward," and "mentally unstable." Independent fact-checkers reported that the clip circulating online was edited, dubbed, or presented out of context; North Korean state media typically uses broad anti‑U.S. rhetoric rather than naming and taunting a sitting U.S. president with those exact insults in a formal speech.

claim: Says Tom Barrett "has directed that tens of millions of City of Milwaukee tax dollars be used for the construction of a downtown trolley at the expense of: health and public safety; repair and replacement of public infrastructure; public education; and, job creation and economic development."
rationale: The claim overstates and misattributes actions. While Milwaukee’s downtown streetcar (“The Hop”) had total costs over $100 million and did include local financing (including tens of millions from city/TIF/bond sources) and Mayor Tom Barrett supported the project, there is no clear evidence he unilaterally “directed” city tax dollars to the trolley specifically by cutting or diverting funds from health/public safety, infrastructure repair, public education, or job-creation budgets. Moreover, K–12 education funding is primarily handled outside the city’s general fund, and municipal budgeting decisions are more complex than the one-to-one tradeoffs asserted here.

claim: Ron Klein "sponsored an amendment that specifically allows price gouging."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Congressman Ron Klein sponsored an amendment that explicitly 'allows price gouging.' Contemporary congressional records and fact-checking do not show Klein authoring any amendment that authorized excessive emergency pricing, and political ads that made this claim mischaracterized other votes or actions. Without a specific bill or amendment text showing explicit authorization, the claim is incorrect.

claim: Insulin prices have "gone THRU THE ROOF for patients/taxpayers bc of manufacturer, health plan & PBM biz practices."
rationale: U.S. insulin list prices have risen sharply over the past decades and many independent investigations and academic studies attribute a large part of the resulting patient out‑of‑pocket costs and public spending to industry practices — including manufacturer list‑price increases, opaque rebate/fee structures and formulary dealings by PBMs, and plan cost‑sharing designs. Those practices have been repeatedly cited as drivers of high consumer prices and taxpayer exposure through public insurance programs. While exact contributions vary by insulin type and payer, the core causal link is supported by multiple sources.

claim: Says the percentage of officers the Chicago Police Board fired after hearing their cases or who chose to resign prior to a board hearing roughly doubled during her tenure.
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as written because it omits who “her” refers to and the exact time period and baseline percentage being compared. Claims about changes in disciplinary outcomes for Chicago Police require specific dates and CPB case statistics to confirm a doubling; without that information this assertion cannot be substantiated.

claim: Says Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T-shirt with progressive slogans on it.
rationale: This claim is rated FALSE because there is no widely reported, verifiable photograph or reliable news coverage confirming Tom Hanks was photographed wearing a T‑shirt emblazoned with progressive slogans. While Hanks is known to express liberal views, the assertion as presented is vague and unverified by reputable sources.

claim: Says the Steele dossier "was—according to (James Comey's) June 2017 testimony—'salacious and unverified.' "
rationale: James Comey, in his June 8, 2017 public testimony to the Senate Intelligence Committee, described the Steele dossier as “salacious and unverified.” Contemporary transcripts and news reports quote him using those words while discussing the dossier’s unverified status and the FBI’s handling of it.

claim: Says an NBC producer at the Olympics was caught on a hot mic saying "60% of people in this stadium will be dead within 10 days."
rationale: The claim has no credible contemporaneous evidence and was debunked by fact-checkers; NBC denied such a statement and no reputable news outlet corroborated a producer saying that on a hot mic. The audio/posting appears to be fabricated or a misattribution circulated on social media rather than an authentic recorded quote.

claim: "Many people every year, sometimes over 100,000, and despite the vaccine, die from the flu … we are learning to live with Covid, in most populations far less lethal."
rationale: The first part is broadly true: seasonal influenza causes many deaths annually worldwide and global respiratory deaths from flu commonly exceed 100,000 in some years, and vaccines do not eliminate all flu deaths. The second part overgeneralizes: while COVID-19 has become less severe for many people due to vaccination and prior infection and some populations now experience lower per-infection severity, COVID-19 remains substantially more lethal than seasonal flu in many populations (especially the elderly, immunocompromised, and areas with low immunity or limited healthcare), so the claim that it is “in most populations far less lethal” is misleading.

claim: Opening the schools "is a local determination, but it’s not a state determination."
rationale: The statement as an absolute is incorrect: authority over school openings varies by jurisdiction and is often a state determination or shared authority, not solely local. In many U.S. states governors, state education departments or legislatures have issued statewide rules or orders (including during COVID), while in other states local school boards control openings. Thus it is inaccurate to claim universally that opening schools is only a local determination and not a state one.

claim: Photo shows Bill Clinton among others not wearing a mask at John Lewis’ funeral.
rationale: Contemporary fact-checking and news reports found that the circulating photo was misattributed and not reliably shown to be from John Lewis's funeral. There is no credible evidence tying the specific image to that service, and multiple outlets flagged the claim as a miscaption or wrong context.

claim: "The claim ... that we plan to set up panels of bureaucrats with the power to  kill off senior citizens ... is a lie, plain and simple."
rationale: The statement refers to the widely circulated allegation that health reform would create "death panels" — bureaucratic panels empowered to kill senior citizens. That allegation has been thoroughly debunked: the Affordable Care Act contained no provision creating such panels, and independent fact‑checkers and government analyses found the claim to be false. The ACA only included provisions for voluntary advance care planning conversations and quality commissions without authority to order death.

claim: "Heitkamp has voted against Trump 68 percent of time."
rationale: This specific numeric claim is not supported by standard vote-tracking sources. Public trackers (e.g., FiveThirtyEight/GovTrack) that measure how often a senator voted with or against President Trump show Heidi Heitkamp voted with Trump roughly around half the time during his presidency, not that she voted against him 68% of the time. The claim therefore misstates widely reported vote-alignment figures.

claim: President Barack Obama "is the first president to keep a dog-trainer on retainer for $102,000 a year at taxpayer expense."
rationale: The claim is false. Past administrations have used paid animal handlers or trainers for presidential pets, and independent fact-checkers found the $102,000 number was misleading or taken out of context (it conflated staffing costs/assignments rather than a unique ‘retainer’ created by Obama). The expense was not a novel sole-purpose taxpayer retainer for a dog trainer reserved only for Obama’s pets.

claim: Fox News changed its accreditation to "entertainment."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Fox News as an organization formally changed an official accreditation status to "entertainment." Claims like this usually conflate legal or promotional language (e.g., labeling some programming as opinion or entertainment in defenses or descriptions) with an official reclassification by a credentialing body. Official press-accreditation listings (e.g., White House press credentials) and reporting by major fact-checkers do not show Fox News being reclassified as "entertainment."

claim: Says Marsha Blackburn "voted against the Reauthorization of the Violence Against Women Act, which attempts to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and date rape."
rationale: Marsha Blackburn voted against the House vote to reauthorize the Violence Against Women Act when a 2013 reauthorization that expanded certain protections came up; she opposed the measure citing objections to its expanded provisions. The Act’s purpose is to protect women from domestic violence, stalking, and sexual assault, so the statement that she voted against a VAWA reauthorization is accurate.

claim: "Spanish was the first European language spoken in this country."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as written because no country is specified, and many countries were first contacted by other European languages (e.g., Portuguese in Brazil, English in parts of North America, Dutch in Suriname). While Spanish was the first European language in some countries (many in Latin America), it was not universally the first in all countries. Without a named country and historical context the blanket statement is false.

claim: "We've seen in this last year tremendous things happening, including our unemployment rate come down 2 percentage points."
rationale: The claim omits any country and a specific 12‑month period, so it is unverifiable as stated. In recent years for major economies like the U.S., year‑over‑year unemployment changes have generally been under one percentage point; a 2‑point drop over a single year is uncommon except during exceptional events (e.g., early COVID‑19 recovery). Given the missing context and typical BLS data patterns, the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: Marc Molinaro "has cut taxes, his budget now is lower than it was six years ago" in Dutchess County
rationale: This is not supported as stated. While Marc Molinaro frequently touted tax restraint and compliance with New York's property tax cap, Dutchess County's total budget in nominal dollars did not fall to a level lower than six years earlier; municipal budgets typically trend up and the claim conflates tax-cap messaging with an absolute budget cut. The statement fails to specify which taxes or whether figures are inflation‑adjusted, making it misleading.

claim: Takes credit for "reining in" state spending when he was governor.
rationale: The claim as written is unverifiable because it does not identify who “he” is or which governorship and timeframe are meant. Without a named individual and specific state/time period, I cannot confirm whether that person publicly took credit or whether state spending was actually reined in. To assess the claim would require checking the individual's public statements and state budget records for the relevant period.

claim: "For the first time in over a decade, business leaders around the world have declared that China is no longer the world’s No. 1 place to invest; America is."
rationale: The statement overgeneralizes and is not supported by a single, verifiable global declaration. While some investor surveys and reports in recent years have shown increased preference for the United States versus China, other surveys and FDI data remain mixed and sector- or region-specific, so there is no clear, once-in-a-decade consensus among "business leaders around the world."

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't make a thing in America."
rationale: The claim presents an exact quote attributed to Donald Trump — "doesn't make a thing in America." There is no verifiable record or reliable transcript of Trump saying that phrase, and it conflicts with his frequent public claims that his businesses and policies support U.S. jobs and manufacturing. Given the lack of sourced evidence and the contradiction with his usual rhetoric, the attribution is likely false.

claim: "Foster children are disproportionately victims of identity theft."
rationale: Multiple government reports, advocacy organizations, and academic studies have found that children and youth in foster care face higher rates of identity theft and misuse of their personal information than peers, driven by frequent placement changes, shared or lost records, and exploitation by caregivers or traffickers. While exact prevalence estimates vary by study and jurisdiction, the pattern of disproportionate vulnerability is well-documented.

claim: "COVID internment camps announced in America: Tennessee governor signs EO authorizing National Guard to carry out COVID medical kidnappings."
rationale: This claim is false. Tennessee did not announce 'COVID internment camps' nor did the governor authorize the National Guard to perform 'medical kidnappings.' Executive actions and National Guard missions referenced during the pandemic authorized support for public-health operations (such as medical transport, logistics, and assistance to health agencies) within legal constraints, not forcible abduction or establishment of internment camps, and independent fact-checkers have debunked the specific allegation as a conspiracy misreading of orders and guidelines.

claim: "Years of economic decay are over" because Trump "reversed the failed economic policies of the previous administration."
rationale: The U.S. economy was not in 'years of economic decay' immediately before Trump—unemployment and GDP growth had been improving through the post‑2009 recovery. While some indicators (stock market, employment) improved during 2017–2019, many of those trends began before his presidency and the effects of his tax cuts and deregulation are disputed; deficits increased and long‑run benefits are uncertain. Thus the absolute causal claim is false.

claim: "When Marcy Kaptur brought home $42 million for new manufacturing jobs, Dennis Kucinich voted 'no'."
rationale: The statement asserts a specific roll-call link but provides no bill or date, and there is no clear public record tying a Dennis Kucinich "no" vote directly to a $42 million award Marcy Kaptur secured. While Kucinich did occasionally vote against large spending measures, that general pattern does not verify this precise claim without a specific appropriation and roll-call to cite.

claim: "Since 1961 … our private economy has produced 66 million private-sector jobs. So what's the jobs score? Republicans 24 million, Democrats 42 (million)."
rationale: The specific totals are not reliably supported by official employment data and depend on ambiguous choices of start/end dates and counting methodology. Official BLS series and independent fact-checkers show different cumulative private‑sector job totals and that attributing simple partisan splits (Republicans 24M, Democrats 42M) is misleading because job growth spans business cycles, multiple administrations, and other factors.

claim: Says Donald Trump "wants to keep big government in charge" of federally-owned land.
rationale: This claim contradicts Donald Trump’s well-documented public positions and administration actions on public lands. Trump and his administration promoted transferring control of federally owned land to states, rolling back national monument designations, and expanding resource development — actions aimed at reducing federal control rather than keeping “big government in charge.”

claim: "About 47 percent of able-bodied people in the state of Maine don’t work."
rationale: This overstates non-employment in Maine. Official labor-force and employment-population measures show a majority of working-age/able-bodied adults are employed (overall participation in the low-60s percent and much higher employment rates for prime-age adults), so a 47% non-work rate for able-bodied people is inconsistent with standard statistics and likely arises from misreading a different metric.

claim: "After filing a lawsuit in Rhode Island, we reached an agreement with state agencies that resulted in more voters being registered in the first full month after our lawsuit than in the entire previous two-year reporting period."
rationale: I cannot verify this specific, concrete numeric claim from available knowledge: there is no widely known or corroborated report up to mid‑2024 showing that a Rhode Island lawsuit and subsequent agreement produced more registrations in the first full month after the suit than in the entire prior two‑year period. The claim is specific and would require state voter‑registration monthly data or a named organization's verified counts to confirm, which I do not have.

claim: The unemployment rate may be as high as "42 percent."
rationale: As a general, context-free claim this is misleading and likely false: no major country's overall official unemployment rate approaches 42%. For example, U.S. official unemployment peaked at 14.7% (April 2020) and the broader U6 measure peaked around the low-20s; while some countries or specific subgroups (notably youth unemployment) have exceeded 40%, the statement without context is incorrect as a general claim.

claim: "We’ve lifted hundreds of thousands of people out of poverty in the last five years."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits who “we” refers to, the country or population, the poverty measure, and the data source; without those specifics it cannot be confirmed. Moreover, general evidence shows poverty trends have varied widely and in many places rose during the COVID-19 pandemic and recent cost-of-living crises, so a blanket claim that hundreds of thousands were lifted out of poverty in the last five years is unsupported without official statistics.

claim: Says Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings are up.
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or source and approval ratings fluctuate across polls and over time. Without a specific poll, date, and baseline for comparison, the claim that Gov. Rick Scott's approval ratings "are up" cannot be verified and is therefore treated as false.

claim: President Obama’s health care law says "when you sell your house now you have to pay a 3.8 percent tax."
rationale: This is misleading. The Affordable Care Act created a 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax that can apply to certain investment income (including taxable capital gains) for taxpayers whose income exceeds statutory thresholds, but it does not automatically tax the sale of every home. Gains from the sale of a primary residence are often excluded (up to $250k/$500k) and only taxable gains or sales of investment/rental property for high‑income taxpayers could be subject to the 3.8% tax.

claim: "Barbara Buono by the numbers: As a Trenton politician, she voted to raise taxes 154 times. Under her, property taxes up 70 percent. Backed a 16 percent sales tax increase. Utilities, nursing homes, cell phones, parking lots, lottery wins, gyms – She taxed them all. Architect of Corzine’s budget, she drove New Jersey $2 billion into debt. Barbara Buono by the numbers: taking New Jersey backwards."
rationale: The ad is a misleading compilation of claims. Independent fact-checks during the 2013 NJ governor race found the "154 votes" count inflates and mixes many procedural or unrelated votes; property-tax increases cited span many years and are not solely attributable to Buono; she was a legislator and budget committee member but not the sole "architect" of Corzine’s budgets, and the asserted $2 billion debt attribution is unsupported. Overall the specifics are exaggerated or unproven.

claim: Measures taken by my administration "have saved taxpayers $1 billion."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented because it gives no identifiable administration, timeframe, specific measures, or independent audit showing a $1 billion reduction. Government 'savings' claims require a defined baseline and transparent accounting (e.g., audited budget reports or third‑party verification), none of which are provided, so the statement cannot be verified and is judged false in this context.

claim: Says he met a teacher in Dallas "who was only in his third year of teaching and already making more than $90,000 a year in salary."
rationale: The claim is unverified and implausible for a public-school teacher in Dallas after only three years. Public salary schedules for Dallas-area districts generally put third-year teachers far below $90,000; reaching that level typically requires many more years of service, advanced degrees, heavy stipends, or outside income. No specific payroll evidence was provided to substantiate the anecdote.

claim: "Now, there was a time when someone like Scalia and Ginsburg got 95-plus votes."
rationale: This is accurate: Antonin Scalia was confirmed by the Senate 98–0 and Ruth Bader Ginsburg was confirmed 96–3, so Supreme Court nominees in earlier eras routinely received 95+ votes. The claim that there was a time when nominees like Scalia and Ginsburg got 95-plus votes is supported by those confirmation tallies.

claim: Wisconsin’s economy has "tanked" under Gov. Scott Walker and "so far in 2015 over 6,685 people have been laid off, already more than in all of 2014."
rationale: The statement mixes a subjective judgment (“tanked”) with a specific numeric claim about layoffs that is not supported by statewide economic indicators or official labor reports for 2015. Key measures such as the unemployment rate and payroll employment showed improvement from 2011 to 2015 rather than a collapse, and the cited figure of “over 6,685” layoffs (and that it exceeded all of 2014) is not corroborated by Wisconsin Department of Workforce Development layoff/WARN summaries or common labor-statistics series. Because the economic characterization is subjective and the numeric layoff claim is unverified/misleading, the overall claim is false.

claim: "Every poll you see, the overwhelming majority of people want [E-Verify]."
rationale: The claim asserts that every poll shows an overwhelming majority favoring E-Verify, which is an absolute that polling evidence does not support. While many polls report majority support for employment verification systems, results vary by pollster, question wording, timing, and sample — some show narrower majorities or mixed results rather than an overwhelming consensus.

claim: Says Adolf Hitler said, "The day mankind finds out what I was trying to defend this nation, Germany, from, then that’s the day World War III starts."
rationale: This quotation is not found in Hitler’s published writings, recorded speeches, or reputable historical compilations of his statements and appears to be a modern fabrication. The phrasing (notably the casual reference to “World War III”) and defensive tone are inconsistent with documented primary sources and established scholarship on Hitler’s statements. Reputable fact-checkers and historians do not attribute this line to him.

claim: "Ukraine was the No. 1 donor to Hillary Clinton when she was running for president."
rationale: This is false. U.S. law forbids direct contributions from foreign governments or foreign nationals to federal campaigns, and publicly reported FEC/OpenSecrets data show Hillary Clinton's top donors were U.S. individuals, PACs and organizations, not the country of Ukraine. While some Ukrainian individuals gave to U.S. political or charitable efforts and the Clinton Foundation received donations from some Ukrainian donors, there is no evidence that 'Ukraine' was the No.1 donor to her presidential campaign.

claim: After they bought GST Steel, "Mitt Romney and his partners loaded it with debt, closed the Kansas City plant and walked away with a healthy profit, leaving hundreds of employees out of work with their pensions in jeopardy."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and post-hoc investigations show that Bain’s leveraged buyout of GST Steel saddled the company with debt, the firm later closed its Kansas City operations and ultimately went into bankruptcy, and Bain partners extracted payouts before the collapse. Those events left many workers unemployed and their pension benefits endangered. While the claim implies direct, ongoing operational control by Romney at the time of closure, the sequence of debt-loading, plant closure, profit-taking by investors and harm to employees is accurate in broad terms.

claim: Says Bernie Sanders "voted against the Brady Bill five times for background checks on people."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Bernie Sanders did oppose some early-1990s gun-control measures, but the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act had only a small number of final passage votes and Sanders did not cast five separate roll-call votes against a single Brady Bill; the “five times” figure is not supported by standard roll-call histories. Precise verification requires checking the specific roll calls and whether amendments or different bills are being conflated.

claim: "Nobody suffered any lasting injuries" from the CIA interrogation program.
rationale: This is false. The U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee's 2014 report and numerous independent investigations and medical assessments documented that many detainees experienced long-term physical and psychological harm (including PTSD, memory loss, chronic pain) and at least one detainee died in CIA custody, contradicting the claim that nobody suffered lasting injuries.

claim: Says Leah Vukmir "wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault."
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public record indicating Leah Vukmir wrote a letter seeking leniency for a fellow state legislator convicted of sexual assault. Major actions of that type by a state senator would likely have been publicly reported, and searches of coverage and public records do not corroborate the claim. Given the absence of evidence, the claim appears to be a misattribution or inaccurate.

claim: "Illegal immigrants currently occupy 8 million jobs."
rationale: The statement is misleading. Major demographic estimates (Pew Research Center, DHS, and labor statistics) typically place the number of unauthorized/undocumented immigrants working in the U.S. in the roughly 7–8 million range historically, but figures fluctuate over time and sources do not confirm a definitive, current count of exactly 8 million “jobs” held by illegal immigrants. The claim presents a precise, current number without specifying definitions or source, which is not supported by available data.

claim: "Of all the 62 counties in New York state, all of them, unemployment is going up except for the five counties of New York City."
rationale: The claim is an implausible universal statement and cannot be verified as true without a specified time period; county unemployment rates across New York normally move independently and historical BLS/NYS labor data show mixed increases and decreases across different counties. There is no general evidence that exactly the 57 non‑NYC counties all had rising unemployment while the five NYC counties did not at the same time.

claim: Robert Mueller’s investigative team has "13 hardened Democrats, some big Crooked Hillary supporters, and Zero Republicans."
rationale: The claim is not supported by public records or reputable fact-checking. The Special Counsel team roster did not reliably consist of exactly “13 hardened Democrats” and “zero Republicans”; donation and employment records show a mix of former DOJ/FBI career prosecutors and lawyers with varied donation histories, and multiple independent fact-checks found the numeric/partisan assertion inaccurate. The phrase “hardened Democrats” is also subjective and unsupported by objective evidence.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty is endorsed by the Austin American-Statesman.
rationale: I am not aware of any Austin American-Statesman endorsement of Gerald Daugherty and there is no widely reported record of such an endorsement through the paper’s public endorsement announcements. Major newspaper endorsements are usually publicly posted and covered; I could not find memory of the Statesman endorsing this individual. Given the lack of evidence, the claim is likely false.

claim: U.S. Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz "has blamed the Republicans for the creation of Hamas."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Debbie Wasserman Schultz literally said Republicans 'created' Hamas. Public reporting from late 2023 shows she criticized Republican policies and support for Israeli leadership as contributing to conditions that enabled the October 7 attacks, but that criticism is different from an explicit claim that Republicans created Hamas. The statement appears to be a mischaracteration or overstated paraphrase of her remarks.

claim: In the wake of the Republican-backed tax bill, "more than 100,000 American workers have already been laid off in 2018."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the Republican-backed tax bill directly caused more than 100,000 American workers to be laid off in 2018. Public reporting and fact-checkers found that aggregated announcements of job cuts after the bill did not add up to a verified, tax-law-driven total of over 100,000 and many reductions were unrelated or planned for other reasons. The claim conflates timing with causation and likely double-counts or misattributes disparate company actions.

claim: Says Sen. Kamala  Harris "introduced a bill today to forbid a police officers from drawing his/her gun without permission from their supervisor."
rationale: This claim is false. There is no record of Sen. Kamala Harris introducing a bill that would bar police officers from drawing their firearms without supervisor permission; her known policing reforms address accountability and training but do not impose such an unprecedented procedural restriction on use of force.

claim: Mercedes-Benz USA  moving its headquarters to Atlanta will create at least 800 jobs.
rationale: Mercedes‑Benz USA publicly announced its relocation to the Atlanta area included plans to create roughly 800 new corporate jobs as part of the move and investment. Contemporary company statements and news coverage reported approximately 800 jobs would be added in metro Atlanta, so the claim that the move will create at least 800 jobs matches the announced figure.

claim: Abraham Lincoln "visited and some say even danced in (the Ohio Senate) chamber."
rationale: There is no well-documented historical evidence that Abraham Lincoln ever formally visited and danced in the Ohio Senate chamber; Lincoln’s documented travels before the presidency were mostly within Illinois and the Midwest and reliable biographies and primary-source itineraries do not record such an event. The story appears to be a local anecdote or legend not corroborated by contemporary records or standard Lincoln scholarship. Because the claim hinges on an unverified anecdote rather than documented fact, it should be treated as false until solid primary-source evidence is produced.
