Florida law and court precedent preserve the public’s rights to the wet‑sand area (generally up to the mean high‑tide line), and the bills signed during Scott’s term did not repeal that public‑trust protection; social posts conflating limited property‑owner provisions or local access rules with wholesale privatization are exaggerations or misinterpretations.

claim: Says Donald Trump’s book "The Art of the Deal" advises: "Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated."
rationale: The Art of the Deal does not contain that exact admonition. The quoted line appears to be a pithy paraphrase of Trump's combative, win-focused style rather than a verbatim passage from the 1987 book; the book emphasizes aggressive deal‑making and projecting strength but does not include the sentence “Never admit defeat. You win. If you don’t win, claim they cheated.”

claim: "Instagram has been limiting our posts so that no more than 7% of our friends see our posts."
rationale: Instagram uses an algorithmic feed and does not publicly impose a fixed rule that limits every post to exactly 7% of an account’s friends/followers. Organic reach varies widely by account, engagement, post type, timing and platform changes; third‑party analyses have reported low median reach for some accounts but not a universal 7% cap. Therefore the categorical claim that Instagram is limiting posts so “no more than 7%” see them is unsupported.

claim: Says Donald Trump "doesn't believe in equal pay."
rationale: There is no clear, verifiable public record of Donald Trump saying the exact sentence “I don't believe in equal pay.” While he has at times questioned the size and causes of the gender wage gap and emphasized merit-based pay, characterizing that as an explicit statement that he doesn’t believe in equal pay appears to be a misleading paraphrase. Without a precise source or verbatim quote, the claim as written is not supported by established public records.

claim: "The race will tighten, just because that's what happens at the end of campaigns. They always have."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute rule — that races always tighten at the end of campaigns — which is inconsistent with historical evidence. Some elections do show late swings or tightening, but many races remain stable or even widen; therefore the universal quantifier "always" is false.

claim: "When I go on Letterman" the "ratings go up."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it names no specific person, episode, or time period and presents a broad causal assertion. TV ratings are affected by many factors (guest profile, promotion, competing programming, lead-in audience), so a single claim that "when I go on Letterman the ratings go up" cannot be confirmed without audience data. Occasional appearances by high-profile guests can coincide with ratings bumps, but that does not validate an unqualified general rule.

claim: Says El Chapo testified in court that he paid off Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.-Mexico border open for drug cartels.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or trial transcript indicating Joaquín “El Chapo” testified that he paid Nancy Pelosi to keep the U.S.–Mexico border open. Reporting and court records from his U.S. prosecution document bribes to Mexican officials and security forces, not to U.S. members of Congress. The claim appears to be a fabricated or misattributed social-media rumor.

claim: Says there is a "traditional 60-vote threshold for confirming Supreme Court nominees."
rationale: There is no constitutional or permanent Senate rule requiring 60 votes to confirm Supreme Court nominees; confirmations have legally required a simple majority. The idea of a "60-vote threshold" refers to the Senate cloture rule used to overcome filibusters (commonly requiring 60 votes for 30 years), but that was a Senate practice rather than a formal confirmation requirement and was changed for Supreme Court nominees in 2017. Thus characterizing a 60-vote rule as a traditional confirmation threshold is misleading.

claim: Says "Every time the Legislature 'suspended' the kicker, most recently the corporate kicker in 2007, Salem spent every penny and failed to stabilize the state's revenues."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes: it asserts that on every occasion the Legislature suspended the kicker (citing 2007) Salem 'spent every penny and failed to stabilize revenues.' Historical practice with Oregon's kicker has varied — when lawmakers diverted or delayed refunds they sometimes used funds for one-time obligations, reserves, or to pay liabilities rather than simply spending every dollar, and the revenue effects differed by episode. The wording “every time” is demonstrably too absolute and the 2007 corporate situation is more complex than a simple suspension-and-spend narrative.

claim: "Last year, there were an additional 81,000 pages of government regulations. If you stack that up, it would be a three-story building."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and appears to overstate the visual height. Stacking 81,000 standard office pages (≈0.004 in per page, or 500 pages ≈2 in) yields roughly 324 inches (~27 feet), about 2.5 stories if a story is ~10 feet, so calling it a three‑story building is an exaggeration. Also annual ‘‘pages of regulations’’ totals vary by jurisdiction and year and do not uniquely support the precise 81,000 figure without attribution.

claim: "When President Obama landed in Cuba on Air Force One, no leader was there, nobody, to greet him -- perhaps an incident without precedent in the long and prestigious history of Air Force One."
rationale: When President Obama arrived in Havana in March 2016 he was met by Cuban officials on the tarmac and was later officially received by President Raúl Castro; contemporary news reports and photographs show Cuban representatives greeting him. The claim that 'no leader was there, nobody, to greet him' is therefore incorrect and the suggestion of unprecedented protocol for Air Force One is exaggerated, since foreign leaders or other officials sometimes do or do not meet arriving heads of state.

claim: Wisconsin is "38th in the country in terms of proficiency standards" in student testing.
rationale: The claim is imprecise and unsupported by a single, widely accepted ranking. "Proficiency standards" can be measured in multiple ways (state cut scores, equivalence to NAEP, year and subject), and I am not aware of an authoritative, current source that ranks Wisconsin specifically as 38th overall. Different studies and metrics produce different state orderings, so the blanket statement is misleading without a cited study and timeframe.

claim: Says Rick Perry's proposal on driver licenses and high school dropouts has been state law since 1989.
rationale: The claim is false. There is no clear evidence that a statewide Texas law matching Rick Perry’s described proposal — a blanket rule denying driver’s licenses to high‑school dropouts — has existed continuously since 1989. Texas statutes tie driving privileges to certain truancy or attendance findings in limited circumstances and have been amended over time, but the broad portrayal as a single 1989 state law is misleading.

claim: "Hillary (Clinton), one time late at night when she was exhausted, misstated and immediately apologized for it, what happened to her in Bosnia in 1995."
rationale: The claim mixes facts and an unsupported detail. Hillary Clinton did visit Bosnia as First Lady (commonly cited as a 1996 trip) and later faced scrutiny for remarks suggesting she landed ‘under sniper fire,’ but the timeline and description in the claim—that this was a one‑time late‑night exhausted misspeaking followed by an immediate apology about Bosnia in 1995—are inaccurate. Reporting shows the visit was in 1996 and the controversy involved later remarks and campaign clarifications, not a single late‑night exhausted instant apology in 1995.

claim: Facebook is changing its hate speech policy to ban "Let’s go Brandon."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Facebook/Meta announced a policy change specifically banning the phrase "Let’s go Brandon." Meta’s hate speech rules target slurs or demeaning content directed at protected characteristics; a political chant like this is generally treated as political expression and would only be removed if used in a way that violates other policies (harassment, threats, or targeted abuse).

claim: "Tony Evers is cutting child support."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Tony Evers has ‘‘cut child support’’ payments. Child support amounts are set and modified by courts and enforced by the state child support agency; governors can propose budget changes to programs but cannot unilaterally reduce individual court-ordered child support. Without a specific policy or budget line cited, the claim is misleading or false.

claim: "Over the past decade, drug prices have risen at three times the rate of inflation."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and overstated. While prescription drug prices in the U.S. have generally risen faster than overall inflation over the last decade, aggregate measures (e.g., CPI for prescription drugs versus overall CPI) do not consistently show a uniform threefold multiple across the entire decade; some drug categories (brand-name or specialty medicines) rose far faster, but overall increases are typically below three times general inflation. Because the statement lacks timeframe, geography, and drug-type specificity, it cannot be validated as a blanket fact.

claim: In the plot to kidnap Michigan Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, "the perps were ANTIFA and BLM anarchists."
rationale: Investigations and federal charges identified the suspects as members or associates of a far‑right militia (often reported as the Wolverine Watchmen) and motivated by anti‑government/extremist views; prosecutors and the FBI did not find evidence linking them to Antifa or Black Lives Matter. Claims that Antifa/BLM were responsible were propagated by misinformation and contradicted the official record and court filings.

claim: Mitt Romney previously believed "that abortion should be safe and legal in this country." Now he is "prolife."
rationale: Romney publicly described himself as supporting legal abortion in earlier campaigns (he made statements in the 1990s and early 2000s indicating abortion should be "safe and legal") but later adopted an explicitly pro-life position during his 2007–2012 presidential runs. Public statements, campaign platforms, and his later advocacy for abortion restrictions document a clear change in stance.

claim: Amazon will ship baby formula to U.S. addresses if you change your preferred country on its website from the U.S. to Canada.
rationale: This is not generally true. Amazon determines whether an item can be shipped to a given address based on the shipping address, seller/fulfillment settings, and cross‑border restrictions, not merely a user’s preferred country display. Infant formula is also subject to import/regulatory limits, so most Amazon.ca formula listings will not ship directly to U.S. addresses despite changing the site country.

claim: "Masks will kill quite a few people, it’s well known that they reduce blood oxygen levels and those with respiratory and cardiac disorders will die."
rationale: The claim is false. Multiple clinical studies and monitoring of healthcare workers show cloth and surgical masks (and most respirators when used properly) do not meaningfully reduce blood oxygen or cause CO2 retention in the general population, and there is no evidence that mask use has led to widespread deaths. While individuals with severe, specific respiratory or cardiac conditions should consult their clinician about mask use, that does not support the assertion that masks will "kill quite a few people."

claim: "As your Lieutenant Governor…I cut your taxes."
rationale: The statement as written is unverifiable and likely false because it gives no name, jurisdiction, timeframe, or tax type. In most U.S. jurisdictions lieutenant governors do not have unilateral authority to cut taxes—tax changes are enacted by legislatures and signed by governors—so a blanket first‑person claim that "I cut your taxes" cannot be confirmed without specific evidence of that officeholder's direct role in enacted tax reductions.

claim: "2 million rounds of ammo that ‘went missing’ under Obama turns up in enemy hands"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a specific cache of “2 million rounds” that went missing during the Obama administration was later definitively found in enemy hands. Fact-checking and government audit records have noted inventory discrepancies and unaccounted-for rounds at times, but investigators have not documented a confirmed transfer of a 2-million-round shipment to hostile groups. The claim conflates inventory shortfalls with proven diversion to enemies and inflates or misstates the available documentation.

claim: Says Texas U.S. Rep. John Culberson "was caught using campaign cash on collectibles, including Civil War memorabilia and fossils."
rationale: Contemporaneous news reports and campaign finance filings show Culberson’s campaign made payments to vendors that sold collectibles, and reporting specifically noted purchases or payments linked to Civil War memorabilia and fossils. These expenditures were documented in public filings and covered by multiple outlets as campaign spending on collectible items. The facts reported support the claim that he used campaign cash for such items, though interpretations of intent and propriety vary.

claim: "I've seen (life) from the factory floor when I was working the graveyard shift ...and I'd be ankle-deep in water at the Murray Ohio bicycle plant where I was running a machine that was so loud I couldn't hear myself yell if I wanted to."
rationale: This is a specific first-person anecdote but the speaker is not identified and I found no independent, verifiable evidence corroborating that this person actually worked the graveyard shift at the Murray Ohio bicycle plant or experienced those exact conditions. While Murray Ohio Manufacturing did exist and factory shifts could be loud and wet, the claim as stated is unverified and cannot be confirmed as factual. Because the statement is a personal claim without supporting documentation, it is treated as false here.

claim: "Military tribunals start Jan. 20, 2021."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official action showing that "military tribunals" began on January 20, 2021. In the United States that date was the presidential inauguration and ordinary civilian legal processes remained in place; widely circulated claims that mass military tribunals would start then have been debunked. The statement appears to reflect a conspiracy claim rather than a documented fact.

claim: "Kenosha car dealer kills himself after insurance won’t cover … damages caused by the riots."
rationale: This claim is false. Multiple fact-checkers and searches of reputable local and national news and official statements found no evidence that a Kenosha car dealer killed himself because insurance refused to cover riot-related damages; the story appears to be a social-media rumor with no corroboration. No authoritative reports linked any suicide to an insurance denial over riot damage in Kenosha.

claim: "Attention hunters: Voting in North Dakota could cost you your out-of-state hunting licenses."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Casting a ballot in North Dakota by itself does not automatically revoke out-of-state hunting licenses, but registering to vote or otherwise establishing legal domicile in ND can be used as evidence of residency change; residency is what some states use to determine hunting-license eligibility. Whether a license is affected depends on the specific residency rules and actions (e.g., changing voter registration or driver's license), not simply voting once in ND.

claim: "We are No. 1 among all large states in having fully vaccinated teenagers. We are No. 2 in all large states for having fully vaccinated five- to 11- year-olds."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it gives no date, no state name, and no definition of “large states” or “fully vaccinated.” Vaccination rankings change over time and depend on the data source (CDC, state dashboards) and the cutoff used, so without a specified timeframe and source the assertion cannot be confirmed. Following the instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain, I mark the claim false pending specific, dated evidence.

claim: The Wisconsin Economic Development Corp. "cannot account for creating one single job."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that WEDC 'cannot account for creating one single job.' Independent state audits and news investigations found that WEDC had significant record‑keeping and verification problems and could not substantiate many claimed jobs, but they did report and document job creation for numerous projects. Therefore the blanket assertion that it could not account for a single job is inaccurate and overstated.

claim: Police are "20.8 times more likely to kill than be killed by a criminal."
rationale: The statement gives a precise ratio without any time frame, country, or data source. US data sources show that annual counts of civilians killed by police (roughly 800–1,100 in recent years depending on source) divided by felonious killings of police officers (about 40–60 per year) yield ratios that vary year-to-year and by definition; while ratios near 20 can occur for specific years and definitions, the claim as stated is unverified and misleading without context.

claim: The $1.9 trillion relief package is "about a bridge for Chuck Schumer, a tunnel for Nancy Pelosi."
rationale: This statement presents a partisan metaphor as factual—that the $1.9 trillion package was primarily intended as a bridge for Schumer and a tunnel for Pelosi. The American Rescue Plan was a broad COVID-19 relief bill with nationwide provisions (stimulus checks, unemployment aid, vaccine and public-health funding, and state/local government aid), not a targeted infrastructure payoff to those two leaders. There is no credible evidence the bill’s main purpose or design was to benefit Schumer or Pelosi personally in the literal sense implied by the quote.

claim: "Before we even passed health care, 4 millions kids got health insurance that didn't have it before, through the Children's Health Insurance Program."
rationale: The statement overstates the documented CHIP gains in the period referenced. CHIP existed since 1997 and was reauthorized/expanded in 2009, but independent data and contemporary fact-checks show CHIP alone did not add 4 million newly insured children in the brief period “before” the Affordable Care Act’s passage; larger multi-million gains often cited combine Medicaid and CHIP or cover a longer time window. Thus the claim as phrased is inaccurate.

claim: ﻿﻿"Since Mayor Kennedy O’Brien took office Sayreville has issued 22,081 building permits! Now O’Brien is holding secret meetings with big developers."
rationale: I cannot verify the specific tally of 22,081 building permits or the allegation of "secret meetings" with developers from available public records; the claim bundles a precise numeric assertion with an unverifiable allegation of clandestine behavior. The permit count appears implausibly high without a clear timeframe or supporting municipal permit data, and accusations of secret meetings require specific evidence (witnesses, minutes, leaked records) which is not provided.

claim: In the 1970s, "the swine flu broke out . . . under another Democrat, President Jimmy Carter."
rationale: The major U.S. swine-flu scare occurred in 1976 after an outbreak at Fort Dix, New Jersey, and the national vaccination program was launched under President Gerald Ford. Jimmy Carter took office in January 1977 and there was no comparable U.S. swine-flu outbreak during his presidency. The claim misattributes the 1976 event to Carter.

claim: Louisiana gets "not one single penny" from Gulf Coast offshore oil revenues.
rationale: The claim is false. Louisiana receives substantial revenue tied to Gulf offshore oil through state royalties and taxes on production in state waters and from federal revenue-sharing created by the Gulf of Mexico Energy Security Act (GOMESA), which directs a portion of certain federal offshore lease revenues to Gulf producing states and coastal parishes; the state also gets money for coastal restoration funded by offshore-related revenues.

claim: Says Joe Biden took a knee during the national anthem.
rationale: There is no verified video or reputable reporting showing President Joe Biden taking a knee during the playing of the U.S. national anthem at a public event; widely circulated images that claim this mischaracterize moments where he briefly bent or knelt for other reasons (e.g., to speak with children or victims) but not during the anthem. Major fact-checkers and contemporaneous coverage of key ceremonies (including the 2021 inauguration) show he stood for the anthem. Given the lack of credible evidence, the claim is false.

claim: "The number of people who just got their voting rights restored in Florida is greater than the populations of Wyoming, Vermont, Alaska, North Dakota, South Dakota, Delaware, Rhode Island, Montana, Maine and New Hampshire."
rationale: The ten states named have a combined population of roughly 9–10 million people. The number of Floridians who recently had voting rights restored (commonly cited figures: ~1.4 million eligible under 2018’s Amendment 4, or later restorations numbering in the tens or low hundreds of thousands) is far smaller than that total, so the claim is not correct.

claim: "With 320,000 net Ohio manufacturing jobs lost, (Sen. Rob) Portman calls NAFTA a ‘proven success’."
rationale: Sen. Rob Portman has publicly defended NAFTA, describing it as a "proven success" in remarks and interviews. Ohio manufacturing employment declined by roughly 300,000–330,000 jobs when comparing post-NAFTA years to earlier benchmarks (depending on the exact start/end years), so the 320,000 figure aligns with BLS state manufacturing employment trends that critics cited.

claim: "Obamacare … means that for up to 20 million Americans, they will lose the insurance they currently have, the insurance that they like and they want to keep."
rationale: The claim substantially exaggerates the effect. Independent analyses and the Congressional Budget Office found that the Affordable Care Act would shift some people between sources of coverage and that a minority would have noncompliant individual or small-group plans cancelled, but the number of people who would lose coverage they could keep is far smaller than 20 million and many of those affected would be offered compliant replacement coverage or gain coverage through exchanges or Medicaid. Major fact‑checks concluded the "up to 20 million" framing was misleading because it mixes different categories and timeframes.

claim: "U.S. agricultural & food exports are expected to increase more than $2 billion annually under #USMCA"
rationale: This statement mirrors official projections made by the U.S. Trade Representative during the USMCA negotiations, which claimed U.S. food and agricultural exports to Canada and Mexico would rise by more than $2 billion annually under the agreement. Independent economic studies and the U.S. International Trade Commission produced different (often smaller or more uncertain) estimates, so the claim is accurate as an expectation attributable to USTR but not an established outcome.

claim: The longest filibuster in U.S. history was 75 days and "took place in 1964, when Democrats tried to block the Civil Rights Act."
rationale: The Senate filibuster opposing the Civil Rights Act of 1964, led by Southern Democrats, lasted roughly 75 days and is widely cited as the longest filibuster in Senate history. (The longest single-person speaking filibuster is a separate event — Strom Thurmond’s 24-hour-plus speech in 1957.)

claim: "The Defense Department received only one-half of 1 percent of the nearly trillion-dollar stimulus package funding."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate or misleading. Public budget breakdowns for the commonly referenced “nearly trillion‑dollar” stimulus (the 2009 ARRA) and later large packages show the Defense Department received more than 0.5% of total stimulus funding; moreover the phrase “nearly trillion‑dollar stimulus” is ambiguous (different packages and accounting methods change the share). Consequently the strict statement that the Defense Department received only one‑half of one percent is false as stated.

claim: "More than half of women under 30 who give birth do so outside of marriage..."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous about country and timeframe and cannot be verified as universally true. In many countries (and in recent U.S. national totals) the share of births to unmarried women is well under 50% overall; while nonmarital birth rates are higher among teenagers and younger adults, it is not clearly established that more than half of all births to women under 30 occur outside marriage. Without a specific location and year the statement overgeneralizes and is not reliably supported by available demographic patterns.

claim: A state report’s "projection is that approximately half of public employees" would live outside municipal boundaries in a decade if the state bans local residency requirements.
rationale: There is no specific, verifiable state report cited and I am not aware of any widely reported state analysis projecting that roughly half of public employees would move outside municipal boundaries within a decade if residency requirements were banned. Such a claim would require a named report, clear methodology, and jurisdiction because outcomes vary widely by state, job type, and local housing markets. Without that supporting evidence the assertion is unverified and likely incorrect.

claim: He "stood up to Barack Obama by passing legislation that prevents you from being forced to join government health plans or buy health insurance against your will."
rationale: The claim is false as stated: state or individual legislation cannot stop a valid federal requirement from applying. The Affordable Care Act’s individual mandate was a federal provision (upheld as a tax by the Supreme Court in 2012) and only Congress and federal courts can change its force; while some state laws limited state cooperation or barred state-level mandates, those do not prevent federal law from applying. Moreover, the federal penalty for the mandate was reduced to zero by Congress in 2017, which is a separate federal action.

claim: "Already, the Affordable Care Act is helping to slow the growth of (Medicare’s) health care costs."
rationale: Empirical federal analyses and academic studies found Medicare spending growth slowed in the years after the ACA and the law contains multiple provisions (e.g., payment-rate adjustments, productivity adjustments, value‑based payment pilots and ACOs) intended to reduce Medicare cost growth. While other factors (the 2008–09 recession, slower medical price inflation, coding changes) also contributed and exact attribution is debated, evidence supports that the ACA has at least partly helped slow Medicare’s cost growth.

claim: Says county parties representing more than half the state’s Republican voters approved resolutions "demanding changes" in Texas House leadership.
rationale: The broad claim is unverified and likely false. While numerous Texas county GOP organizations have passed resolutions criticizing or calling for changes in House leadership, there is no reliable evidence that those specific county parties collectively represent more than half of the state’s Republican voters; aggregating county resolutions into a majority-of-voters claim requires up-to-date, vote-weighted tallies that have not been substantiated. The statement conflates local resolutions with statewide voter representation without providing the necessary population or primary-vote calculations.

claim: "I haven't switched my position" on the Trans-Pacific Partnership trade deal.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it lacks the identity of the speaker and a time frame; without knowing who 'I' refers to and when the statement was made, we cannot confirm consistency of position. Many public figures have changed positions on the Trans-Pacific Partnership over time, so a generic assertion of 'I haven't switched my position' cannot be validated from this isolated quote.

claim: "Texas now has the second-highest high school graduation rate in the country. And it has the highest graduation rate for African Americans and Hispanics."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not clearly supported by consistent national data. While Texas has reported record-high overall graduation rates in recent years and gains for Black and Hispanic students, national rankings change by cohort and data source; other states (e.g., New Jersey, Iowa, New York) often rank equal to or above Texas overall, and states that lead overall do not always match the claim about highest Black and Hispanic rates. Without a specific year and data source, the broad assertion that Texas is now second-highest overall and highest for both African Americans and Hispanics is not reliably verifiable.

claim: "David McCormick paid for attacks on Donald Trump."
rationale: There is no well-documented public evidence that David McCormick personally paid for attacks on Donald Trump as an explicit, verified fact. While candidates and allied outside groups sometimes run negative ads in primary contests, attributing payment requires clear documentary proof (campaign or PAC spending records) which is not established here. Without a specific time frame, mechanism (personal payment vs. campaign/PAC expenditure), or cited spending record, the blanket claim is unsupported.

claim: Photos show "diesel generators" at the COP26 climate change conference.
rationale: Independent fact-checkers reviewed the widely shared photos and found they were misidentified; the pictured white boxes and cabinets were temporary electrical or infrastructure equipment, not diesel generators. Organizers and reporting indicated COP26 was powered from the grid with only occasional backup generators, so the claim that the photos show diesel generators is inaccurate.

claim: The book Little Red Riding Hood is something "that’s been banned in America," but not assault weapons.
rationale: The folk tale Little Red Riding Hood and some specific editions have been challenged or removed from U.S. schools and libraries at various times for violent or sexual content, so it has been banned in parts of America. By contrast there is no current nationwide federal ban on assault weapons in the United States (the 1994 federal assault-weapons ban expired in 2004), though some states do restrict them.

claim: Sen. Mark Kelly voted "for benefits to illegals."
rationale: The claim is vague and framed as a blanket statement; there is no clear evidence that Sen. Mark Kelly voted to provide universal or unspecified “benefits to illegals.” U.S. senators vote on specific bills and amendments, and while Kelly has supported Democratic immigration and social-policy measures that expand benefits for certain immigrant groups, that is not equivalent to a general vote for benefits to undocumented people without context. Without a identified vote or bill the statement is misleading.

claim: "George Bush never suggested that we eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood."
rationale: The blanket claim that “George Bush never suggested” eliminating Planned Parenthood funding is false. The George W. Bush administration consistently supported policies that cut or barred federal funding to organizations that provide abortions (e.g., backing the Hyde Amendment approach and related restrictions) and supported legislative efforts to block Planned Parenthood from receiving certain federal funds. Those positions amount to advocating elimination or restriction of federal funding to Planned Parenthood.

claim: Says the CEO of Camping World told Trump supporters "Frankly, don’t shop at my business."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the CEO of Camping World publicly said the quoted line exactly as presented. While Marcus Lemonis (CEO) has criticized former President Trump and commented on customers and politics, the specific phrasing “Frankly, don’t shop at my business.” is not substantiated by credible contemporaneous reporting or a verifiable direct quote. The claim appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase rather than a documented statement.

claim: "8 Syrians caught at Texas border in Laredo."
rationale: The statement gives a specific count but provides no date, source, or official confirmation; I could not corroborate a widely reported incident of exactly eight Syrians being apprehended in Laredo. Encounters with migrants of various nationalities at the Texas border do occur, but specific claims require DHS/CBP or credible news confirmation, which is missing here. Without that verification the claim is unreliable.

claim: Data on violent crime shows Wisconsin "has become less safe than it was when Scott Walker took office."
rationale: State and federal crime-reporting data show that Wisconsin's violent-crime rate was lower in the early 2010s (when Walker took office in January 2011) and rose in later years, particularly around 2020–2021, so by recent reporting the state experienced higher violent crime than at the start of his tenure. While there were year-to-year fluctuations and some periods of decline, the overall comparison to 2011 shows an increase in reported violent crime.

claim: No openly gay man has ever been elected to the Georgia Legislature.
rationale: This claim is false. In 2016 Sam Park, an openly gay man, was elected to the Georgia House of Representatives and is widely reported as the first openly gay man to win election to the Georgia General Assembly. Other openly gay men have served in Georgia state government since then.

claim: The "president of Drag Queen Story Hour" was "arrested, charged with child pornography."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the national president of Drag Queen Story Hour was arrested and charged with child pornography. Major news outlets and contemporary fact-checkers found no records substantiating that claim; posts making the allegation appear to conflate or misidentify unrelated arrests of individual performers.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. Sean Casten has held numerous "invite-only" town halls.
rationale: There is no clear, consistent evidence that Rep. Sean Casten regularly held numerous "invite-only" town halls. Public reporting and his event history indicate a mix of open town halls, virtual calls, and smaller constituent meetings, but not a pattern of repeatedly holding invite-only town halls as claimed. Without documentation of repeated, widespread invite-only events the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: Bernie Sanders has "never taken corporate lobbyist money in his *entire political career.*"
rationale: The statement is too absolute. Sanders has consistently refused corporate PAC money, but multiple fact-checks and reporting have documented that his campaigns have accepted donations from individual registered lobbyists, law‑firm employees, and corporate employees at times during his House and Senate campaigns. Therefore the claim that he has 'never' taken corporate lobbyist money is inaccurate.

claim: "Not only is there no scientific evidence that CO2 is a pollutant, higher CO2 concentrations actually help ecosystems support more plant and animal life."
rationale: The claim is false: abundant scientific evidence shows CO2 is a potent greenhouse gas driving climate change and many negative ecological impacts (heat stress, drought, wildfire, shifting ranges, and ocean acidification). While elevated CO2 can stimulate plant growth in some controlled or nutrient-rich contexts (the “CO2 fertilization” effect), those benefits are limited by nutrients, water, pests and can reduce crop nutritional quality and do not compensate for the broad harms of higher atmospheric CO2.

claim: Says private-sector job growth in 2011 "places New Jersey in the top third among all of the states."
rationale: Contemporary BLS and state employment data for 2011 show New Jersey experienced modest private-sector job gains after the recession and did not rank among the top third of states by private-sector job growth that year. Top-third rankings were occupied by faster-growing states (e.g., energy- and tech-leaning states and Sun Belt states), while New Jersey’s growth was near or below the national average, placing it in the middle or lower half rather than the top third.

claim: "8% of the votes cast" in Michigan’s Aug. 4 primary, 864 mailed ballots, came from dead voters. "NOTHING TO SEE HERE!!!"
rationale: The claim is incorrect as stated. 864 ballots is not 8% of votes cast in Michigan’s Aug. 4 primary — the statewide turnout was orders of magnitude larger, so 864 would be a tiny fraction, not 8%. Additionally, reports about ballots tied to deceased registrants have typically reflected data-entry or registration-matching errors or posthumous deaths, not evidence of widespread fraud.

claim: "Moderna has been pulled in Iceland and pulled for everyone under age 30 in Finland, Sweden, Norway, Denmark due to heart issues."
rationale: This is inaccurate in important details. In late 2021 several Nordic countries limited use of Moderna's Spikevax in younger age groups because of a small increased myocarditis/pericarditis risk, but the age cut-offs and scope differed by country and by dose (primary vs booster) rather than a uniform ban 'for everyone under age 30'. Iceland did not universally 'pull' Moderna for the whole population; restrictions were age‑limited and policies have changed over time.

claim: "As a 27 year old staff attorney for the House Judiciary Committee during the Watergate investigation, Hillary Rodham was fired by her supervisor, lifelong Democrat Jerry Zeifman. When asked why Hillary Rodham was fired, Zeifman said in an interview, ‘Because she was a liar. She was an unethical, dishonest lawyer, she conspired to violate the Constitution, the rules of the House, the rules of the Committee, and the rules of confidentiality.’"
rationale: Jerry Zeifman, who supervised Hillary Rodham (later Clinton) on the House Judiciary Committee during the Watergate period, has publicly said he fired her and in a 1994 interview described her as "a liar" and "an unethical, dishonest lawyer" who violated confidentiality and committee rules. Contemporary reporting and Zeifman's own statements corroborate that he fired her and made those criticisms, though others have disputed his characterization and context.

claim: "Violent crime is now going down for the first time in a long while."
rationale: The claim is too general and misleading: trends in violent crime vary by country, city, and time period. In the U.S., violent crime rose sharply around 2020–2021 and some measures fell again in 2022–2023 in many jurisdictions, but that is not universally true and is not "the first time in a long while" given the long-term decline since the 1990s and frequent local fluctuations. Without a specified place and timeframe the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: Says Quaden Bayles committed suicide.
rationale: There are no credible reports that Quaden Bayles committed suicide; past rumors about his death were publicly denied by his family and not corroborated by reliable news outlets. Bayles is known for a widely reported 2020 bullying incident and subsequent fundraising and family statements refuting death claims.

claim: Gov. Scott Walker received a $7,300 pay raise.
rationale: There is no clear, corroborated evidence that Gov. Scott Walker personally received a one-time $7,300 pay raise; gubernatorial salaries are set by law and any increases are publicly documented. The claim may conflate changes in benefits, pension contributions, or budget line items with a direct pay raise to Walker himself, but available public records and reporting do not support the specific $7,300 raise as stated.

claim: Officials "recommend that women who get one of these (COVID-19) shots should absolutely not get pregnant for at least the first two months after they’ve been injected."
rationale: Major public‑health agencies (CDC, WHO, ACOG) did not issue a blanket recommendation that women avoid pregnancy for two months after COVID‑19 vaccination. Guidance generally allowed vaccination in people trying to conceive or who are pregnant, and did not require an absolute two‑month delay; isolated, temporary cautions for specific vaccines or jurisdictions early in rollout do not support the broad quoted statement.

claim: During the lead-up to the American Revolutionary War, "some guy in Boston got his head blown off because he tried to secretly raise the tax on tea."
rationale: There is no historical record of anyone in Boston having their "head blown off" for secretly raising the tax on tea. Key events in the lead-up to the Revolution include the publicly imposed Townshend Acts and Tea Act, the Boston Massacre (colonists shot by British soldiers) and the Boston Tea Party (colonial protestors destroying tea); none describe a secret tax-raiser being decapitated. A related killing was the 1770 shooting of 11-year-old Christopher Seider by a customs informer, but that was a firearm killing of a boy amid protests, not a secret tax increase or a person literally having their head blown off.

claim: "They tried to give us $400 million to build a high-speed train that goes 39 miles an hour."
rationale: This characterisation is inaccurate. Federal and state support for California high-speed rail involved funding in the hundreds of millions to billions (not a single isolated $400 million “offer”), and the planned system’s top speeds were targeted around 200+ mph; 39 mph is not the design operating speed. The 39 mph figure appears to be a misleading reference to an average or interim segment speed or to construction-phase conditions, not the intended high‑speed train performance.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker doesn't make his calendar public -- "he's on our dime and we don't know where he is."
rationale: During Scott Walker’s time as governor his office routinely declined to release a full, detailed public calendar and resisted public-records requests, prompting frequent criticism that taxpayers could not see his full whereabouts. The administration did provide partial schedules and daily public events but did not make comprehensive appointment books publicly available, citing security and privacy concerns.

claim: Says Virginia Gov. Ralph Northam said, ‘You will give up your guns, if you don’t I’ll have the National Guard cut your power, your phone lines, and your internet. Then, if you still refuse to comply I’ll have you killed.’"
rationale: There is no credible record—no transcript, audio, or reputable news reporting—showing Gov. Ralph Northam ever made that statement. The quote is inconsistent with his public remarks and policy positions and matches patterns of fabricated or misattributed inflammatory quotes circulated online.

claim: Says Josh Mandel bet against Ohio families
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported by publicly available evidence. There are no credible reports or financial disclosures showing Josh Mandel made investments or financial trades that explicitly constituted "betting against Ohio families," and the phrase appears to be a political attack without documented transactions or clear meaning. Without specific, verifiable evidence of such a bet, the assertion is unproven and likely false.

claim: "The EPA has tried to define a puddle or a drainage ditch on your farm to be navigable waters and thus subject to massive environmental regulations."
rationale: Federal agencies (EPA and the Army Corps of Engineers) have proposed and issued broad definitions of “waters of the United States” that could bring small features such as certain ditches, intermittent streams, and some puddle-like wetlands within Clean Water Act jurisdiction. Critics correctly argued those definitions might cover puddles or farm drainage ditches in some circumstances; agency guidance and courts, however, apply tests (like “significant nexus”) and exemptions so not every puddle or ditch is automatically regulated.

claim: State budget cuts for local schools resulted in "nearly 4,000 educator layoffs"
rationale: The claim is missing key context (which state and what year) and I cannot corroborate a specific, statewide total of “nearly 4,000 educator layoffs” from general knowledge. Layoff counts from state budget cuts vary widely by state and year and are typically reported by state education departments or local news; without a cited source this precise number cannot be verified. Given the ambiguity and lack of corroborating data, the precise claim is not supported.

claim: Says this photo shows Joe Biden kissing and biting a child on the cheek.
rationale: Reliable reporting and image analysis of the widely circulated photo show Biden leaning in and appearing to kiss or touch the child's cheek or hair, but there is no credible evidence that he is 'biting' the child. Multiple fact-checks concluded the claim exaggerates and misinterprets the angle and timing of a brief close contact.

claim: Says the case of a Texas judge who refused to perform heterosexual weddings exposes a double standard in the case against Kentucky clerk Kim Davis.
rationale: There is no reliable, widely reported evidence that a Texas judge refused to perform heterosexual weddings in a way that was invoked to expose a double standard in the Kim Davis case. Kim Davis refused to issue marriage licenses to same-sex couples in 2015; while commentators sometimes argued double standards by citing other officials, the specific claim about a Texas judge refusing heterosexual weddings and being used as such an example is not supported by mainstream reporting.

claim: "America’s least-trusted news sources are also its most popular."
rationale: This claim is an overbroad generalization. Public-opinion surveys show trust and popularity do not align neatly: some widely used sources (local TV, network news) tend to score relatively high on trust, while some low-trust venues (social media, fringe sites) have large reach but are not the single most popular news sources overall. Partisan cable channels like Fox News are highly watched despite polarized trust, but that does not make "America's least-trusted" outlets identical to its most popular ones.

claim: Georgia ranks 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices.
rationale: I cannot confirm that Georgia ranks exactly 49th for women serving in elected state and federal offices. Reliable trackers (e.g., the Center for American Women and Politics and similar annual tallies) show state rankings vary by year and by whether the metric is share in state legislatures, Congress, or a combined measure, and Georgia is not consistently listed as 49th. Without a specific year and source, the precise rank claim is unsupported.

claim: "An economic impact study found that for every $1 invested in pre-K in Pennsylvania, a total of $1.79 is generated in total spending within the state."
rationale: I could not corroborate a Pennsylvania economic impact study that specifically concluded every $1 invested in pre-K generated $1.79 in total in-state spending. Reports and studies on pre-K typically report different kinds of metrics (short-term economic output multipliers, longer-term benefit–cost ratios, or fiscal returns) and the specific 1.79 figure does not match the major Pennsylvania analyses I’m aware of and may be a misquote or from a different jurisdiction or metric. Without a cited source the claim appears to conflate or misstate common measures used in early childhood investment studies.

claim: "Phony" ballots "were printed without my name on it."
rationale: The claim is unverified and lacks supporting evidence or specific context (who, where, when). Additionally, routine ballots are generally anonymous and do not include a voter’s name on the ballot itself, so saying ‘phony ballots were printed without my name’ is either tautological or requires specific proof which is not provided. Without corroborating documentation or an investigatory finding, the assertion cannot be treated as factual.

claim: Says that politicians who approved collective bargaining restrictions for public employees "exploited a loophole exempting themselves from Senate Bill 5."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that lawmakers inserted a secret "loophole" in Senate Bill 5 to exempt themselves from its collective bargaining restrictions. Most statutes and SB5-type measures already treat elected officials differently than rank-and-file public employees, and the widely reported controversy around SB5 concerned its broad limits on unions and its subsequent repeal by referendum rather than a self-exemption by legislators. Without specific proof of a deliberate, unique exemption created by those politicians, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "Before Congress, (Tom) Cotton got paid handsomely working for insurance companies and corporate interests."
rationale: Public biographies and reporting show Tom Cotton’s pre‑Congress career was primarily military service (Army infantry officer), then Harvard Law School followed by judicial clerkships and brief private‑law practice; there is no clear evidence he was a highly paid executive or lobbyist for insurance companies. While he did work in the private sector after law school, available records identify legal and clerkship roles rather than lucrative positions with insurers or major corporate lobbying posts.

claim: "We could build 30 walls with the $150 billion Obama gave to Iran."
rationale: The claim misstates both the money and who paid it. The roughly $100–150 billion figure widely cited refers to Iranian assets that were unfrozen worldwide after the 2015 nuclear agreement (access to Iran’s own oil revenue), not a $150 billion cash gift from President Obama or the U.S. Treasury. The second part—that those funds could instead build “30 walls”—is speculative and depends on undefined costs per wall, so the asserted equivalence is unsupported.

claim: Says Andrew Gillum is running "from the FBI."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Andrew Gillum is literally "running from the FBI." While Gillum was the subject of federal scrutiny after his 2018 campaign, he has not been reported as a fugitive or as actively evading investigators; the phrasing appears to be a political attack or figurative language rather than a factual description of flight from law enforcement.

claim: Says Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez said, "We must block Trump from stopping the return of the heroic Alabama mother from ISIS. In many ways she is more of a hero then our veterans. Welcome home sister!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez ever made this statement. An assertion praising an ISIS-affiliated person as "more of a hero than our veterans" would have been widely reported and debunked; it does not appear in her verified social media, speeches, or reliable news transcripts and matches patterns of misattributed or fabricated quotes. Therefore the claim is false.

claim: "Nancy Pelosi, Adam Schiff, and the rest of the corrupt Democrats made a promise to their crazy left-wing base that they would impeach me even BEFORE I took office."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Nancy Pelosi, Adam Schiff, or House Democrats formally promised to impeach Trump before he was inaugurated. Pelosi publicly cautioned against impeachment without evidence, and Democrats moved toward impeachment only after later investigations (Mueller, then the 2019 Ukraine call) rather than as a pre-inauguration pledge.

claim: Says "Donald Trump himself contributed $100,000" to the Clinton Foundation.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or contemporaneous donor record showing Donald J. Trump personally gave $100,000 to the Clinton Foundation. Multiple fact‑checking outlets and public Clinton Foundation donor lists do not include a $100,000 donation from Trump, and reporting on Trump’s charitable giving does not corroborate this specific claim.

claim: Photo shows Rihanna is pregnant
rationale: No photo was provided to verify, and a single image alone is an unreliable basis to conclude someone is pregnant because angles, clothing, editing, or unrelated factors can create the appearance of pregnancy. Determining pregnancy requires confirmation from the person involved or reputable reporting, neither of which is present here. Without that, the claim cannot be substantiated.

claim: "If you want out of the individual mandate... all you have to do now is tick off the box that says 'hardship' and you're out."
rationale: This is misleading. While the ACA and some state rules include a "hardship" exemption, you cannot legally evade the individual mandate simply by ticking a box unless you actually qualify for that exemption; some exemptions require an application, approval, or supporting documentation and false claims can be challenged or penalized. Also, the federal penalty for the individual mandate was reduced to $0 starting in 2019, and several states have their own, different rules.

claim: "We jumped 11 places since beginning this year in terms of being job-friendly."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it gives no country, ranking index, source, or precise timeframe. Assertions of an 11-place jump in “job-friendliness” would normally be supported by a specific published ranking or labor-market report; without that citation the claim cannot be confirmed. Because the statement lacks necessary detail and evidence, it is judged false for the purposes of fact-checking.

claim: The Baucus health care bill "would drastically restrict the use of flexible spending accounts (FSAs) in order to help pay for health care reform."
rationale: The claim overstates the proposal. The Baucus Senate Finance Committee drafts included provisions to limit tax-advantaged contributions (critically, proposals to cap FSA/HSA-style pretax contributions around $2,500 at the time) as a revenue offset, but did not seek to eliminate FSAs or broadly ban their use. Describing that modest cap as a “drastic restriction” is partisan framing rather than an accurate description of the actual proposal.

claim: Says author J.K. Rowling was the first billionaire to fall off Forbes billionaire list because of charitable giving.
rationale: While Forbes did report that J.K. Rowling fell off its billionaire list in 2012 in part because of large charitable donations, she was not the first billionaire to lose billionaire status due to philanthropy. Earlier philanthropists (for example Chuck Feeney and others who gave away large portions of their fortunes) had long reduced or exited billionaire rankings for the same reason. Forbes itself did not credibly establish Rowling as the first-ever case.

claim: Wisconsin was embroiled in a "constitutional crisis" brought on by the Democratic senators fleeing the state for Illinois to block Gov. Scott Walker's budget-repair bill.
rationale: In February 2011 fourteen Democratic Wisconsin state senators left the state for Illinois (and later other locations) to deny quorum and block consideration of Governor Scott Walker's budget-repair bill. The departures produced a prolonged legislative impasse, large protests, legal battles and widespread media and political commentary characterizing the standoff as a constitutional crisis over the functioning of state government.

claim: "Registered Republican not allowed to vote."
rationale: The blanket claim that a registered Republican is not allowed to vote is false. In the U.S. and most democratic systems, party registration does not bar a person from voting in general elections; it typically only affects which party primary they may participate in. Only narrow, non-party-based exceptions (e.g., felony disenfranchisement in some jurisdictions, court orders, or administrative issues) can prevent an individual from voting.

claim: "So that 2005 energy bill was a big step backwards on the path to clean, renewable energy. That's why I voted against it."
rationale: The statement mixes a normative judgment (“big step backwards”) with an asserted personal vote (“I voted against it”), but no speaker or voting record is provided to verify the latter. The 2005 Energy Policy Act included provisions both criticized as favoring fossil fuels (tax incentives, royalty relief) and provisions that supported some renewable and efficiency measures, so labeling it unequivocally a “big step backwards” is subjective and not verifiable as an objective fact. Because the claim lacks identifying context and contains a value judgment, I rate it as false for factual verification purposes.

claim: Federal spending is "the highest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years (and) revenue is the lowest it's been as a share of our economy in 60 years."
rationale: The statement mixes a largely-accurate claim about spending with an inaccurate claim about revenue. Federal outlays as a share of GDP did spike around the COVID-era and reached levels not seen in many decades (approaching the highest since World War II), but federal receipts as a share of GDP were not uniquely the lowest in 60 years—there were similarly low or lower revenue-to-GDP ratios during the Great Recession and other years. The exact truth also depends on the precise 60-year window and whether one uses gross receipts or a particular accounting series.

claim: The number of children in seven countries "missing so far this year" range from 20,000 to 460,000.
rationale: I could not verify a credible source reporting that in seven specific countries the number of children “missing so far this year” ranges from 20,000 to 460,000. The claim is vague about which seven countries and what definition of “missing” is used (e.g., abducted, disappeared, unregistered, displaced), and I am not aware of an authoritative dataset that produces those per-country ranges. Because the statement lacks identifiable sourcing and context it is not supported as presented.

claim: Says Keanu Reeves gave a speech that began, "I cannot be part of a world where men dress their wives as prostitutes by showing everything that should be cherished ..."
rationale: The quoted line is not found in any reliable transcript or reputable news report of Keanu Reeves speaking and has been circulated on social media and quote sites without verifiable sourcing. Independent fact-checkers have investigated similar attributions and concluded the quote is fabricated or misattributed to Reeves.

claim: "I investigated Abramoff and people ended up in jail."
rationale: The statement asserts a personal role and a consequence. It is true that federal investigations into lobbyist Jack Abramoff resulted in guilty pleas and prison sentences for Abramoff and several associates, but there is no verifiable evidence here that the speaker personally conducted that investigation. Because the claim as phrased attributes personal investigative action that cannot be substantiated, the overall claim is not supported.

claim: "While (Chris Christie) talks about job creation, we don't see jobs being created in this state."
rationale: The claim is an absolute assertion that no jobs were created in the state while Chris Christie talked about job creation. That is not supported: state employment levels during Christie's tenure and other periods show mixed but measurable job gains in many months/years, so a blanket 'we don't see jobs being created' is false as stated. The claim is also vague about which state and time period, making the absolute assertion unsupportable.

claim: "Before Leaving, Obama Enacts Rules to Take $3,000 From EVERY American."
rationale: This claim is false. There is no record of President Obama issuing any rule that deducted $3,000 from every American, and the executive branch cannot unilaterally impose a broad new federal tax or universal levy without Congress. Viral versions of this story misrepresent or fabricate administrative actions from the end of the Obama administration.

claim: Says Virginia Republican "Scott Taylor has been convicted in at least four different courts across the country, at times failing to even appear, and having a warrant issued for his arrest."
rationale: This overstates and conflates different records. Public reporting and court records show Scott Taylor had some civil judgments, unpaid fines/traffic citations and at least one temporary failure-to-appear/warrant tied to a minor matter, but not criminal convictions in four separate courts across the country. The claim mixes civil judgments, traffic issues and a short-lived warrant into an allegation of multiple criminal convictions, which is unsupported.

claim: In Liberia, "a girl is more likely to be married by 18 than to know how to read."
rationale: Available national survey and education data indicate that the share of young Liberian women who can read (youth female literacy) is higher than the share who were married before 18. Estimates vary by source and year, but literacy among younger cohorts in Liberia exceeds the measured child‑marriage prevalence, so the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: According to a recent CDC report, "almost everyone — 85% — who got the coronavirus in July was wearing a mask, and they were infected anyway. So clearly (wearing a mask) doesn’t work the way they tell us it works."
rationale: The statement misrepresents CDC evidence. The cited CDC analyses reported self‑reported mask use among people who became infected in a period and did not conclude that masks are ineffective; prevalence of mask use among cases alone does not show masks don’t work because it ignores denominators, exposure intensity, and comparison to infection rates among non‑mask wearers. Controlled studies and CDC guidance evaluate relative risk reductions, not raw counts of cases who happened to report mask use.

claim: "The Clinton Foundation folded."
rationale: The claim is false — the Clinton Foundation did not "fold" (cease to exist). The organization has remained legally active and continued to report activities publicly, maintain programs and communications, and file required nonprofit tax documents rather than formally closing.

claim: "More than half of last year's U.S. college graduates are unemployed or underemployed."
rationale: This claim is not supported by available labor statistics. BLS and other reputable surveys show unemployment for recent U.S. college graduates is typically low (single digits), and even with broader measures of underemployment included, most authoritative estimates put the combined share below 50%, so “more than half” is an overstatement.

claim: "Medicare does just as good, if not better, at keeping people healthy" as Medicare Advantage.
rationale: The bulk of comparative research finds Medicare Advantage enrollees often have equal or better preventive care use and in many studies lower hospitalization and mortality rates than traditional Medicare; differences are sometimes reduced after adjusting for selection and coding, but the overall evidence does not support a clear claim that traditional Medicare performs as well-or-better across health outcomes. The statement is overly broad and ignores substantial empirical findings favoring Medicare Advantage on several common quality measures as well as important confounding factors.

claim: Says a video shows Iranian rockets being launched toward U.S. airbases in Iraq.
rationale: The claim cannot be confirmed: the video is not independently geolocated, time-stamped, or corroborated by reputable news outlets or official sources linking it to Iranian rocket launches toward U.S. airbases in Iraq. Visual footage alone is frequently misattributed or filmed elsewhere, so without verification the assertion is unproven and evaluated as false.

claim: "By any measure, New Jersey has one of the most segregated school systems in the country."
rationale: The claim is overly absolute. New Jersey consistently ranks among the states with high levels of school segregation on many common metrics (racial isolation, poverty concentration, dissimilarity), but saying "by any measure" is too broad: different indices, definitions, and years can yield different state rankings and other states sometimes score higher on particular measures.

claim: "From 1990 to 2015 under (Democratic) control, W. Va. teacher pay rank plummeted from 30th in the nation to 48th."
rationale: The numeric part is roughly but not precisely framed: national teacher-salary rankings (NEA/BLS measures) show West Virginia declined from roughly the low-30s in the early 1990s to the high-40s by 2015. However the claim’s attribution “under (Democratic) control” is misleading and incorrect because West Virginia did not have uninterrupted Democratic control over that whole period (a Republican governor served 1997–2001 and Republicans won legislative control in the 2014 elections, taking office in 2015).

claim: Says Jennifer Aniston said, "Me and all the Trump supporter celebrities decide to make a company named ‘celebrities for Trump’"
rationale: There is no credible reporting or reliable source that Jennifer Aniston ever said she and Trump-supporting celebrities would form a company called “celebrities for Trump.” The quote appears to be a fabricated or misattributed statement circulated on social media; Aniston has not publicly endorsed Trump or announced such an organization.

claim: Says "$30 million gap" in stadium funding forced the Portland Beavers to leave.
rationale: The Portland Beavers left because the city opted to convert PGE Park for MLS use and the team owner failed to secure a replacement ballpark, not solely because of a proven "$30 million" funding shortfall. Contemporary reporting and public discussions cite multiple cost estimates and political negotiations over financing, but there is no clear, authoritative source establishing a specific $30 million gap as the singular, definitive reason the team relocated.

claim: "A [bank] surveillance camera capturing a criminal’s face and other identifiable traits would certainly discourage robbery attempts and serve as a deterrent to robbers."
rationale: The claim is stated with certitude ('certainly') but is empirically overstated. Empirical research and practical experience show visible cameras can deter some opportunistic property crimes, but their effect on robberies is mixed and depends on factors like camera visibility, live monitoring, signage, and offender determination; criminals can and do mask faces or target businesses despite cameras.

claim: Atlanta Tea Party co-founder Debbie Dooley "wants gas taxes raised."
rationale: This characterization is misleading. Debbie Dooley has backed specific regional transportation funding measures and toll/user-fee solutions and has at times supported targeted local sales-tax measures for transit, but she has not broadly advocated a general statewide gas-tax increase as a primary policy demand. Reporting that she simply “wants gas taxes raised” omits important context about the forms of funding she supported.

claim: The seven nations identified in Donald Trump's travel ban were "identified by the Obama administration as the seven most dangerous countries in the world in regard to harboring terrorists."
rationale: The seven countries in Trump’s 2017 travel ban (Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Yemen) were not designated by the Obama administration as a single ‘seven most dangerous’ list. While Obama-era agencies produced terrorism reports, travel warnings, and lists of areas with terrorist activity—some of these countries appear in those documents—there was no official Obama-issued ranked list labeling those seven as the most dangerous for harboring terrorists. The claim conflates overlap in concern about certain countries with a non-existent Obama designation.

claim: America’s federal business tax rate is the highest "in the world."
rationale: This is false. The U.S. federal corporate tax rate was cut to 21% by the 2017 tax reform and is not the highest in the world; many countries have equal or higher combined statutory corporate tax rates (for example, several jurisdictions have national or combined rates in the high-20s to mid-30s percent range). The statement would only be true under a narrow, specific, and time-bound definition that is not stated (and even historically the U.S. was not uniquely highest).

claim: Says she is a registered nurse.
rationale: The claim provides no identifying information or source — it merely says “she is a registered nurse.” Without a named person or evidence (e.g., a verifiable statement, license record, or authoritative biography) the statement cannot be confirmed. Because verification of professional credentials requires checking official licensure records or reliable sources, I treat an unsupported claim as false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "The amount of money that we put into running our own state legislature is nearly as much as we put into the University of Rhode Island."
rationale: The claim is unlikely: the operating budget and state appropriation for a public university like the University of Rhode Island are generally much larger than the administrative/operational budget for a state legislature. State legislatures are small agencies with relatively modest staffing and operating costs, whereas a university’s budget covers thousands of students, faculty, staff, facilities, research, and financial aid. Without a specific year or definition (total university budget vs. state appropriation) the comparison is not supported and is misleading.

claim: "U.S. Department of Homeland Security has told banks -- in writing -- it may inspect safe deposit boxes without warrant and seize any gold, silver, guns or other valuables it finds inside those boxes!"
rationale: There is no credible evidence DHS issued a written directive telling banks they may inspect customers' safe deposit boxes without a warrant and seize valuables. Searches of private safe-deposit boxes are generally subject to customers' contracts, state abandoned-property laws, and constitutional protections; law enforcement ordinarily must obtain a warrant or follow legal forfeiture procedures except in narrowly defined exceptions. Claims like this have circulated as rumors and conflate other authorities (e.g., border searches or civil asset forfeiture) with a blanket DHS power to inspect bank safe-deposit boxes without legal process.

claim: "As we near the 10th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, we should not forget that some of the hijackers used New Jersey driver’s licenses to board those aircraft."
rationale: Authoritative investigations and contemporary news reporting list various state-issued photo IDs carried by the 9/11 hijackers (for example Florida and Virginia credentials appear in records), but there is no documented evidence that any of the hijackers used New Jersey driver's licenses to board the aircraft. The claim appears to conflate the general fact that hijackers used state IDs with a specific, unsupported assertion about New Jersey-issued licenses.

claim: "The Republican from Georgia [U.S. Rep. Jack Kingston], he hasn’t even been to a NASCAR race."
rationale: The absolute claim that Rep. Jack Kingston “hasn’t even been to a NASCAR race” is unsubstantiated and unlikely. Kingston represented Georgia for decades, a state with prominent NASCAR events, and public officials from the region commonly attend such races; there is no credible record supporting the assertion that he never attended one.

claim: "We have pay equity. When you think about that wage gap, we all know it's 78 cents to the dollar. Well, in New York state it's 90 cents to the dollar."
rationale: The claim is misleading. The oft-cited '78 cents' figure reflects a particular year and measure; recent federal data usually put the national female-to-male median earnings ratio closer to about 80–82 cents on the dollar. New York State's ratio in most recent annual estimates is generally in the mid-to-high 80s, not a clear 90 cents, and the exact number depends on the year and whether one uses median annual or weekly/full-time measures.

claim: "NFL attendance and ratings are WAY DOWN. Boring games yes, but many stay away because they love our country."
rationale: The claim mixes a partly true observation (TV ratings have declined from earlier peaks) with overstatement and an unsupported causal claim. NFL ratings have fallen somewhat in recent years but not uniformly or “WAY DOWN” across all platforms, and stadium attendance has largely remained near pre-pandemic levels for many teams. There is no solid evidence that a large portion of fans are staying away primarily out of “love of country.”

claim: Says "we are overcharging students . . . to help pay for the health care law."
rationale: The statement presents a general claim that students are being deliberately overcharged specifically to pay for the health care law. There is no broad evidence that the Affordable Care Act required or produced a systematic policy of institutions overcharging students; while some colleges raised student health fees or premiums after insurance/administration changes, those increases were typically to cover higher insurer costs or compliance, not an explicit scheme of overcharging students to fund the law. As a universal claim it is unsupported and therefore false.

claim: Photo shows Kim Jong Un’s weight loss
rationale: A single photo by itself does not reliably demonstrate that Kim Jong Un has lost weight. Images can be affected by angle, clothing, lighting, posture, cropping, or editing, and similar viral claims about his appearance have previously relied on misattributed or misleading photos. Without independent, dated sources or multiple corroborating images from credible outlets, the claim is unproven.

claim: "Over 97 percent of the scientific community … believe that humans are contributing to climate change."
rationale: Multiple peer‑reviewed studies and surveys of climate scientists and of published climate papers report that about 97% (or more) of actively publishing climate researchers endorse the consensus that humans are a major driver of recent global warming. Thus the statement is accurate when 'scientific community' is taken to mean climate scientists or authors of climate science papers; it is misleading if interpreted to mean every discipline across all sciences.

claim: The federal government only ordered BP to pay "to do one of those six segments" of sand barriers for Louisiana.
rationale: This claim is inaccurate. In the aftermath of the Deepwater Horizon spill federal authorities and the Army Corps of Engineers approved a multi-segment sand-berm response in Louisiana and BP agreed to fund berm construction and other response/recovery costs rather than being ordered to pay for only a single segment. Statements that BP was directed to pay for “one of those six segments” misstate the scope and timing of federal directives and funding agreements.

claim: Paul Ryan would "outlaw in vitro fertilization."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Paul Ryan has said he believes life begins at conception and has supported policies restricting embryonic stem cell research, which critics say could threaten IVF, but he has not advocated explicitly for or introduced legislation to outlaw in vitro fertilization. Fact-checkers have judged blanket claims that he would ‘outlaw IVF’ as overstated given his public record and lack of specific proposals to ban the procedure.

claim: Says Scott Walker rejected legislation to make college loan payments tax deductible and the result was "to raise taxes on students."
rationale: Rejecting or vetoing a bill that would have allowed student loan payments to be tax-deductible is not the same as actively "raising taxes on students." At most a veto preserves the existing tax treatment (no new deduction); it does not itself increase tax rates or create a new tax burden on students. Without a specific bill and documented offsetting tax increases targeted at students, the claim misstates cause and effect and is misleading.

claim: "Hillary Clinton invented ISIS with her stupid policies. She is responsible for ISIS."
rationale: The claim is false. ISIS emerged from al‑Qaeda in Iraq (AQI), which formed after the 2003 U.S. invasion and later grew during the Iraqi sectarian conflict and the Syrian civil war under leaders like Abu Musab al‑Zarqawi and Abu Bakr al‑Baghdadi. Although some U.S. and regional policies (and specific decisions in various administrations) are debated as contributing factors, there is no evidence that Hillary Clinton "invented" or is solely responsible for ISIS.

claim: "The national unemployment rate has been above 8 percent for a record 36 months."
rationale: The claim is false as stated because it gives no country or timeframe and is inconsistent with known historical unemployment records. For the U.S., unemployment exceeded 8% for extended periods in the 1930s (Great Depression) and more recently around 2009–2012, and there is no clear record uniquely identified as “36 months” being the longest. Without specifying which nation and period, the statement is misleading and not supported by historical data.

claim: Says "Karen Handel’s office budget increased a whopping 42 percent."
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and unsupported as stated: it does not specify which "office" (state secretary of state office, congressional office, or campaign office) or the timeframe. Publicly available budget processes make a one-person-driven 42% increase unlikely—congressional office allowances are set centrally by House rules and state agency budgets are set by legislatures; no clear record shows a 42% jump attributable to Karen Handel. Without a specific budget line and period, the claim lacks verifiable evidence and is therefore judged false.

claim: A video shows "Dems caught not wearing masks" at the White House.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated: a short viral clip alone does not prove the people are Democratic officeholders or that it was filmed at the White House. Viral videos are frequently misattributed, and party affiliation and location cannot reliably be determined from appearance alone without corroborating context or sourcing. Because the claim asserts a specific partisan identification and location without supporting evidence, it is judged false as presented.

claim: The federal deficit is "growing."
rationale: The claim is too vague to be taken as universally true: whether the federal deficit is "growing" depends on the timeframe and which country is meant. For the U.S., annual deficits rose from FY2022 to FY2023 and many projections show future increases, but deficits have fluctuated year-to-year and are not monotonically growing without a specified period. Because the statement lacks context it cannot be accepted as fact as written.

claim: Bill Nelson’s vote for the Affordable Care Act "cuts $500 billion from Medicare to pay for new government programs."
