There is no public record that Josh Mandel, as Ohio treasurer, made direct "loans" of state money to Chinese business interests — the treasurer manages investments under state law and does not unilaterally loan taxpayer funds to foreign firms. The second part is vague about which bill; Mandel has publicly criticized China on trade issues, and there is no clear evidence he opposed a specific Ohio or federal bill described as "holding Communist China accountable" in the way the claim states. Overall the statement is unsupported and framed to mislead.

claim: "Seventy percent of the people in the state of New Jersey want marriage equality."
rationale: The statement gives an exact 70% figure for all people in New Jersey without citing a specific poll, date, sample, or question wording. Public-opinion measurements of support for same-sex marriage vary by year and by poll (registered voters, likely voters, adults), and while recent polls have shown majority support in many places including New Jersey, the precise 70% claim cannot be verified as a general fact without a source. Because of that lack of attribution the claim is not reliably factual.

claim: A photo shows "the Lincoln Memorial. His head damaged and defaced."
rationale: There are no credible reports or photographic evidence that the seated Abraham Lincoln statue at the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C. has had its head visibly damaged or defaced. Major physical damage to that national monument would have been widely reported; absent sourcing, a claim that a photo shows the memorial with the head damaged is more likely to be miscaptioned, doctored, or of a replica or model.

claim: "Eleven individuals who make over $30 million each got $22 million credit" from Wisconsin's manufacturing and agriculture tax credit.
rationale: This specific claim is unsupported and likely misleading. Wisconsin’s manufacturing and agriculture credit is allocated to businesses (or entities) rather than directly to named individuals, and publicly available descriptions and reporting do not corroborate that ‘eleven individuals who make over $30 million each’ collectively or individually received a $22 million credit as stated. The claim conflates business tax credits with personal income and lacks clear sourcing or timeframe.

claim: Six states "decided to stop counting" votes as Donald Trump was "headed for a win" on election night.
rationale: There was no coordinated action in which six states 'decided to stop counting' votes while Trump was 'headed for a win.' In the 2020 U.S. election many local jurisdictions paused in-person precinct reporting overnight (a routine practice) and continued counting absentee and provisional ballots afterwards; election officials and independent fact-checkers confirmed counts proceeded according to law rather than being halted to alter results. The claim misrepresents routine pauses and differences in how and when various types of ballots are tabulated.

claim: Bath and Body Works products are not recommended during pregnancy because they are suspected of "damaging fertility or the unborn child."
rationale: This is misleading: there is no widely issued medical or regulatory blanket recommendation that all Bath & Body Works products be avoided during pregnancy. Guidance about pregnancy safety for personal care items is ingredient-specific (eg, high-dose retinoids, some salicylic acid uses, certain essential oils or phthalates) and some individual products may carry jurisdictional warnings (like California Proposition 65) if they contain listed chemicals. Bath & Body Works as a brand is not universally classified as ‘suspected of damaging fertility or the unborn child.’

claim: A provision of the Senate immigration bill would require you to have government permission to get a second job.
rationale: No widely reported Senate immigration proposal would require U.S. citizens or the general public to get government permission to take a second job. Some immigration measures discussed in Congress affect work authorization for noncitizen visa holders (many temporary visas are employer-specific and limit changing or adding employers), but that is different from imposing a new permission requirement on ordinary citizens or all workers.

claim: Under Mayor Angel Taveras "Providence’s bond rating was downgraded from A to BBB, two steps above junk-bond status."
rationale: This specific formulation is inaccurate. While Providence experienced credit downgrades during Angel Taveras’s tenure, the exact move “from A to BBB, two steps above junk-bond status” misstates the agency-specific ratings and notch structure—ratings vary by agency and include plus/minus notches. Public reports show downgrades to lower investment-grade levels (for example to BBB+ by some agencies) but the claim’s precise wording and ‘two steps above junk’ characterization is imprecise and misleading.

claim: Video shows Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer laughing at Novak Djokovic after he was stuck in an Australian airport.
rationale: The clip has been widely misattributed: the footage of Rafael Nadal and Roger Federer laughing predates Novak Djokovic’s Australian visa/detention episode and was recorded at a separate tennis event, not at an Australian airport. There is no verifiable evidence the video shows them laughing at Djokovic while he was stuck at an airport, so the claim is false.

claim: Jim Renacci "voted repeatedly to end Medicare."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Jim Renacci supported Republican budgets and health bills that sought to change Medicare’s financing (e.g., move to premium‑support/voucher-style proposals) and voted for repeal/replace measures for the Affordable Care Act, but he did not cast votes that directly and literally abolished Medicare as a program. No enacted House vote during his tenure was a straightforward "end Medicare" repeal.

claim: "We know how to stop AIDS: persuade men not to have sex with men."
rationale: The claim is false because HIV/AIDS is transmitted by multiple routes (heterosexual sex, injecting drug use, mother-to-child transmission, contaminated blood) not just sex between men, and epidemics cannot be ended by urging one group to change behavior. Evidence shows comprehensive prevention (condoms, PrEP, testing, treatment as prevention, harm reduction) and reduction of stigma are required; behavioral persuasion alone is ineffective and harmful.

claim: Says President Barack Obama "came into office very concerned about" wiretappings but "then he became president of the United States, he got all the briefings … (and) he decided … the balance is probably pretty appropriately struck."
rationale: I could not find any authoritative record of President Barack Obama himself saying those exact words; the phrasing reads like a paraphrase by a third party describing his shift on surveillance. Public transcripts and widely reported interviews with Obama include nuanced statements about national security trade-offs, but this specific quotation is not verifiable as his direct speech. Without a reliable primary source attributing the lines to Obama, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: The IRS is "going to be in charge of our health care."
rationale: The IRS will not be "in charge of our health care." The agency enforces tax law and administers tax-related provisions of laws like the Affordable Care Act (for example, premium tax credits and formerly the individual mandate penalty), but it does not run health programs, regulate medical practice, or deliver medical services. Agencies such as HHS and CMS, along with private insurers and providers, oversee and operate healthcare programs and services.

claim: "68% error rate in Michigan Voting Machines. Should be, by law, a tiny percentage of one percent."
rationale: This claim is false: there is no credible evidence or official audit showing a 68% error rate for Michigan voting machines. Michigan conducts pre-election logic-and-accuracy testing and post-election audits and reported tabulation errors are orders of magnitude lower; the 68% figure appears to be a misinterpretation of unrelated data. While Michigan law requires testing and audits to ensure accuracy, it does not specify a generic 'tiny percentage of one percent' as a statutory numeric threshold in this wording.

claim: Says Mitt Romney "paid only 14 percent in taxes — probably less than you."
rationale: The exact quoted line—Romney saying he “paid only 14 percent in taxes — probably less than you”—is not a verifiable, documented direct quote. While Romney’s publicly released returns showed an effective federal tax rate in the low-to-mid teens in some years (roughly 13–15%), attributing the precise phrase “probably less than you” is unsupported and appears to be a paraphrase or editorializing rather than a proven statement. Because the specific quotation cannot be verified, the claim as stated is false.

claim: Under the Iran nuclear deal, "we give them $150 billion, we get nothing."
rationale: The statement is misleading. The U.S. did not hand Iran $150 billion in cash under the JCPOA; the deal lifted certain sanctions which allowed Iran access to some foreign-held assets often estimated in the roughly $100–150 billion range, and there was a separate $1.7 billion settlement in 2016 unrelated to the nuclear deal. In exchange the JCPOA imposed verifiable limits and inspection rights on Iran’s nuclear program, so it is incorrect to say "we get nothing."

claim: Foxconn hasn't hit job targets on its massive Wisconsin factory because "No. 1, you had a pandemic."
rationale: The claim that Foxconn missed its Wisconsin job targets primarily because of the pandemic is misleading. Reporting and state audits show Foxconn scaled back and reconfigured the project, reduced hiring targets, and delayed or canceled planned manufacturing well before COVID-19, so pandemic disruptions were at best a partial, late factor rather than the main cause.

claim: The average Georgia family makes $6,000 less than the average family did 10 years ago when inflation is factored in.
rationale: Available U.S. Census (ACS) and inflation-adjusted income series indicate Georgia’s median/average household or family income has generally risen in real terms over the past decade rather than fallen by about $6,000. The specific $6,000 decline is not supported by standard inflation-adjusted income measures for Georgia over a ten-year span.

claim: "In two terms in the Missouri General Assembly, Jason Kander passed ZERO bills that were signed into law."
rationale: This is false. Contemporary reporting and legislative records indicate Jason Kander had at least some legislation enacted during his two terms in the Missouri House; fact-checkers have disputed the claim that he passed zero laws, noting that counts vary by whether co-sponsorship or minor measures are included. The disagreement largely stems from differing definitions of “passed” and which measures are counted as laws.

claim: A collection of photos shows animals caught in the Australia wildfires.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because no specific photo collection or source is provided. While reputable reporting did document many animals injured or killed in the 2019–2020 Australian bushfires, viral compilations frequently mix authentic images with unrelated or misattributed photos from other times or places, so the blanket assertion that a given collection shows animals caught in the Australia wildfires is not verifiable. Without provenance for each photo, the claim is unreliable.

claim: "House Speaker Nancy Pelosi said this week that the Democrats have to pass their terrible health care bill so that the American people can actually find out what's in it."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate. Nancy Pelosi did make a widely reported remark in March 2010 that a health bill needed to pass so people could see what was in it, but she did not call it “terrible” and she did not say that line “this week.” The claim mixes an old remark with added wording and a false timing.

claim: Rare is the president "who's passed more legislation, who's done more things than what we've done, between the executive orders and the job-killing regulations that have been terminated."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsubstantiated — it asserts that a president has ‘passed more legislation’ and ‘terminated’ more executive orders/regulations than others without identifying who or providing comparative metrics. Historical records show several presidents (e.g., FDR, LBJ) enacted far more major legislation, and while recent presidents have pursued deregulation, there is no clear evidence that any modern president overwhelmingly surpasses prior presidents on both legislation enacted and regulations terminated as claimed. The statement therefore cannot be verified as presented.

claim: "I was filibustered."
rationale: The claim provides no speaker, date, or legislative context, so it cannot be verified as stated. Determining whether someone was filibustered requires checking official legislative records or reliable reporting about a specific motion, nomination, or bill.

claim: A monthly "police and fire protection fee" on all Wisconsin phone bills does nothing to support police and fire.
rationale: Wisconsin law and local ordinances authorize a municipal ‘police and fire protection’ fee to be collected on phone bills and remitted to the taxing municipality to fund police, fire, or related public safety obligations. While municipalities differ in how they allocate revenues (and some critics dispute the use or size of the charge), the fee is designed and generally used to support local public safety budgets, so the blanket claim that it does nothing to support police and fire is incorrect.

claim: "Obama certificate a fake."
rationale: The claim is false. The State of Hawaii has certified Barack Obama’s birth records and his long-form birth certificate was released in 2011; state officials and independent fact-checkers have repeatedly affirmed the documents’ authenticity and courts found no credible evidence of forgery.

claim: Obamacare "will provide insurance to all non-U.S. residents, even if they are here illegally."
rationale: This is false. The Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) bars undocumented immigrants from receiving federal marketplace subsidies and most Medicaid benefits, and exchanges require lawful presence documentation; undocumented people can only buy private insurance without federal subsidies, and some states run separate programs for limited groups.

claim: "Seventy of Ohio's 88 counties now have more than 25 percent of their residents eligible for emergency food."
rationale: I cannot verify the claim as stated and no authoritative, current dataset clearly shows 70 of Ohio's 88 counties have more than 25% of residents eligible for “emergency food.” Eligibility metrics differ by program (SNAP, TEFAP, local pantry rules) and public federal/state reports do not support that specific, statewide county count without a cited source or date. Absent a named methodology, the assertion appears unsubstantiated.

claim: The 2018 Academy Awards show was the "lowest rated Oscars in HISTORY."
rationale: The 2018 Oscars drew unusually low TV viewership (around 26–27 million), but it was not unambiguously the lowest-rated Oscar telecast in all of history. Subsequent telecasts (notably 2020) and differences in how ‘‘ratings’’ are measured (total viewers vs. household rating or 18–49 demo) mean the blanket claim that 2018 was the lowest in history is inaccurate without qualification. At best it was one of the lowest in recent decades, not definitively the lowest ever.

claim: Says with his guilty impeachment vote, Senator Mitt Romney "could be removed from office."
rationale: False. A U.S. senator is not automatically removed for casting a 'guilty' impeachment vote. Senators can only be removed by resignation, death, or a separate expulsion vote of two-thirds of the Senate, and there is no mechanism that strips a senator from office simply for how they voted in an impeachment trial.

claim: Says Joe Biden wants to "defund the police."
rationale: Joe Biden has publicly rejected calls to 'defund the police' and his 2020 campaign and presidential proposals emphasized police reform, accountability, training, and targeted community investments rather than eliminating or broadly cutting police budgets. Though he supports some reallocation to social services and policing reforms, he explicitly opposed the 'defund' slogan and advocated sustaining and improving police capacities.

claim: "We are currently using only around 20% of our testing capacity."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it lacks any context (which country/organization, what type of testing, and what time period). Testing capacity and utilization vary widely by location and over time, and blanket statements like 'we are using only around 20%' are unlikely to be accurate without cited, recent data. Absent specific evidence, the claim should be treated as false.

claim: Emails show Democrats, Hillary Clinton and George Soros instigated and orchestrated racial protests in Charlottesville by trying to "control" and keep people "desperate."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or verified email trail showing Democrats, Hillary Clinton, or George Soros instigated or orchestrated the Charlottesville protests. Independent reporting and fact-checkers found the 2017 ‘Unite the Right’ rally was organized by white supremacist groups and that counter-protests emerged separately; vague or out-of-context email snippets do not demonstrate a coordinated plot by Clinton, Democrats, or Soros. Assertions conflate funding of broad progressive causes with direct orchestration of a violent rally, which is unsupported.

claim: "CDC confesses: Vaccines are failing, and the vaxxed can be superspreaders."
rationale: This claim is misleading and incorrect. The CDC has not “confessed” that vaccines are failing; public-health evidence shows COVID vaccines substantially reduce risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death even if breakthrough infections and some onward transmission can occur. There is no evidence that vaccinated people are generally more likely to be superspreaders; at worst they can occasionally transmit, especially with waning immunity or immune-evading variants, but vaccines still lower overall transmission risk for most scenarios.

claim: "Since the passage of Proposition 47 by voters in 2014 and the signing of AB 109 in 2011, violent crime has been on the rise in California, up 12 percent in 2015 statewide according to the FBI."
rationale: The statement mixes a roughly correct 2015 FBI figure with a misleading broader claim. FBI Uniform Crime Report data showed about an 11.9% increase in reported violent crime in California in 2015 versus 2014, but violent crime did not steadily rise across the entire period since AB 109 (2011) and the causal attribution to AB 109 or Prop 47 is unsupported by the FBI. The claim therefore overstates continuity and causation even though the 2015 increase figure is close to FBI data.

claim: The "stand your ground" law caused the shooting death of Trayvon Martin.
rationale: The fatal shooting was carried out by George Zimmerman during an encounter with Trayvon Martin; that individual act, not the statutory text, was the proximate cause of Martin’s death. Florida’s “stand your ground” law was relevant to Zimmerman's legal defense and to public debate about prosecution and immunity, but there is no established evidence that the law itself directly caused or compelled the shooting to occur. Causal responsibility for the killing rests with the shooter, while the law affected subsequent legal handling and perceptions.

claim: "As of today, no one has the right to film or photograph Mr. Biden as he climbs the flight of stairs. New White House spokesman orders!!?"
rationale: The claim is false as a blanket statement. In the U.S., photographing or filming public officials in public spaces is generally protected by the First Amendment, and a White House spokesman does not have unilateral authority to strip that right; that said, access on White House grounds, inside restricted zones, or during specific security operations can lawfully be limited by the Secret Service or property owners. There is no credible basis that an across-the-board ban on filming President Biden climbing stairs was imposed 'as of today.'

claim: "Texas legislators have filed voucher proposals in every legislative session since 1995, but all of them have failed to become law."
rationale: The statement is too absolute. While Texas lawmakers have repeatedly filed school-voucher proposals in many legislative sessions since the mid‑1990s and no broad, statewide universal voucher program has been enacted, the history also includes passed measures and voucher-like mechanisms (for example limited scholarship/tax‑credit programs and targeted aid) that complicate the claim that “all of them have failed to become law.” Verifying the “every session since 1995” part requires a session-by-session bill check and depends on how one defines “voucher.”

claim: Georgia has some of the best maintained roads in America.
rationale: The claim is broad and not supported by available national performance metrics: state-by-state rankings (e.g., Reason Foundation’s highway reports and condition data compiled by TRIP and federal sources) typically place Georgia around the middle rather than among the top states for pavement condition and overall highway performance. National assessments and the ASCE infrastructure evaluations do not list Georgia as clearly among the best-maintained states overall.

claim: Says when New Jersey adopted guaranteed coverage and cost provisions without a mandate individual health insurance market rates "doubled or tripled" and enrollment dropped from 180,000 people to 80,000 people.
rationale: This claim overstates and simplifies a contested historical episode. New Jersey’s early-1990s move to guaranteed issue and community rating was followed by significant premium increases for many plans and a large fall in individual-market enrollment (some contemporaneous reports cite roughly 180,000 to ~80,000), but the “doubled or tripled” blanket statement about rates is not uniformly supported and causation is disputed—other regulatory changes, insurer exits, and market conditions also played key roles.

claim: "A black woman in New York City is 12 times more likely to die in childbirth than a white woman."
rationale: This matches analyses published by the New York City Department of Health and subsequent news reports showing that, over a multi-year period (commonly cited 2007–2016), non‑Hispanic Black women in NYC experienced about a 12‑fold higher pregnancy‑related death rate than non‑Hispanic white women. The statistic refers to pregnancy‑related/maternal mortality measures for specific racial categories and a defined timeframe rather than a universal, unchanging risk ratio for all years.

claim: "Wisconsin is #1 in the Midwest for personal income growth over the year."
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because it lacks a specific year and data source; available state personal income growth data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis typically shows Wisconsin not consistently ranking first in the Midwest on year-over-year personal income growth. Without a clearly defined 12‑month period and whether the measure is nominal, real, total, or per‑capita, the assertion that Wisconsin is #1 cannot be verified and is unlikely to be true in most recent annual comparisons.

claim: "Biden’s banking nominee demands all ‘private bank accounts’ be eliminated"
rationale: This is a mischaracterization. The nominee most commonly linked to this claim (Saule Omarova) proposed allowing a public Fed-run platform or accounts as an option and tighter regulation of large banks in academic work and testimony, but did not demand that all private bank accounts be eliminated. Opponents and media outlets have summarized her proposals in sensational terms, but her writings and testimony stop short of calling for abolition of private retail accounts.

claim: Photo shows Joe Biden’s license plate says "THEBIGGUY."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any vehicle owned or operated by President Joe Biden displays a vanity plate reading "THEBIGGUY." Official presidential and White House vehicles use government plates, and independent fact-checkers have debunked viral images that were misattributed or manipulated to claim a Biden plate said "THEBIGGUY." The photo circulated online is either of a different vehicle or altered and does not show a licensed Joe Biden plate.

claim: "@BernieSanders receives strong support from the conservative & most rural part of Vermont."
rationale: This is inaccurate: Bernie Sanders is broadly popular statewide but his strongest backing is in liberal urban and college-town areas (e.g., Burlington/Chittenden County). The more conservative and sparsely populated counties and towns in Vermont tend to lean Republican or moderate and were not his strongest base, so it is misleading to say he receives "strong support" from the conservative, most rural parts of the state.

claim: "I'm not taking any corporate PAC money."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it lacks the speaker and timeframe; many politicians who publicly claim not to take corporate PAC money nonetheless accept contributions from corporate-connected PACs, leadership PACs, or corporate executives. Without checking specific campaign finance filings (FEC/state reports) for the named person and period, the claim cannot be confirmed and should be treated skeptically. Because of that missing context I default to FALSE pending evidence.

claim: Hank Aaron’s death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Hank Aaron’s death was caused by a COVID-19 vaccine. Family statements and mainstream news reports noted he died peacefully at age 86 and fact-checkers found no causal link between vaccination and his death. Claims tying the vaccine to his death rely on temporal association and unverified speculation rather than documented medical proof.

claim: "Over the last several years, 40 percent (of) the jobs created in Texas were created for illegal aliens."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that 40% of jobs created in Texas over recent years were created for unauthorized immigrants. Estimates from government and research groups show unauthorized immigrants are a minority share of the Texas workforce and of net job gains; while they are concentrated in some industries, their overall share is far below 40%. The claim appears to conflate or misstate workforce shares without verifiable data.

claim: Abigail Spanberger and other Democrats "voted to spend public funds on their political campaigns; up to $5 million..."
rationale: There is no evidence that Rep. Abigail Spanberger voted for a measure to directly spend public taxpayer funds for her or other Democrats' political campaigns up to $5 million. Federal law and longstanding rules prohibit the use of general federal funds for partisan campaign activity, and votes by Democrats in Congress on relief or election-related bills have not authorized direct public funding of campaigns in that manner. The claim appears to mischaracterize or conflate other funding votes (e.g., election administration or public outreach) with direct campaign financing.

claim: "59 people die as pastor gives them dettol to drink in church to prevent coronavirus."
rationale: This claim is false — there are no credible reports or official records that 59 people died after a pastor gave congregants Dettol to drink to prevent coronavirus. Major news organizations and independent fact-checkers investigated similar viral posts and found no evidence to support the mass-fatality allegation; the story appears to be a rumor or a conflation with unrelated poisoning incidents. Given the scale alleged, such an event would have been documented by local authorities and national media, which it was not.

claim: "A rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months. The legislature’s failure to expand Medicaid has brought crisis to many of Missouri’s rural health care providers."
rationale: The precise statistic that “a rural hospital in Missouri closes every 8 months” cannot be corroborated by authoritative statewide data and appears to be an overgeneralization—closure rates have varied over time and I find no reliable source confirming that exact interval. The second part has factual support in that Missouri’s delay in expanding Medicaid (until voter approval in 2020) increased uncompensated care and financial strain on many rural providers and contributed to closures, but the causal statement is broad and other factors also play roles.

claim: Says President Barack Obama told a room of students, "Children, every time I clap my hands together, a child in America dies from gun violence," and then a child told him he could solve the problem by not clapping any more.
rationale: There is no credible record, transcript, or reliable news report showing President Obama ever said that line; it appears to be a fabricated anecdote circulated on social media. The phrasing is inconsistent with documented public remarks and resembles satirical/misattributed content rather than a verifiable quote.

claim: "Barnes opposed the creation of the HOPE Scholarship and campaigned against Zell Miller on the issue."
rationale: There is no well-known record that a politician surnamed 'Barnes' led opposition to creation of Georgia's HOPE Scholarship or conducted a campaign against Governor Zell Miller over it. The HOPE Scholarship is widely credited to Miller and was broadly popular; opposition was not prominently identified with any notable 'Barnes'. Without a specific individual named, the claim appears inaccurate.

claim: "They eliminated the funding for community policing."
rationale: The claim is too general and lacks a named actor, jurisdiction, or time period; there is no single, universal action by 'they' that eliminated community policing funding everywhere. Decisions about community-policing budgets have varied by city, county, and federal levels—some places proposed cuts, others reallocated or increased funding—so the blanket statement is unsupported. Without specific context it cannot be verified as true.

claim: "Bill White used D.C. connections from his job in the Clinton administration to form a company that did business in the Middle East and defaulted on a $60 million loan."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Bill White used Clinton-era D.C. connections to form a company that did business in the Middle East and subsequently defaulted on a $60 million loan. Public records and contemporary reporting about Bill White (the former Houston mayor and Clinton administration appointee) do not document such a firm or a $60 million default; the claim appears to conflate or misattribute actions. Absent specific corroborating sources, the allegation is unsubstantiated.

claim: Quotes Andy Borowitz as saying "stopping Hillary is a short-term solution. The long-term solution — and it will be more difficult — is fixing the educational system that has created so many people ignorant enough to vote for Hillary."
rationale: There is no credible record of Andy Borowitz — a New Yorker satirist whose work is archived — making this exact statement. The line reads like a social-media fabrication or misattribution; a distinctive, inflammatory quote of this sort would be traceable to an article or column but is not found in reliable archives. Given Borowitz's known satirical voice, it's more plausible the text was fabricated or taken out of context rather than actually published by him.

claim: Says 2010 was the "worst year ever for America's doctors" reimbursed by Medicare.
rationale: The claim is hyperbolic and not supported by clear evidence. While 2010 involved Medicare payment pressure (the Sustainable Growth Rate threatened large cuts that Congress repeatedly delayed), lawmakers enacted temporary fixes and no objective metric shows 2010 as definitively the "worst year ever" for physicians reimbursed by Medicare. Historical payment volatility, earlier cuts and later sequester effects make the absolute claim inaccurate without a specific measure or data.

claim: "The video doesn't show the broader picture of the firing that was going on at American troops."
rationale: The claim asserts a specific video omits broader context about firing at American troops but provides no identification of the footage or corroborating evidence. Because the exact video, time, location and independent sources are unspecified, the assertion cannot be verified; per instruction, I mark it false when uncertain. If the video were identified and independently corroborated, the assessment could change.

claim: Says two-thirds of groups targeted for IRS scrutiny were not conservative.
rationale: Major investigative reports (notably the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration and subsequent congressional reviews) found that many of the applications singled out for extra IRS scrutiny bore conservative identifiers (e.g., Tea Party) and that while some non-conservative or politically neutral groups were also reviewed, they did not compose two-thirds of the targeted set. In short, the evidence does not support the claim that two-thirds of targeted groups were not conservative.

claim: "The VA negotiates prescription drug prices. Medicare doesn't do that."
rationale: The Department of Veterans Affairs has statutory authority and routinely negotiates prices and obtains mandatory discounts for drugs it covers. By contrast, the Medicare program historically could not directly negotiate prices for most outpatient prescription drugs (private Medicare Part D plans negotiate with manufacturers), though a recent law (the Inflation Reduction Act) created a limited Medicare negotiation authority to take effect for selected drugs starting in the mid-2020s.

claim: "If we manufactured 5-million of these 2.5-meg windmills across the country, we could electrify the entire nation — the entire nation."
rationale: Five million 2.5 MW turbines equals 12.5 terawatts of nameplate capacity. Even at modest wind capacity factors (20–35%) that fleet would produce on the order of 20,000–40,000 TWh per year, far exceeding U.S. annual electricity consumption (~3,500–4,500 TWh), so in raw generation terms the claim is correct. However this ignores practical constraints like siting, transmission, storage, and manufacturing limits.

claim: Decriminalizing marijuana "will save the state anywhere from $4 (million) to $11 million dollars."
rationale: The claim gives a specific savings range without naming a state, timeframe, or which costs are counted, so it cannot be verified as universally true. Estimates of savings from decriminalization vary widely by jurisdiction and methodology (law enforcement, courts, corrections, regulatory costs, and lost/future tax revenue), so a single $4–$11 million range is not reliably factual without context.

claim: TriMet is "spending 4.2 million in fed funds to save $168K per year."
rationale: I could not verify any public TriMet item that matches the exact claim that $4.2 million in federal funds was spent to achieve only $168,000 per year in savings. The specific dollar figures and purported payback are not documented in TriMet budget reports or news coverage I can find, and such a poor annual return on a federal capital grant would typically be explained or justified in public materials. Without a clear project, timeframe, or source, the claim appears to misstate or omit key context and is not supported by available information.

claim: Says Gerald Daugherty advocated lowering the penalty for crimes like strangulation in domestic violence cases because "they just ‘throw more people into the’" jail "‘system."
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence or a reliable citation that Gerald Daugherty voiced that specific position or used the quoted phrasing about lowering penalties for strangulation in domestic violence cases because they "just throw more people into the jail system." The wording resembles general arguments made by some criminal-justice reform advocates, but without a primary source attributing this statement to Daugherty the claim is unverified and likely misattributed.

claim: "The ‘tax plan’ rolled out by @realDonaldTrump would have cut his taxes by $30 million in 2005 (the only year we have returns for)."
rationale: Multiple independent analyses of Trump’s publicly released 2005 tax return using the 2016 Trump tax-plan parameters found his federal tax liability that year would have fallen by roughly $30 million (estimates clustered around $30–33 million). Those calculations were reported by major news outlets and tax-policy analysts who applied his plan’s lower rates, pass‑through provisions and other changes to his 2005 income profile. The exact number varies with assumptions and incomplete public data.

claim: "CBO reports that delaying the Obamacare individual mandate will reduce the deficit by $35 billion over ten years."
rationale: This specific claim is incorrect as stated. The Congressional Budget Office did not report a clean $35 billion deficit reduction from delaying the Obamacare individual mandate over ten years; CBO’s published cost estimates varied by which mandate (individual vs. employer), the length of any delay, and the year, and in many scenarios delaying mandates produced different or opposite budgetary effects. The $35 billion figure has been misattributed or conflated with other estimates about different delays or provisions.

claim: "Maybe (the COVID-19 vaccine) doesn't work, and they're simply not telling you that."
rationale: This claim is false. Large randomized trials and extensive real-world evidence across many countries have shown COVID-19 vaccines substantially reduce the risk of symptomatic infection, severe disease, hospitalization, and death; while breakthrough infections occur and effectiveness can wane or vary by variant, that does not support the assertion that vaccines "don't work" or that authorities are concealing that fact.

claim: "Beginning in the early 1990s, we built barriers in 4 sectors at our southern border. Since each was built, those sectors have seen massive drops in apprehensions of people crossing the border illegally," including 90 percent to 95 percent decreases in the Tucson, Yuma, San Diego and El Paso sectors. ​
rationale: The claim mixes a true element (barriers were built starting in the early 1990s and some sectors later saw large drops in apprehensions) with an overbroad, inaccurate conclusion. While San Diego and El Paso experienced very large declines from their early-1990s highs, sector trends differ (Tucson in particular later saw higher crossings) and attributing uniform 90–95% decreases across Tucson, Yuma, San Diego and El Paso solely to barriers is misleading. Multiple studies show fencing had localized effects and often displaced crossings rather than producing identical, sustained 90–95% drops in every named sector.

claim: Georgia is the second-fastest growing state for international tourists.
rationale: The claim is unsupported as stated because it gives no timeframe or source and is ambiguous about whether it refers to the U.S. state of Georgia or the country of Georgia. Public tourism statistics and rankings do not commonly list Georgia (U.S. state) as the second-fastest-growing destination for international tourists, and without a specific period or citation the statement cannot be verified.

claim:
Says 
"With nearly 75 percent of Americans supportive of the construction of the pipeline, Schrader needs to explain to Oregon families why he voted against this needed project."
rationale: The statement that “nearly 75 percent of Americans” support construction of “the pipeline” is not substantiated; public polling on specific pipeline projects has varied widely (often around 50–60% at peaks) and depends on wording and the exact project. The claim also ambiguously attributes a vote by “Schrader” without specifying which pipeline or providing a roll-call reference. Because the assertion mixes an unverified blanket support figure with an unclear allegation about a particular vote, it cannot be treated as fact.

claim: Says a photo shows a "lithium mine for hybrid cars."
rationale: There is no image or provenance provided, so the assertion that a photo depicts a 'lithium mine for hybrid cars' cannot be corroborated. Many landscapes—salt evaporation ponds, tailings or clay pits, aquaculture ponds, and other mining sites—are frequently misidentified as lithium operations. Without geolocation, metadata or expert analysis, the claim is unverified and should be treated as false.

claim: "The nine-day deer hunt contributes more than $1.3 billion in revenue to the state of Wisconsin."
rationale: The frequently cited ~$1.3 billion figure refers to the hunt's estimated economic impact (spending and economic activity) in Wisconsin, not to direct revenue collected by the state government. Framing it as "revenue to the state" conflates total economic activity with actual state tax or fee receipts, so the claim is misleading/incorrect as stated.

claim: "The gas station where they initially attacked" Kyle Rittenhouse "is owned by his grandparents."
rationale: This claim is false: reputable news reports, court records, and available property records about the Kenosha incidents do not identify Kyle Rittenhouse's grandparents as the owners of the gas station where he was initially confronted. The assertion appears to have circulated on social media without supporting documentation or confirmation from reporting or public records.

claim: "[Hillary Clinton]'s not trusted -- virtually at all."
rationale: The claim that Hillary Clinton is "not trusted -- virtually at all" is false. Multiple public opinion polls and her electoral support (including winning the 2016 popular vote and strong backing from Democratic voters) show substantial segments of the public do trust or support her; while she has had notable distrust among some groups, it is not near-zero or universally absent. The phrase "virtually at all" overstates the level of distrust and ignores measurable pockets of trust and support.

claim: "New York, for all of their complaining, Gov. Cuomo's complaining, has only had a 1.5% decrease in revenue" due to the coronavirus pandemic.
rationale: This is false. New York’s official budget reporting and widely reported tax-collection data from 2020 show much larger coronavirus-driven declines and multibillion-dollar budget gaps — monthly income and sales tax receipts plunged in spring 2020 and the state projected double-digit percentage drops in some categories, not a 1.5% overall decline. A 1.5% figure is inconsistent with New York Division of Budget summaries and the governor’s own statements seeking large federal relief.

claim: Photo shows Ice Cube and 50 Cent wearing Donald Trump hats.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that an authentic photo shows Ice Cube and 50 Cent both wearing Donald Trump hats; versions of this image that circulated were digitally altered or miscaptioned. Trusted reporting and image checks of the original pictures show the subjects were not photographed wearing MAGA hats together, indicating the claim is false.

claim: Tim Tebow used to "kneel in prayer and the NFL complained."
rationale: Tim Tebow did frequently kneel in prayer on the field, but there is no clear evidence that the NFL as an organization formally complained or punished him for praying. Most criticisms came from commentators, opponents, or fans rather than an official league complaint or sanction.

claim: Says Sen. Chuck Schumer in 2014 "helped put together and signed a $25 billion deal to fund a border wall" and now opposes Trump's $5 billion request for a border wall "just because he's a Republican." ​
rationale: Contemporary records and reporting do not support that Sen. Schumer "helped put together and signed a $25 billion deal to fund a border wall" in 2014; bipartisan immigration and budget discussions at that time included border-security provisions but did not authorize a $25 billion wall package. Likewise, there is no reliable attribution of Schumer saying he opposes Trump’s wall funding "just because he's a Republican." The claim mixes incorrect dollar figures and a likely misquote or fabrication of Schumer’s comments.

claim: "Space X’s Starlink internet constellation has angered Russia as it was reported that the Starlink satellite constellation was used to guide the fire" on the Russian ship Moskva.
rationale: There is no credible, independently verified evidence that SpaceX’s Starlink system directly “guided” the fire or strike on the Russian ship Moskva. Russian officials and state media alleged foreign involvement and criticized Starlink, but open-source investigations and mainstream reporting indicate the Moskva was likely struck by Ukrainian missiles or suffered an internal ammunition fire, and do not show Starlink was used as a weapon guidance system.

claim: "In 2009, Mitch McConnell was the person that’s saying, 'Hey, we should get all the ethics information in before we do the hearings.' "
rationale: I find no clear public record or widely reported attribution of Mitch McConnell saying that exact line in 2009. The quote appears to be misattributed or lacking context — major coverage of 2009 confirmation hearings does not show McConnell publicly urging to ‘get all the ethics information in before we do the hearings’ in those terms. Given the absence of a verifiable source, the claim is likely false or at least unproven.

claim: Says the majority of candidates in Texas’ 25th Congressional District live outside the district.
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated; it provides no date or election cycle and I am not aware of reliable evidence showing a majority of TX-25 candidates lived outside the district for any recent race. U.S. House candidates need only reside in the same state, so some may live outside the specific district, but available historical candidate lists for TX-25 generally show many contenders who were district residents. Without a specific election and a verifiable count, the assertion that a majority live outside the district is not substantiated.

claim: "Obama administration kept illegal Mexican kids in detention camps as ‘experiment’"
rationale: While the Obama administration did detain large numbers of undocumented and unaccompanied children in border and family detention facilities and faced court challenges and criticism over conditions, there is no credible evidence that those children were kept as part of an intentional "experiment." Reports documented detention, overcrowding, and use of emergency shelters and family detention centers, but not systematic experimental use of children as research subjects.

claim: "They (Clinton and Obama) have never to my knowledge been involved in legislation nor hearings nor engagement on this issue (climate change)."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: both Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton have a well-documented record of involvement on climate change. Obama, as a Senator and especially as President, pursued climate policy through executive actions and regulation (e.g., Clean Power Plan), and led U.S. participation in major international negotiations (Copenhagen 2009, Paris 2015). Clinton, as a U.S. Senator, as Secretary of State, and as a presidential candidate, participated in hearings, sponsored or supported climate-related measures, and engaged in international climate diplomacy.

claim: "I can send every qualified person to a four-year college in their state for $150 billion."
rationale: The claim is misleading and unlikely to be true as stated. Rough demographic and cost math shows the figure is sensitive to definitions: about 3–4 million U.S. high‑school graduates per year and typical in‑state public four‑year tuition plus fees runs into the thousands per year, so fully funding four years for all qualified students (and covering room/board, administrative costs, existing enrollees, nontraditional students, etc.) would push costs well beyond $150 billion. Independent policy estimates for universal four‑year tuition programs have generally been much larger when realistic costs are included.

claim: Kelly Loeffler has a "long history of donating to abortion-on-demand Democrats."
rationale: Public campaign finance records and news reporting show Kelly Loeffler (and her husband) have overwhelmingly funded Republican candidates and conservative causes; while there are a few isolated donations to Democrats in the past, there is not a documented "long history" of routinely giving to pro‑choice Democrats. The claim therefore exaggerates and mischaracterizes her giving patterns.

claim: A poll conducted in Egypt revealed that 80 percent of Egyptians oppose receiving foreign aid from the United States.
rationale: There is no well-documented, reputable poll widely reported that finds 80% of Egyptians oppose receiving U.S. foreign aid. Major survey organizations (e.g., Pew, Arab Barometer, Gallup) that regularly poll attitudes in the region have reported varied and context-dependent views rather than a single finding at that magnitude. The claim likely misstates or misinterprets a different survey question, time period, or subgroup.

claim: "We are in the sixth year of recovery, and median income is below what it was at the start of the recovery."
rationale: The claim is not reliably true as stated. Using the commonly accepted end of the U.S. Great Recession (June 2009) the “sixth year” would fall in 2014–2015, and by that period official series such as the Census Bureau’s real (inflation‑adjusted) median household income had largely recovered toward or above 2009 levels; therefore the blanket assertion that median income was below its start‑of‑recovery level is inaccurate. The statement also omits key definitional choices (which country, which recovery dating, nominal vs real income).

claim: The state crime lab under Attorney General Josh Kaul "is testing significantly less items than former AG Brad Schimel and is still taking longer to test many categories of key items in comparison to Schimel, including DNA."
rationale: Publicly available reporting and lab throughput data indicate mixed outcomes rather than a uniform, across-the-board drop in testing or universal slower processing under AG Josh Kaul compared with Brad Schimel. Some categories saw fewer items tested or longer turnaround at certain times, but other categories showed similar or improved volume and speed; the claim overstates and generalizes these mixed trends as a broad decline that explicitly includes DNA.

claim: Says that Mitt Romney's response to the crisis in the auto industry was, "Let Detroit go bankrupt."
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly opposed a taxpayer bailout of the U.S. auto industry and repeatedly argued that automakers should go through the bankruptcy process rather than be rescued by the federal government. Media coverage and Romney’s own statements during 2008–2012 summarized and sometimes quoted his position as “let Detroit go bankrupt,” so the claim accurately reflects his stated response to the crisis.

claim: "There are communities under Sharia law right now in our country. Up in Illinois. ... There’s Sharia law, as I understand it, in Illinois, Indiana -- up there. I don't know."
rationale: There are no U.S. municipalities or communities legally governed by Sharia as a parallel legal system in Illinois, Indiana, or elsewhere. Some Muslim communities use private religious arbitration or mediation (religious councils) by mutual consent, but those operate within and under U.S. and state law and are not government-imposed Sharia jurisdictions. Claims of official "Sharia law" zones in the U.S. have been repeatedly debunked.

claim: A congressional laundry closed due to the partial government shutdown.
rationale: I could not verify that a distinct 'congressional laundry' was closed as a result of a partial government shutdown. Reporting on past U.S. shutdowns commonly notes closures of cafeterias, gift shops, and nonessential federal services, but I am not aware of credible sources confirming a dedicated congressional laundry closure. Without a specific time or facility name this claim appears unverified.

claim: "We're No. 46 out of 50 states... we're 46th in terms of percentage of deaths in nursing homes."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it omits which state and which time period or data source are meant; rankings of the share of deaths occurring in nursing homes have varied over time and by dataset (state reports vs. federal compilations). Without a specific state and date/source, the statement cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false. If a precise state and date are provided, the ranking could be checked against CMS/CDC or state health department data.

claim: Says Democratic obstruction is the reason why "many important positions in government are unfilled."
rationale: The claim misattributes sole responsibility to Democratic obstruction. Vacancies in important government positions commonly result from a mix of factors: the administration's pace of nominations and vetting, Senate procedural delays by both parties, retirements and reassignments, and resource limits. Historical evidence shows both parties have used holds and other tactics to slow confirmations, so blaming only Democrats is inaccurate without more specifics.

claim: "As Virginia lost over 65,000 jobs, (Tim) Kaine put partisan ambitions first" by serving as DNC chairman during the last year of his governorship.
rationale: The factual kernel — Kaine began serving as DNC chair in June 2009 while he was still governor (his term ended January 2010) — is correct; however the claim frames this as him putting "partisan ambitions first" because "Virginia lost over 65,000 jobs," which is a causal and evaluative assertion not established by the facts. Job losses in 2009 were driven by the national Great Recession and exact job-change totals depend on the specific period and series cited; the statement conflates coincidence with culpability and relies on an ambiguous job-loss number.

claim: Says "President Obama’s proposed oil tax would cost consumers 24 cents a gallon."
rationale: The statement is misleading. While a per-barrel fee can be converted to a per-gallon number (a $10/barrel fee equals about $0.24/gallon because 1 barrel = 42 gallons), President Obama did not put forward a single, clear 'oil tax' described only as costing consumers 24¢/gal, and whether any tax would be passed fully to consumers depends on market dynamics and the specific policy. Without naming a specific proposal and accounting for incidence and market effects, the flat 24¢/gal claim is unsupported.

claim: Says Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones told players: "Stand for the Anthem or you’re off team."
rationale: In September 2018 Jerry Jones publicly said he had told Cowboys players they must stand for the national anthem or not play for the team. In a pregame news conference he said players who would not stand should not be with the team and indicated they would be benched or asked not to play. This statement matches the claim’s substance, even if word-for-word phrasing varies.

claim: "Mike Trainor...still owes $250,000 to the state."
rationale: I cannot verify the assertion that “Mike Trainor…still owes $250,000 to the state.” My training-data knowledge up to mid-2024 does not contain reliable, corroborated reporting or public-record evidence that a person named Mike Trainor currently has a $250,000 debt to a state. The claim may conflate individuals, be outdated, or lack necessary jurisdictional and documentary support.

claim: "There's a loophole where you can sell guns without a background check … 40 percent of guns are sold that way" at gun shows and over the Internet.
rationale: There is a recognized federal ‘‘private sale’’ gap (private-party transfers are not federally required to use NICS), but the specific claim that 40% of guns are sold without background checks at gun shows or online is not supported by reliable national data. Estimates of how many transfers occur without checks vary widely by study, time period, and how ‘sale’ and ‘background check’ are defined, and many transfers at gun shows are conducted by licensed dealers who do run checks. Because of that variability and lack of a solid, current national estimate at 40%, the precise numeric claim is misleading.

claim: "Last year we lost $500 billion on trade with China."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate or misleading. In recent years the U.S. annual merchandise trade deficit with China has typically been in the low-to-mid hundreds of billions (commonly reported around $300–$420 billion depending on the year) and the overall goods-and-services deficit is smaller because the U.S. runs a services surplus with China; it is not a $500 billion 'loss.' Also calling a trade deficit a 'loss' misstates what the statistic means economically.

claim: Says the USMCA is the "biggest trade deal ever made."
rationale: The USMCA is a significant three-country North American trade agreement but it is not the "biggest trade deal ever made." Larger and broader arrangements exist — for example the EU single market and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) involve more countries and larger combined populations, trade volumes, and economic output. The term “biggest” is also ambiguous without specifying a metric (GDP, population, trade volume, etc.).

claim: John McCain "began his career in Washington as a lobbyist when he was appointed in 1976 as the Navy's liaison to the United States Senate."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate. John McCain was assigned in the mid-1970s as a uniformed Navy liaison to the U.S. Senate, a military staff role while he was still on active duty, not a civilian lobbyist job; he remained in the Navy until 1981 and only later entered electoral politics. Calling that appointment the start of a Washington career 'as a lobbyist' mischaracterizes his role and timing.

claim: Under changes being debated, state employees in Wisconsin "who earn $30,000, $40,000, $50,000 a year might have 20 percent of their income just disappear overnight."
rationale: The statement is broadly accurate in context: the 2011 Wisconsin proposals required state employees to begin paying sizable shares of pension and health insurance costs (roughly a 5.8% pension contribution plus a new employee share of health premiums), which for lower‑paid workers could equal roughly 18–20% of pay and take effect almost immediately, sharply reducing take‑home pay. It is a summary claim with some simplification — the exact percentage varies by employee’s salary and coverage.

claim: Says Barbara Buono "voted to raise her own pay 40 percent."
rationale: This statement is misleading. Contemporaneous fact-checks and legislative records show Buono did not cast a straightforward vote to raise her own salary by 40%; the cited votes and measures were more complex (involving pay formulas, judges or broader compensation provisions) and have been mischaracterized as a direct 40% pay raise for legislators. In short, the claim distorts the substance and effect of the actual votes.

claim: Says he and Mitt Romney "always said that we agree with the 2014 deadline" for leaving Afghanistan.
rationale: The claim as presented is unverifiable because it omits who "he" is and provides no source for the quoted line. Without a named speaker, date, or citation, I cannot confirm that any person publicly said "we agree with the 2014 deadline" alongside Mitt Romney. Given the missing context and lack of evidence, the statement should be treated as false until a reliable source is provided.

claim: Black cats in Vietnam are being killed and consumed as a COVID-19 cure.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Vietnamese people are widely killing and eating black cats as a cure for COVID-19. Independent fact-checkers and Vietnamese officials reported that the social-media claim was unsubstantiated; while isolated cases of animal cruelty or consumption have occurred in the region, they were not verified as a COVID-19 remedy or a widespread practice.

claim: Says that under the law, New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio "can’t open" the city’s schools.
rationale: The claim is false as an absolute statement. New York City public schools operate under mayoral control (the mayor appoints the schools chancellor) so the mayor does have authority over opening schools, although that authority is limited by state education law and state or public-health emergency orders which can restrict local action.

claim: Cher "is moving to Canada because of President Trump."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that Cher has actually relocated to Canada because of Donald Trump. She made public comments around the 2016 election saying she might move if Trump were elected, but those statements were conditional and widely reported as rhetorical; subsequent coverage does not show an actual move. Therefore the claim that she "is moving to Canada because of President Trump" is false as stated.

claim: Says Gov. Tony Evers has declared Wisconsin "permanently closed" for business.
rationale: This is false. Governor Tony Evers issued temporary COVID-19 restrictions and phased reopening plans, but he never declared Wisconsin "permanently closed" for business in any official order or press statement. The phrase appears to be a misquote or social-media misinformation rather than an actual gubernatorial declaration.

claim: "This past (legislative) session, we passed out of the Legislature a resolution requiring Congress to pass a balanced-budget amendment to the (U.S.) Constitution."
rationale: No state legislature can legally 'require' Congress to pass a constitutional amendment. Under Article V, states can request or apply for a convention or pass resolutions urging Congress to propose an amendment (including a balanced-budget amendment), but those resolutions are requests or expressions of opinion, not binding commands on Congress.

claim: Says Pope Francis "was arrested Saturday in connection with an 80-count indictment of charges including possession of child pornography, human trafficking, incest, possession of drug paraphernalia and felony fraud."
rationale: No credible evidence or reporting from major news organizations or official Vatican sources indicates Pope Francis was arrested or indicted on any charges. Claims that he was arrested in connection with an “80-count” indictment have circulated on social media and satirical websites but are fabricated. The absence of corroboration from reliable outlets and the implausibility given the office and jurisdiction make the claim false.

claim: "In her short time in the United States Senate, the senator from New York, Senator Clinton, got $500-million worth of pork barrel projects."
rationale: This claim conflates and exaggerates funding tied to Senator Hillary Clinton. Public records and contemporary fact-checking found no credible evidence that Clinton personally secured $500 million in “pork barrel” earmarks in a short time after arriving in the Senate; large numbers often cited refer to broader federal spending to New York over multiple years or to grants not solely attributable to her. The statement is therefore misleading and not supported by reliable sourcing.

claim: "Unvaccinated, you can get COVID and have over 99% chance of survival. Get vaccinated and you can still get COVID and will still have over 99% chance of survival."
rationale: The claim is an oversimplification and misleading. COVID-19 infection fatality rates vary substantially by age, comorbidities and variant—many older or medically vulnerable people have well under 99% survival if unvaccinated. Vaccination does reduce the risk of severe illness and death, often raising survival probability for high-risk people, but stating a blanket “over 99%” survival for all unvaccinated and vaccinated infections is not accurate.

claim: Says "we know" Erika Harold would "discriminate against a loving gay couple who want to adopt a child, favoring an abusive straight couple instead."
rationale: The statement asserts definitive knowledge that Erika Harold would choose an abusive straight couple over a loving gay couple for adoption. While Harold has opposed same-sex marriage and supported religious-liberty positions critics say could permit discrimination, there is no public record of her explicitly pledging to place children with abusive heterosexual parents or otherwise promising that outcome. That makes the categorical “we know” claim unsupported by available evidence.

claim: "(Brendan) Doherty wants to raise the eligibility age for Social Security benefits for anyone born after 1960, with no regard for the challenges it would cause for people working in physically demanding occupations."
rationale: There is no clear public evidence that Brendan Doherty explicitly proposed raising Social Security eligibility for everyone born after 1960, and I could not find a documented policy statement with that specific cutoff. The additional assertion that he acted 'with no regard' for workers in physically demanding jobs attributes motive and a judgment that is not supported by available public statements or policy texts.

claim: After pushing through a red flag law in the New Mexico Senate, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham "has had the firearms of her guards and household seized."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham had firearms belonging to her guards or household seized after a New Mexico Senate red‑flag measure. Red‑flag (extreme risk) orders require individual court proceedings and typically exempt on‑duty law enforcement/security arms; mainstream reporting and official statements do not corroborate the asserted seizure. The claim appears to be a misrepresentation or rumor rather than documented fact.

claim: Military spending cuts, known as the sequester, were President Barack Obama’s idea.
rationale: The automatic defense and non-defense cuts known as the 'sequester' were created by the 2011 Budget Control Act—a bipartisan compromise in the wake of the debt-ceiling fight—not originally proposed solely by President Obama. The sequester was an enforcement mechanism written into the law after negotiations among Congressional leaders and the White House; it resulted from the supercommittee failure to agree, not as a unilateral Obama initiative.

claim: The Democratic health care plan is a "government takeover of our health programs."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Democrats have proposed a range of policies: the Affordable Care Act (the major enacted Democratic plan) expanded coverage through subsidies, exchanges, and Medicaid expansion while preserving private insurers rather than nationalizing health care. Some Democrats have proposed single‑payer 'Medicare for All,' which would substantially expand government provision, but that was not the enacted Democratic plan and not universally supported within the party.

claim: "More than 90 percent of the gains have gone to the top 1 percent."
rationale: The statement is presented without a timeframe or definition of “gains,” so as a blanket claim it is false. Whether the top 1% received more than 90% of gains depends on the period and whether one measures pre‑tax income, after‑tax income, wealth, or stock-market gains; some short windows have shown such concentration but it is not universally true. The claim is misleading without specifying metric and dates.

claim: Says a change in law he carried stopped a $100 million tax increase in the Dallas school district.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify who “he” is, which law changed, or when this occurred, and there are no widely reported records directly linking a specific legislative change carried by a named individual to stopping a $100 million tax increase for Dallas ISD. School tax revenue and changes are driven by local taxing decisions, property valuations, and specific state statutory mechanisms; attributing prevention of a specific $100M increase requires clear documentary evidence which is not provided.

claim: "The higher the education level, the more likely they are to vote Democratic."
rationale: The claim is an overgeneralization. While recent U.S. election data show higher education (especially postgraduate degrees) has become more Democratic-leaning, the relationship is not strictly monotonic across all education levels, demographic groups, regions, or historical periods; for example, college-educated voters historically leaned Republican and patterns differ by race and locality. Therefore the blanket statement that higher education always increases likelihood of voting Democratic is false without qualifiers.

claim: Before the coronavirus pandemic, the United States had "the greatest economy in the history of our country."
rationale: The statement is a subjective superlative and cannot be proven as an objective fact. While the U.S. economy immediately before the COVID-19 pandemic showed strong indicators (very low unemployment and high stock markets), whether it was the “greatest in history” depends on which metrics and time periods you compare and is therefore not a verifiable factual claim. Given competing historical eras with different strengths (post‑WWII expansion, Gilded Age industrial growth, etc.), the blanket statement is misleading.

claim: "Science says that being single will kill you faster than obesity."
rationale: This statement is an overgeneralization. While some observational studies and meta-analyses report that being unmarried or socially isolated is associated with higher mortality risk, obesity is also clearly linked to increased mortality and the relative risks vary by age, sex, BMI category and other health behaviours. No consensus 'science says' that being single universally causes faster death than obesity; comparisons depend on definitions and confounding factors, and causality is not established.

claim: President Barack Obama’s latest executive order "mandates the apprehension and detention of Americans who merely show signs of ‘respiratory illness.’ "
rationale: The claim is false. There is no Obama executive order that authorizes blanket apprehension and detention of Americans merely for showing signs of a respiratory illness. Federal quarantine/isolation powers exist under statute and CDC regulations for specific communicable diseases and include legal safeguards and procedures; an executive order would not unilaterally create a broad authority to detain people based solely on symptoms.

claim: "David Dewhurst currently owes more than $1 million to vendors for services provided to his 2012 U.S. Senate campaign."
rationale: The claim is presented without a date and cannot be confirmed as true 'currently.' Contemporary news coverage and campaign finance records did show Dewhurst's 2012 Senate campaign carried unpaid vendor bills in the years after the race, but reported amounts and repayment status varied and were not consistently verified as exceeding $1 million at a given present time. Because the statement lacks a specific timeframe and up-to-date verification, it cannot be treated as a verified fact now.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was literally present when we pressed the reset button with Russia just a few months after Russia had invaded Georgia."
rationale: Russia invaded Georgia in August 2008, and Hillary Clinton, as Secretary of State, traveled to Moscow in March 2009 and participated in the well-publicized symbolic "reset" with Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, including presenting a physical 'reset' button. Thus she was literally present when the U.S. enacted that diplomatic 'reset' a few months after the invasion.

claim: "This election marks the largest Senate gains for a president's party in a first midterm election since at least President Kennedy's in 1962."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because a president’s party gained more Senate seats in a first midterm after 1962 — most notably in 2002, when Republicans under President George W. Bush netted Senate gains (larger than the single-seat gain often cited for more recent midterms). Therefore this election cannot be the largest Senate gain for a president’s party in a first midterm since 1962.

claim: "News report accidentally reveals doctors giving ‘banned’ COVID treatment to the Queen."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or reporting that a news broadcast accidentally revealed doctors giving a ‘banned’ COVID treatment to the Queen. Major fact-checkers and reputable outlets have debunked viral claims that the late Queen Elizabeth II received ivermectin or other prohibited COVID therapies, and no reliable media organization has published such an accidental revelation. Royal medical care is private, but extraordinary claims like this would require verifiable sourcing, which is absent.

claim: A recent Gallup poll found that 72 percent of Americans and 56 percent of Democrats "say the biggest threat to our nation's security is big government."
rationale: I could find no evidence of a recent Gallup poll asking Americans whether the biggest threat to the nation's security is “big government,” and the cited percentages (72% overall, 56% of Democrats) are inconsistent with typical Gallup findings and partisan patterns. Gallup’s recent threat and priority polls have emphasized issues like the economy, terrorism, China, and climate rather than “big government,” and Democrats rarely register a majority labeling big government the top security threat. Given the lack of a matching Gallup question or reported results, the claim appears to misattribute or misstate poll findings.

claim: "The cost-of-living increase in Social Security is tied to wage inflation."
rationale: This is false for U.S. Social Security: the annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) is tied to the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W), which measures changes in consumer prices, not wage inflation. Wage measures do affect how initial benefits and bend points are indexed, so people sometimes confuse wage-indexing for benefit formulas with the separate CPI-based COLA.

claim: "Reagan took the deficit from $70 billion to $175 billion. Bush 41 took it to $300 billion. Clinton got it to zero. Bush 43 took it from zero to $1.2 trillion. Obama halved it to $600 billion. Trump’s got it back to a trillion."
rationale: The statement mixes approximate annual deficit figures, rounding, and confuses surpluses/deficits in ways that make several claims inaccurate. Clinton produced multi-year federal budget surpluses (not merely “to zero”), George W. Bush-era deficits peaked around $1.2–1.4 trillion in FY2009 (timing overlaps with the Obama transition), and other numbers (Reagan/Bush41) are rough approximations rather than precise accounting. While some elements (Obama-era deficits falling to roughly $600B by mid-2010s, Trump-era deficits near $1T pre-pandemic) are directionally correct, the overall string of exact figures is incorrect.

claim: "This week the House of Representatives voted to remove the word ‘lunatic’ from federal law."
rationale: I cannot verify that the House voted this week to remove the word 'lunatic' from federal law. Up to my last reliable information (June 2024) there were proposals to modernize archaic or stigmatizing language in statutes, but I have no confirmed record of a contemporary House vote specifically deleting the word 'lunatic.' Without a specific date or current news source, the claim is unverified and likely false as stated.

claim: Ivermectin is an effective treatment for COVID-19.
rationale: High-quality randomized controlled trials and multiple systematic reviews/meta-analyses have found no convincing evidence that ivermectin provides a clinically meaningful benefit for treating or preventing COVID-19. Early studies suggesting benefit were small, methodologically flawed, or retracted, and major public-health agencies advise against using ivermectin for COVID-19 outside of properly conducted clinical trials.

claim: "Hidden in the CARES Act was an obscure $135 billion tax break for 43,000 millionaires."
rationale: The CARES Act did include business tax-relief measures (notably temporary net operating loss carrybacks and interest-deduction loosening) but it did not secretly grant a $135 billion tax cut specifically to 43,000 millionaires. Independent fact-checkers and tax analysts found the $135 billion/43,000 figure stems from flawed counting and misattribution (mixing corporate benefits and aggregate estimates) rather than a discrete, targeted break for a specific set of millionaires.

claim: The newly drawn congressional district map in Arkansas "keeps communities together."
rationale: The statement is misleading: whether a map “keeps communities together” is subjective but independent analysis and reporting around Arkansas’s latest map noted numerous splits of cities and communities of interest and described the plan as politically driven. Supporters’ claims that it preserves communities conflict with critiques and objective measures (e.g., municipal boundaries and community-of-interest groupings) showing many divisions. Given the contested evidence, the blanket claim that it keeps communities together is not supported.

claim: The debt ceiling deal will result in "the lowest level of annual domestic spending since Dwight Eisenhower was president."
rationale: The claim is not supported by the actual terms or typical measures of the debt ceiling deal. The agreement largely caps or modestly trims current discretionary spending levels rather than rolling federal domestic outlays back to the very low shares of GDP seen under Eisenhower in the 1950s; federal domestic spending as a share of GDP remains far higher today. Therefore it is incorrect to say the deal will produce the lowest annual domestic spending since Eisenhower.

claim: The EPA "wants to hire 230,000 new government regulators that will cost the taxpayer $21 billion."
rationale: This claim misstates EPA plans; the agency has not proposed hiring 230,000 new regulators for $21 billion. The figure appears to come from a misreading or conflation of regulatory-impact estimates, potential compliance-enforcement activities, or broader workforce-gap discussions rather than a concrete EPA hiring proposal; the EPA's actual workforce is on the order of tens of thousands, not hundreds of thousands.

claim: Says Obama said black people have the "worst jobs, the worst housing" and face rampant police brutality, "but when so-called black committeemen came around election time we’d all line up and vote the straight Democratic ticket, sell our souls for a Christmas turkey."
rationale: There is no credible record or transcript of Barack Obama saying this passage. The phrasing and imagery do not match his known speeches or writings (including Dreams from My Father and public addresses), and fact-check coverage and archival speech records do not show that quote.
