claim: "During his 18-year Senate career, (Russ Feingold) supported judges who voted to deny your individual Second Amendment right. … (He) promises to protect those rights, but that's not what his record shows."
rationale: The claim is vague and unsupported as stated: Russ Feingold served in the Senate from 1993–2011, a period when courts’ Second Amendment doctrine shifted (notably with DC v. Heller in 2008), but there is no clear, documented list tying Feingold’s confirmation votes to specific judges who later authored published opinions explicitly denying an individual Second Amendment right. Feingold also opposed many conservative nominees and supported various Democratic or bipartisan nominees, so a blanket statement that his record shows he backed judges who denied the individual right is misleading without named judges and cases.

claim: Says Tom Hughes supports paving over thousands of acres with over-development and sprawl.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated as presented: it alleges that 'Tom Hughes supports paving over thousands of acres with over-development and sprawl' but provides no source, quote, jurisdiction, or evidence. I cannot verify a public record attributing such a sweeping policy endorsement to a specific individual named Tom Hughes, so the assertion is not supported by available information.

claim: "For perspective, Special Session costs you $50k, every single day. That’s roughly the average teacher’s salary in NC."
rationale: The statement bundles two uncertain figures. Estimates of how much an individual “special session” costs per day depend heavily on which session and which expenses are included (staff, agency overtime, security, lost economic activity), and I cannot verify a standardized $50,000/day figure. North Carolina’s average teacher salary is generally reported in the low-to-mid $50,000s, so $50k is in the general ballpark for a single-year teacher pay but the per-day special-session cost claim is unverified and framed ambiguously.

claim: North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Thom Tillis would let insurance companies "deny coverage for pre-existing conditions."
rationale: This specific claim overstates Tillis’s publicly stated position. Thom Tillis has supported Republican repeal/waiver approaches to the Affordable Care Act that critics said could make it easier for insurers to avoid covering people with pre-existing conditions, but he has publicly denied supporting direct denials and said he would protect people with pre-existing conditions. Thus the binary statement that he “would let” insurers deny coverage is misleading without noting the legislative mechanisms he supported that critics argue could have that effect.

claim: "No one visiting Disney can get in" because of protest.
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that no one can enter Disney because of a protest. In general, protests at Disney properties have sometimes caused localized disruptions or temporary delays, but they do not typically prevent all visitors from entering; a full-park closure would be rare and widely reported. Without a specific location and time, the blanket assertion is false.

claim: "In the last five years only one out of 60 -- one out of 60 -- appropriations bills has been passed on time before the end of the fiscal year."
rationale: The claim is almost certainly false because it provides no specific five‑year window and over recent years Congress has still enacted more than a single one of the 60 regular appropriations bills on time. While continuing resolutions and omnibus packages are common, historical patterns show multiple individual appropriations enacted before Oct 1 in many years, so the extreme “1 out of 60” figure is not supported without precise dating or definition.

claim: Says the government has "gotten the TARP money back plus a profit."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While the Treasury ultimately recovered a large share of TARP cash and reported nominal receipts that slightly exceeded some measures of disbursements, independent accounting (for example CBO/GAO-style net-cost analyses) shows the program produced net costs on several measures and some TARP programs lost money. Saying the government simply “gotten the TARP money back plus a profit” ignores differing accounting methods and program-level losses.

claim: Says Donald Trump "himself has a financial stake in the French company that makes the brand-name version of hydroxychloroquine."
rationale: Sanofi, a French company, makes the brand-name hydroxychloroquine (Plaquenil), but there is no credible evidence that Donald Trump personally owned or directly held Sanofi stock. His publicly released financial disclosures and reporting by fact-checkers found no indication of a personal equity stake in Sanofi; at most any indirect exposure would be via pooled funds or mutual funds, which is not the same as a personal stake. Therefore the claim that he "himself has a financial stake" is unsupported.

claim: Dan McCready backed state legislation that raised consumers "$149 million a year in higher energy costs."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Dan McCready sponsored or voted for a specific state bill that directly imposed $149 million per year in higher energy costs on consumers. McCready was a congressional candidate and businessman rather than a state legislator, and the $149 million figure appears tied to analyses of separate state-level energy proposals that were enacted or debated by other lawmakers and later used in political ads. Without naming a specific bill or direct record of his backing, the claim is unsubstantiated and likely misleading.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton called the Trans-Pacific Partnership "the gold standard. You called it the gold standard of trade deals. You said it’s the finest deal you’ve ever seen."
rationale: Hillary Clinton publicly praised the Trans-Pacific Partnership on multiple occasions, describing it as the “gold standard” or the “gold standard of trade agreements” in speeches and interviews before she later opposed the deal. While the precise phrase “the finest deal you’ve ever seen” is a paraphrase, it reflects the same positive endorsements she made prior to changing her position in 2015–2016.

claim: Says 19,000 text messages exchanged between former FBI officials that were "purposely and illegally deleted ... would have explained (the special counsel investigation) hoax."
rationale: DOJ Office of the Inspector General and FBI records acknowledged roughly 19,000 FBI text messages from a 2016–2017 period were unavailable after device upgrades, but investigators found the loss was due to technical/upgrade issues and not purposeful, illegal deletion. The claim that those texts ‘would have explained’ that the special counsel probe was a ‘hoax’ is speculative and unsupported by evidence.

claim: Says Betsy DeVos is the "most unpopular person in our government."
rationale: The statement is a subjective superlative that cannot be definitively proven. While Betsy DeVos received very low approval ratings at times (particularly among cabinet members), there is no comprehensive, time‑bound evidence showing she was objectively the single "most unpopular" person across the entire government. Popularity rankings vary by poll, population, and date, so the absolute claim is unsupported.

claim: "Every day, 34 Americans are murdered with guns."
rationale: The statement is misleading. The figure of about 34 firearm homicides per day is an approximate average cited for certain past years, but it is not a precise daily count and annual totals vary year-to-year (recent years have been higher than that average). Without a specified time period the blanket claim "Every day, 34 Americans are murdered with guns" is inaccurate.

claim: "Ohio student suspended for staying in class during National Walkout Day"
rationale: There are no credible, verifiable news reports or official statements documenting an Ohio student being suspended specifically for remaining in class during a National Walkout Day. Numerous widely circulated social-media claims around school walkouts were later debunked or were misreports of different incidents (e.g., students disciplined for disrupting class or for participating in walkouts). Without a named student, date, or school district, the claim appears to be unsubstantiated.

claim: "Women still earn about 77 cents for every dollar a man earns for working the same job."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate because the frequently quoted '77 cents' is an older, unadjusted figure for overall median earnings and does not measure pay for "the same job." Recent U.S. data show women earn roughly 80–83 cents on the dollar on average for full-time work, and analyses that control for occupation, hours, experience and education find a much smaller unexplained gap (often near parity). Thus saying women earn about 77 cents for the same job conflates different measures and overstates the gap for like-for-like work.

claim: In the primary election, a "right-wing group spent more than $100,000,000 to support" Supreme Court Justice Rebecca Bradley.
rationale: There is no evidence that any right‑wing group spent over $100 million specifically to support Justice Rebecca Bradley in a primary. Spending at that scale for a single state supreme court primary would be unprecedented and reporting on Wisconsin judicial races recorded far smaller, though still substantial, expenditures. The claim appears to wildly overstate the actual reported spending.

claim: "Since 1990, in inflation-adjusted dollars, per-student funding of the (Florida) state university system from general revenue has dropped by about $4,000."
rationale: Multiple state and higher-education budget analyses show that inflation-adjusted state general-revenue appropriations per student for Florida’s public university system fell substantially between 1990 and the 2010s, on the order of several thousand dollars. Using standard inflation adjustments and per‑FTE (or per‑student) measures produces a decline close to $4,000, so the claim is consistent with published trend figures.

claim: The Buffalo Billion is "still breaking every job promise"
rationale: The statement is an absolute claim that the Buffalo Billion is “still breaking every job promise,” which is inaccurate. Independent audits and reporting show a mixed record: some projects and employers did not meet pledged job targets and the program was marred by corruption and underperformance, but other investments produced jobs or partially met commitments. Thus it is incorrect to say it is breaking every job promise.

claim: The Red Sox waited "87 long years" to win the World Series.
rationale: False — Boston's previous World Series win before 2004 was in 1918, so the gap between championships was 2004 − 1918 = 86 years, not 87. Saying "87 years" is off by one year unless using a nonstandard inclusive counting convention.

claim: Says Mitt Romney and Bain Capital are to blame in a woman’s premature death when they closed the plant where her husband worked.
rationale: There is no credible, documented evidence that Mitt Romney or Bain Capital directly caused a specific woman’s premature death by closing a plant where her husband worked. While Bain, as a private equity owner, has been involved in restructurings and plant closures that led to job loss, attributing a particular death to those corporate actions requires medical and legal proof that has not been substantiated in reliable reporting. Romney’s role at Bain was also limited and historically separated from many later transactions.

claim: Multnomah County has faced "11 straight years" of cuts
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and not verifiable as stated because it gives no timeframe or definition of what counts as “cuts.” County budgets and individual program appropriations fluctuate year-to-year; while some departments may have seen reductions in certain years, there is no clear public record showing 11 consecutive years of countywide cuts. Without specific dates and what was cut, the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: The New York Police Department used to have "surveillance going on in and around mosques in New York City. ... Our mayor totally cut that out."
rationale: The NYPD did conduct targeted surveillance of Muslim communities and mosques (notably via the post‑9/11 “Demographics Unit”), so the first part is accurate. However, the claim that the mayor “totally cut that out” is misleading: Mayor Bill de Blasio’s administration disbanded the Demographics Unit and agreed to reforms and a settlement, but the NYPD retained counterterrorism intelligence functions and critics say mosque‑related monitoring continued in other forms.

claim: A Georgia law has not "criminalized giving people bottles of water." It pertains to political organizations.
rationale: Georgia’s 2021 election law (SB 202) contains a provision that prohibits giving, offering, or promising “anything of value” to a voter within a fixed buffer near polling places — language that can and was interpreted to include food and bottled water. The restriction is not limited to formal political organizations and carries criminal penalties in certain circumstances, though there are narrow exemptions (for election officials or water stations authorized by poll workers).

claim: This year’s state budget and my spending proposal for Fiscal Year 2016 represent an infusion of more than $1 billion in additional money for K-12 education.
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it omits the state and speaker, and mixes “this year’s state budget” with a separate FY2016 proposal. K‑12 funding changes vary widely by state and whether proposals were enacted. Without specifying the state and the enacted budget figures (and the baseline used), the asserted “more than $1 billion” infusion cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says Ted Strickland admits his record on jobs and taxes is "mixed and spotty."
rationale: There is no clear, attributable public quote in which Ted Strickland characterizes his own record on jobs and taxes as 'mixed and spotty.' Public statements and campaign materials show he generally defended his record and highlighted job and tax initiatives; the wording appears to be an opponent's paraphrase or out-of-context summary. Without a primary-source citation of Strickland using that phrase, the claim is unverified and likely false.

claim: Exporters are using a federal loophole to "deceptively sell products made from cat and dog fur" to U.S. consumers.
rationale: There is no clear evidence of a lawful federal ‘loophole’ that authorizes exporters to deceptively sell cat or dog fur to U.S. consumers. U.S. law (the Fur Products Labeling Act and related regulations) requires species labeling and prohibits misbranding, and while enforcement gaps and isolated incidents of mislabeled fur have been reported, those are illegal mislabeling rather than an authorized loophole. The claim overstates the situation by implying a systemic, lawful pathway for deceptive sales.

claim: An app called Talking Angela asks children personal questions and takes their photo.
rationale: The widespread 2014 claim was a hoax: investigations (and the app maker Outfit7) showed Talking Angela does not secretly take photos or remotely record children. The app will display chat-like responses and can access the camera only if a user taps the camera icon and grants permission, and its responses are largely automated rather than constituting targeted data collection.

claim: Four million women have fallen into poverty in the last six years.
rationale: The claim lacks any location, timeframe start/end dates, or definition of poverty and is not supported by a known, single authoritative statistic. Poverty changes are reported by country and by specific measures (income thresholds, relative poverty, etc.), and I am not aware of a widely reported, verified figure that exactly matches "four million women have fallen into poverty in the last six years." Without a source, the statement is unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: "No one was taken into custody" for feeding the homeless.
rationale: The claim, stated without any time or location, is not verifiable and is likely false because there are well-documented cases in which volunteers distributing food to people experiencing homelessness were cited, detained, or had encounters with police. Without specific context the universal negative (“No one”) is implausible.

claim: Romney refused to pardon "a decorated soldier" returning from Iraq who had been charged with a crime involving a BB gun when he was 13.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or public-record evidence that Mitt Romney refused to pardon a “decorated soldier” returning from Iraq whose only offense was a BB-gun incident at age 13. A denial of clemency for a veteran under those circumstances would have been a notable, well-covered story, but summaries of Romney’s gubernatorial pardon actions and contemporary news do not document such a case. The claim appears unsubstantiated without a named petitioner or primary-source citations.

claim: Says extras are needed to portray aliens in a Star Wars movie being shot near Rosenberg, Texas.
rationale: There is no credible reporting or official announcement that a Lucasfilm/Disney Star Wars movie is being shot near Rosenberg, Texas, nor any verified casting notice for alien extras linked to such a production. Major Star Wars productions and casting calls are widely publicized and filmed in well-known locations; a local casting post is more likely a hoax or an unrelated indie project misrepresented as Star Wars.

claim: There are fewer wars, there are fewer people dying in wars "now than there have been in quite some time."
rationale: Long-term quantitative datasets and scholarly analyses show that large-scale interstate wars and aggregate battle deaths peaked in the mid-20th century and have been generally lower in recent decades compared with World War II-era levels. While civil conflicts have persisted and there have been regional spikes (e.g., Syria, Yemen, Ukraine), the overall global trend in war frequency and deaths per year is lower than in much of the 20th century.

claim: Senate Democrats who left the state for weeks to delay a vote on union bargaining power exercised a "Wisconsin filibuster" provided by the state’s constitution.
rationale: The senators' departure was a quorum‑busting tactic—leaving the state to deny the Senate the number required to hold a vote—not a filibuster in the traditional sense of extended debate. Wisconsin’s constitution sets quorum rules that made the tactic possible, but it does not provide a distinct "filibuster" mechanism; calling the action a "Wisconsin filibuster" is a colloquial mischaracterization.

claim: Says Paul Ryan's budget relies on the same $700 billion in savings from Medicare that Mitt Romney and other Republicans have been attacking Democrats about.
rationale: This is inaccurate as stated. The roughly $700–$716 billion figure Republicans attacked refers to Medicare provider-payment reductions embodied in the Affordable Care Act and some Democratic budgets; Paul Ryan’s budget relied on a different set of Medicare changes (converting Medicare to a premium‑support/voucher model and other structural cuts) rather than simply adopting the ACA’s $700B provider‑payment savings as the core of its plan. Thus Ryan’s proposals are not the “same $700 billion” Republican critics were pointing to.

claim: "Amazon accepts Dogecoin."
rationale: This is false. Amazon has not publicly announced that it directly accepts Dogecoin (or other major cryptocurrencies) as a payment method at checkout. While customers can sometimes buy Amazon gift cards from third‑party services that accept crypto and then use those gift cards on Amazon, that is an indirect workaround rather than official Dogecoin acceptance by Amazon.

claim: "U.S. comedian Kevin Hart in critical condition after gory car crash."
rationale: This claim is false. The well‑known incident involving Kevin Hart (September 2019) left him with serious back injuries and hospitalized, but contemporary reputable news reports indicated he was conscious and treated for fractures rather than being in 'critical condition' and the crash was not widely described as 'gory.' There are no credible, recent reports substantiating the claim that he is currently in critical condition after such a crash.

claim: Says Rep. Justin Amash "votes more with the Democrats than with the Republicans."
rationale: As a blanket statement this is misleading. While Justin Amash did vote with House Democrats more often than Republicans in some limited periods after he left the GOP in 2019, for most of his tenure as a Republican (2011–2019) he voted with Republicans far more often; overall alignment depends on the specific time period and vote set. Without a time frame the claim is inaccurate.

claim: "We admit more than 100,000 lifetime migrants from the Middle East each year."
rationale: The claim is false as stated because reasonable reading of “we” (e.g., the United States) and “lifetime migrants” (permanent immigrants/green‑card holders or refugees resettled) yields far fewer than 100,000 people from Middle Eastern countries admitted in a typical year. Annual lawful permanent resident admissions overall are roughly on the order of hundreds of thousands to about a million, but immigrants from Middle Eastern countries constitute only a small fraction (typically tens of thousands or less), and refugee resettlement from the region has also been well under 100,000 in recent years.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton sold 20 percent of America’s uranium to Russia and then "the Russian government gave $145 million to the Clinton Foundation." Former FBI Director and special counsel Robert Mueller "delivered it."
rationale: This mixes several false or misleading assertions. The 2010 Uranium One transaction involved a Canadian firm with U.S. assets and was reviewed and approved by the multi-agency CFIUS panel (not a unilateral sale by Hillary Clinton), and the “20% of America’s uranium” claim misstates the scope (it referenced production capacity, not ownership of all U.S. uranium). There is no credible evidence that the Russian government gave $145 million to the Clinton Foundation as a quid pro quo, and Robert Mueller had no role in “delivering” any such funds or in approving the deal.

claim: "Thanks in part to our all-of-the-above strategy for American energy," the United States generates "more natural gas than anybody."
rationale: The United States has been the world’s largest natural gas producer in recent years, a rise driven largely by shale gas and hydraulic fracturing that expanded U.S. output. Saying the U.S. produces "more natural gas than anybody" is accurate in the contemporary context and is plausibly linked to an "all-of-the-above" energy approach that included expanding domestic gas production.

claim: Says his administration has made "progress" on border enforcement by "putting more boots on the southern border than at any time in our history and reducing illegal crossings to their lowest levels in 40 years."
rationale: The claim bundles two factual assertions that do not hold up. Public CBP/Border Patrol staffing and historical deployments have varied and are not clearly the highest “at any time in our history,” and encounter statistics show recent years fluctuate (with a pandemic-related dip in 2020) but do not establish that illegal crossings are at their lowest level in 40 years. These statements therefore overstate and mischaracterize the available data.

claim: "It's just outrageous that under President Bush, the National Institutes of Health have been basically decreased in funding."
rationale: The claim that NIH funding was "basically decreased" under President Bush is misleading. In nominal-dollar terms the NIH budget did not fall during George W. Bush’s presidency (it rose in the early years and then largely plateaued), but when adjusted for inflation the agency’s purchasing power declined over much of his term. Thus the statement is inaccurate unless one explicitly means inflation‑adjusted funding.

claim: "White people control almost 90 percent of the nation's wealth."
rationale: This claim is an exaggeration. In the United States, the share of aggregate household wealth held by non‑Hispanic white households is substantially below 90% — recent Federal Reserve and academic data place it roughly around the low 70s percent (varies by year and definition). While whites hold a clear majority of wealth, it is not “almost 90%.”

claim: Says "Rob Portman voted for the bipartisan bill to affirm climate change is real, humans significantly contribute to it and it needs to be addressed."
rationale: I find no clear roll-call or authoritative record showing Rob Portman voted for a specific bipartisan bill that explicitly states the three clauses as quoted (that climate change is real, humans significantly contribute, and it needs to be addressed). Portman has at times acknowledged human-driven climate change and supported some related measures, but there is no unambiguous bipartisan bill vote matching the claim's precise formulation.

claim: After J.D. Hayworth "was voted out of Congress, he became a registered lobbyist" who was "paid thousands by a Florida corporation to lobby the very committee he used to serve on."
rationale: I could not find corroborating public-record evidence that J.D. Hayworth registered as a lobbyist after leaving Congress and was paid by a Florida corporation to lobby the committee he once served on. Public lobbying registrations and disclosures are searchable and widely reported for former members doing such work; Hayworth’s known post‑Congress activities were media work and later political campaigns rather than documented registered lobbying for a Florida firm. Without a specific company, dates, or disclosure records, the claim is unverified and likely false as stated.

claim: A video shows a nurse pretending to vaccinate actor Anthony Hopkins before squirting fluid in the syringe on the floor.
rationale: There is no corroborating evidence from reputable news or fact‑checking organizations that a nurse pretended to vaccinate Sir Anthony Hopkins and then squirted fluid onto the floor. Viral clips like this are often misattributed, edited, or taken out of context, and without independent verification the claim is unsupported.

claim: Says "I’ve been proven right" about "Hillary Clinton's radical call for open borders, meaning anyone in the world can enter the United States without any limit at all."
rationale: Hillary Clinton has not called for unrestricted “open borders” allowing anyone in the world to enter the U.S. without limit. Her public policy positions and proposals have supported comprehensive immigration reform, pathways to citizenship for certain immigrants, and measures for border security and legal immigration channels — not unlimited, unrestricted entry. Claims describing her as advocating no limits misrepresent her documented positions.

claim: Says he has "more executive experience than the vice president."
rationale: The claim as written is unverified because it does not identify who 'he' or which vice president is being compared. Whether one person has "more executive experience" depends on specific offices held and durations (e.g., governor, CEO, cabinet roles, versus time served as vice president), information that is not provided. Without those specifics the assertion cannot be substantiated and should be treated as false.

claim: Republican state Sens. Paul Newton and Warren Daniel "refused to even give testimony" in North Carolina’s latest redistricting case.
rationale: The claim is inaccurate: Warren Daniel is a West Virginia state senator, not a North Carolina senator, so the statement misidentifies at least one individual. I am not aware of credible reporting showing both Paul Newton and a North Carolina "Warren Daniel" jointly refusing to testify in North Carolina redistricting litigation; such disputes over subpoenas and legislative privilege have occurred, but this specific claim appears incorrect or confused.

claim: Says state schools superintendent candidate Don Pridemore "voted for the largest cuts to public education in our state history" and for "$2.3 billion in tax breaks for corporations and the wealthy."
rationale: The claim mixes a politically charged superlative and a dollar figure that are not clearly supported. It is true Pridemore, as a Republican state legislator, voted for GOP budgets that reduced K–12 funding and enacted tax cuts, but calling those the “largest cuts in our state history” is subjective and not verifiable as an uncontested fact, and the stated $2.3 billion figure and attribution specifically to “corporations and the wealthy” is ambiguous and not precisely attributable to a single vote by Pridemore. Because the wording overstates and lacks necessary context, the claim as presented is misleading.

claim: "We must deal with the here and now and assure affordable fuel for America by increasing domestic production."
rationale: The statement presents a policy opinion as a guaranteed outcome — that increasing domestic production will assuredly make fuel affordable. In reality, retail fuel prices are set by global crude prices, refining and distribution capacity, taxes, and demand; domestic production can influence but does not unilaterally determine affordability. Therefore the claim that increased domestic production will assure affordable fuel is not reliably true.

claim: Says Mike Enzi is "getting about 84 percent of his campaign funds from Washington-based PACs. That's more than any senator of either party."
rationale: The claim gives a very specific and extraordinary percentage (about 84%) and a superlative (more than any senator) but there is no clear corroborating FEC/OpenSecrets data indicating Enzi received that share from Washington-based PACs in any single election cycle. Campaign-finance totals are reported by cycle and by PAC address, and while Enzi has received PAC funding, an 84% share from DC-based PACs would be unusually large and would have been widely noted; absent a cited year or data source the claim appears inaccurate or misleading. The statement also conflates different possible definitions of “Washington-based PACs,” which can distort percentages.

claim: Says "your Legislative Assembly was within one vote of enacting each of those bills into Oregon law."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it references unspecified “those bills” and a particular Legislative Assembly without giving bill names or a session. Legislative passage margins are public and vary by bill; it is unlikely that every referenced bill would have failed or passed by only a single vote across all required votes without specific evidence. Without the exact bills and vote tallies, the assertion that each was within one vote of enactment cannot be confirmed and is therefore treated as false.

claim: "All" University of Texas "student-athletes get an iPad."
rationale: This claim is incorrect as a blanket statement. Athletic departments commonly provide tablets or other tech to many teams for coaching and film study, but distribution varies by sport, role, scholarship status, and over time; there is no evidence that every University of Texas student-athlete is universally issued an iPad. Policies and equipment allocations differ by program and can be loans rather than personal property.

claim: "Almost 1 million children ... have no health insurance in this state."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it fails to name which state or specify a time period; without that context it cannot be confirmed. Generally, most U.S. states do not have nearly one million uninsured children, and child uninsured counts vary substantially by state and over time, so the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: "An April study found that about 70 percent of ads in this election cycle have been negative [due to SuperPACs], up from only 9 percent through the same period in 2008."
rationale: An April 2012 study (Wesleyan Media Project) did report that roughly 70% of ads in the early 2012 cycle were negative, up from about 9% through the same point in 2008. The study also documented that independent groups/Super PACs were responsible for a large share of the negative advertising, though saying they were the sole cause is an oversimplification.

claim: "I certainly supported Barack Obama and Joe Biden. ... I was there both times for them."
rationale: There is insufficient publicly verifiable information in the claim to confirm that the unnamed speaker supported both Barack Obama and Joe Biden and was physically or politically 'there both times.' Without a named individual or documentary evidence (endorsements, voting records, attendance at events), the claim cannot be substantiated. Because verification is not possible from the provided text, I rate the claim as unsupported.

claim: "In sanctuary cities, local officials order police to release dangerous criminal aliens to prey upon the public instead of handing them over to ICE to be safely removed."
rationale: The claim is a broad, value-laden generalization that misstates how sanctuary policies operate. Sanctuary jurisdictions generally limit local cooperation with civil immigration enforcement (for example, declining to honor ICE detainers without a warrant) but do not have a uniform policy of instructing police to release violent criminals to 'prey upon the public'; many jurisdictions still hold or transfer people charged with serious crimes, and ICE detainers are requests rather than binding orders. While isolated cases exist where non-cooperation coincided with later crimes, that does not prove a systemic, intentional directive to release dangerous offenders.

claim: "Part of the increase in the cost (of higher education) has been because state support has dropped. We now spend, under Governor Walker, more on corrections than we do on higher education."
rationale: The first part — that reduced state support contributed to rising higher-education costs — is correct and a documented driver of tuition increases. However, the specific claim that under Governor Walker the state spent more on corrections than on higher education is not supported by statewide budget totals: higher-education appropriations (when counting the University System and related higher-ed funding) remained larger than corrections spending in the relevant budgets. Therefore the combined claim is false.

claim: Says Georgia’s secretary of state won’t let the people recounting ballots check the signatures for fraud.
rationale: The statement is misleading. Georgia law requires signature matching be done by election officials when absentee ballots are processed, and recount procedures focus on counting votes rather than re-checking voter signatures; the secretary of state permitted accredited observers but did not authorize private individuals to independently handle or inspect ballots or signature envelopes in ways that would break chain-of-custody or voter privacy. Thus it is incorrect to say the secretary simply ‘won’t let’ people recounting ballots check signatures as if signature rechecks are a standard part of recounts and open to arbitrary individuals.

claim: "The Clintons' foundation took millions from foreign governments" including United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia.
rationale: Contemporaneous tax filings and investigative reporting show the Clinton Foundation accepted donations from foreign governments and government-linked entities, and several of those donations from sources tied to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates totaled millions of dollars. While reporting distinguishes between direct government treasuries and state-linked charities or wealthy individuals, the core claim that the foundation received millions from foreign-government-associated sources including Saudi Arabia and the UAE is supported by available records.

claim: "Malia Obama just got arrested buying cocaine"
rationale: There are no credible reports from major news organizations or law enforcement that Malia Obama was arrested for buying cocaine. Claims like this have circulated on social media but have not been substantiated by verified sources, which is what would be expected for a high‑profile arrest. Given the lack of reliable confirmation, the claim is false as presented.

claim: "We were promised (the stimulus) would provide 'green jobs' for Americans, but 80% of the $2 billion they spent on alternative energy went to purchase wind turbines built in China!"
rationale: The claim mixes incorrect totals and an unsupported percentage. The 2009 stimulus (ARRA) funded tens of billions for clean energy overall, not a single $2 billion pot that was 80% spent on Chinese-made turbines, and independent fact-checking found no evidence that 80% of stimulus clean-energy spending bought wind turbines built in China. While some stimulus-funded projects used imported components, the available records show a diverse mix of domestic and foreign suppliers rather than the sweeping 80% figure alleged.

claim: "Every day in the United States, we are losing 15 factories."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that the U.S. is continuously losing 15 factories every single day. Official data on manufacturing establishments and plant openings/closings (from sources such as the Census Bureau and BLS) show variable year-to-year net changes that are much smaller than a sustained loss of ~5,475 plants per year and depend on definitions and time periods. The claim appears to be a rounded, context-free political shorthand rather than a verified current statistic.

claim: Florida has "more concealed weapons permits than any other state."
rationale: The claim is not reliably true as stated. While Florida has historically been among the states with a very large number of concealed-carry licenses, other large states (notably Texas) have had comparable or higher totals at different times and recent policy changes (permitless carry in some states) make direct comparisons time-dependent. Without a specific date or definition of the metric, the absolute claim that Florida has more permits than any other state is unsupported.

claim: David Beckham’s proposed soccer stadium at Miami’s Port "threatens the 207,000 jobs and $27 billion economic impact tied to the cargo and cruise industries."
rationale: The numbers cited (about 207,000 jobs and $27 billion) reflect the broad, county‑wide economic contribution of Miami's cargo and cruise sectors, not the portion that would be directly displaced by a single stadium parcel. Beckham's proposed stadium occupied a relatively small terminal area and port/authority analyses and reporting indicated localized impacts could be managed, not elimination of the entire sector's jobs or economic output.

claim: "Six justices" on the U.S. Supreme Court have been "confirmed in presidential election years since 1912."
rationale: I cannot confirm the claim that exactly six justices were confirmed in presidential election years since 1912. Well-known confirmations in election years include Louis Brandeis (1916), Benjamin Cardozo (1932), Anthony Kennedy (1988) and Amy Coney Barrett (2020), but I do not find a reliable memory of a total of six without consulting a full historical confirmation list. Because the statement gives a precise count and the phrasing “since 1912” is ambiguous (inclusive/exclusive), the claim should be treated as unverified and likely inaccurate.

claim: The FBI lost Hunter Biden’s laptop.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that the FBI “lost” Hunter Biden’s laptop. Reporting and statements indicate the FBI seized the device (or forensic images of it) from the Delaware repair shop in 2019 and retained evidence as part of investigations; disputes have focused on chain-of-custody and multiple copies, not a confirmed loss of the laptop by the FBI.

claim: "I'm probably one of the four or five best-known Americans in the world."
rationale: The statement is a subjective, self-assessed claim about global fame that cannot be objectively verified. Global recognition varies by time, region, and demographic, and there are multiple Americans (e.g., recent presidents, global entertainers and athletes) who are plausibly better known worldwide, so the claim cannot be reliably established as fact.

claim: "Nearly half of African-American children under the age of 6 are living in abject poverty."
rationale: This claim is not supported by U.S. poverty data. Recent Census Bureau figures show the overall poverty rate for Black children is well below 50%, and measures of “deep” or extreme poverty (e.g., incomes below 50% of the poverty threshold) affect a much smaller share, typically in the single- to low-double digits. Therefore saying ‘nearly half’ of African‑American children under 6 live in abject poverty is inaccurate nationally.

claim: Says that PolitiFact Ohio confirms that Betty Sutton "maxed out federal debt"
rationale: There is no known PolitiFact Ohio fact-check that literally 'confirms' Betty Sutton 'maxed out federal debt.' PolitiFact typically evaluates specific votes or claims and would rate such a statement with context; the phrasing is hyperbolic and no article endorses that exact assertion. Without a cited PolitiFact item, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "There's no court session between now and the end of this election."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement with no jurisdiction or timeframe; such blanket assertions are implausible. Courts at multiple levels routinely hold scheduled and emergency hearings, and election-related litigation frequently produces expedited sessions or temporary injunctive proceedings before an election concludes.

claim: "There are hit squads being trained all over this country" to violently oppose a second term for President Donald Trump.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or authoritative reporting that 'hit squads' are being trained all over the United States to violently oppose a second Trump term. Public reporting and law-enforcement statements have documented isolated plots and threats from extremist actors, but not a coordinated, nationwide program of trained 'hit squads' as described in the claim.

claim: I spent only $36.29 on my campaign for governor.
rationale: The claim is implausible and unsupported given typical campaign activity and legal reporting requirements. Running for governor generally incurs substantial expenses (filing fees, travel, staff, communications) far exceeding $36.29, and campaign finance reports are required and publicly filed, yet no credible example of a bona fide gubernatorial campaign reporting only $36.29 is known. Without specific candidate, state, and filing evidence, the claim is not credible.

claim: "Pot today is not the weed baby boomers were smoking."
rationale: Contemporary cannabis products are materially different from the average marijuana commonly consumed by baby boomers: average THC concentrations have risen substantially over decades and modern markets produce specially bred high-THC strains, concentrates (oils, waxes, shatter) and engineered hybrids that were uncommon or unavailable in the 1960s–70s. While there is variation and some low-potency flower still exists, the overall profile and potency of widely used products today are meaningfully different.

claim: "Nearly 2/3 of rural Missourians don’t have access to broadband. That needs to change."
rationale: The claim overstates the gap. Authoritative availability estimates (FCC and state broadband maps and reporting) do not show that roughly two-thirds of rural Missourians lack access to basic fixed broadband; published figures are substantially lower and vary by the speed threshold and date. The statement likely mixes definitions or outdated data, producing an exaggerated share.

claim: Says the Georgia Dome would need up to $350 million in work over the next five to seven years.
rationale: Contemporaneous public reports and stadium assessments during the debate over replacing the Georgia Dome estimated several hundred million dollars in deferred maintenance and upgrades; figures cited in news coverage frequently peaked around $300–$350 million projected over a multi‑year period (often framed as five to seven years). That estimate was used by officials and stakeholders arguing for a new stadium rather than renovating the Dome.

claim: "I was totally against the war in Iraq, saying for many years that it would destabilize the Middle East."
rationale: The statement is an unverified first‑person claim of long-standing opposition to the Iraq War but provides no speaker or timeline, so it cannot be corroborated as presented. Verifying such a claim requires checking that specific individual's contemporaneous public statements, votes, or records showing they repeatedly warned the war would destabilize the Middle East.

claim: Says the Obama administration purged "training courses and information about Islamism, jihad, Sharia, and the Muslim Brotherhood."
rationale: This claim overstates and generalizes limited, documented actions. Inspector‑General and news reports show that during the Obama years some individual training slides and materials at agencies such as DHS were reviewed and in some cases removed or revised because they were inaccurate or could stigmatize Muslims; however there is no evidence of an administration‑wide, systematic purge of all training or information about Islamism, jihad, Sharia, and the Muslim Brotherhood. Many federal counter‑extremism programs continued to study Islamist extremism and related topics.

claim: "Some of the wealthiest Americans are African-American now."
rationale: Current wealth rankings and reporting show multiple African-American individuals among the wealthiest Americans. High-net-worth African-Americans such as Oprah Winfrey, Michael Jordan, Robert F. Smith, David Steward and Jay-Z have appeared on Forbes and other lists as billionaires or multi-hundred-millionaires, so the statement is true.

claim: Every child in Colorado who has been given medical marijuana for treatment for seizures has had diminished seizure activity.
rationale: The claim is an absolute universal statement that is not supported by medical evidence. Clinical trials and observational data show that cannabidiol-containing medicines can reduce seizures in some children with specific epilepsy syndromes, but not all children given medical marijuana experience diminished seizure activity and some have no benefit or adverse effects. Variability in formulations, doses, seizure types, and individual response contradicts the claim that every treated child improves.

claim: It’s "typical" for a presidential candidate to release 10 or 11 years of tax returns.
rationale: There is no standard or legal requirement that presidential candidates release 10–11 years of tax returns, and historical practice has varied widely. While some recent candidates have voluntarily released a decade or more, others released fewer years or none at all, so claiming that 10–11 years is "typical" overstates common practice.

claim: Gwinnett County government has made "significant cutbacks in staffing."
rationale: I cannot find authoritative, corroborated evidence that Gwinnett County government implemented widespread, large-scale staffing cuts described as "significant cutbacks." Public records and typical reporting that would note major layoffs or furloughs are not reflected in my training data up to mid‑2024; isolated hiring slowdowns or departmental adjustments are plausible but do not equal countywide significant cuts. Without a specific timeframe or source, the blanket claim is not supported.

claim: "Total deaths from COVID MUCH LOWER than reported."
rationale: The claim is false because multiple independent analyses (including excess-mortality studies and WHO assessments) find that global COVID-related deaths are generally higher than the officially reported counts, not much lower. While some individual jurisdictions may have misattribution or reporting quirks that could overstate deaths locally, the dominant pattern worldwide has been undercounting due to limited testing, incomplete vital registration, and reporting delays.

claim: Says the Trump administration’s new policy for legal immigrants on welfare "has been around for a while. This is not a new thing that the president is trying to implement here, that the United States has been this way."
rationale: The general ‘public charge’ doctrine (inadmissibility for likely reliance on government support) has long existed, but the Trump administration’s 2019–2020 policy materially broadened that test to include many non‑cash benefits (Medicaid, SNAP, housing) and stricter criteria. That expansion was a significant change from prior practice, so saying the specific policy “has been around for a while” is misleading.

claim: "When did the decline of coal start? It started when natural gas took off … that started to begin in (President George W.) Bush’s administration."
rationale: The major U.S. decline in coal-fired generation and coal production began in the late 2000s, coinciding with the rise of inexpensive shale natural gas produced by fracking that ramped up during the George W. Bush administration. Falling natural gas prices and fuel-switching by power plants were primary drivers of coal’s decline, though other factors also contributed later on.

claim: Small businesses "create 70 percent of the jobs in America."
rationale: The claim is false as stated. Small businesses do not account for 70% of all jobs in the U.S.; they employ roughly half of the private-sector workforce (around 45–50%). The 70% figure is sometimes cited for the share of net new jobs created by small firms over certain periods, so the claim conflates total jobs with historical job-creation percentages and lacks a time frame.

claim: "As a city, we currently use about 4 percent less electricity today than we used in 1989."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it names no city and gives no date for “currently.” Aggregate electricity use comparisons require specific location and a defined present year; without those the precise figure (about 4% less than 1989) cannot be confirmed. Additionally, general knowledge shows city electricity use trends vary widely over time due to population, economic activity, efficiency gains, and electrification, so a blanket assertion is unlikely to be universally true.

claim: Says the Ohio Consumers’ Council office employs 74 lawyers and that the funding them is wasteful duplication.
rationale: The factual portion of the claim—that the Ohio Consumers' Counsel (Consumers’ Counsel) office employs 74 lawyers—is incorrect. The Consumers’ Counsel is a relatively small state consumer-advocacy office with far fewer attorneys (its legal staff is in the low dozens, well below 74). The characterization that funding them is “wasteful duplication” is an opinion and not a verifiable fact.

claim: "Snitker has been virtually ignored by the major media."
rationale: The claim is false as stated because Brian Snitker (Braves manager) has received substantial national media coverage — profiles, interviews, and reporting around his 2018 NL Manager of the Year award and leading the Braves to postseason success including the 2021 World Series. Major sports outlets and general national media have regularly covered his career and decisions, so saying he has been “virtually ignored” is not accurate. If the claim intended a specific short timeframe or a different person named Snitker, the statement could be more ambiguous.

claim: A new Republican litmus test "would have resulted in (the GOP) kicking out Ronald Reagan."
rationale: This is a speculative counterfactual without evidence. Ronald Reagan was broadly popular and influential within the GOP during and after his presidency, and there is no record that applying an undefined “new Republican litmus test” retroactively would have produced party expulsion of Reagan. The outcome depends entirely on what the test was and how party institutions would have enforced it, so the claim is unprovable and misleading.

claim: Annual precipitation "has increased in Rhode Island by over 12 inches in the last century."
rationale: Federal climate summaries and state analyses show that Rhode Island’s annual precipitation has increased over the 20th century, but the magnitude reported in authoritative datasets is far smaller than 12 inches (typically a few inches to under ten inches). Therefore the specific claim that precipitation “has increased in Rhode Island by over 12 inches in the last century” is not supported by the major federal datasets and summaries.

claim: John McCain and George W. Bush want to spend "a trillion dollars in Iraq over the next 10 years."
rationale: This specific quoted claim is misleading. While independent analysts (CBO, academic studies) estimated that the Iraq war could cost on the order of a trillion dollars or more over a decade, neither George W. Bush nor John McCain publicly framed a formal policy pledge that they "want to spend a trillion dollars in Iraq over the next 10 years" as an explicit stated goal. Both supported continued funding for operations and reconstruction, but the "trillion dollars" figure was an analyst projection, not a direct joint policy statement by the two men.

claim: "$360 million of our tax dollars went straight to ... the Taliban."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that $360 million of U.S. tax dollars was paid directly to the Taliban. Reporting around Afghanistan finances after the 2021 collapse shows frozen Afghan central‑bank reserves and limited humanitarian transfers or settlements that critics have sometimes conflated with direct payments to the Taliban, but authoritative sources do not document a straight $360M direct payment to the Taliban.

claim: Says Steve Spinnett has court judgments against him for trespass and harassment.
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence or public records confirming that a person named Steve Spinnett has court judgments for trespass and harassment. Without specific jurisdiction, dates, or docket numbers, the claim is unsubstantiated and cannot be confirmed, so I treat it as false pending corroborating court documents or reliable reporting.

claim: Says the State Department has "had half a year" to respond to a Benghazi document request, yet "I have not gotten a single, solitary scrap of paper."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented and likely false: it omits the speaker, date, and which specific document request is meant, while publicly known record shows multiple rounds of Benghazi-related document releases and congressional productions over months and years. Without a precise request and timeline, the blanket claim that the State Department had 'half a year' to respond yet produced 'not a single, solitary scrap of paper' is unsupported.

claim: In 2008, "only 54 percent of Latinos in Texas were registered to vote and only 35 percent actually turned out."
rationale: The stated numbers are inconsistent with post‑2008 analyses: nationwide Hispanic turnout in 2008 was substantially higher than 35% and state analyses do not support that only 54% of Texas Latinos were registered. Major sources (U.S. Census/CPS and Pew) reported Hispanic registration and turnout rates well above the low figure attributed here, and Texas figures are not consistent with such a low turnout share.

claim: Says Charlie Crist "stood there, over 3 African-American prisoners in chains, on their knees, on the side of the road. Saying that it was a great sight. Saying we needed to bring it to Florida. And you did this — whether you know or not — on the eve of Juneteenth, the day the African-American community celebrates the end of slavery."
rationale: I could not find credible, contemporaneous evidence or reputable news reporting that Charlie Crist ever stood over three African‑American prisoners in chains, praised the sight, and said it should be brought to Florida on the eve of Juneteenth. Such a dramatic incident would have been documented and widely reported; the claim appears to be an unverified political attack or misattribution. Without a verifiable source, the assertion should be treated as false.

claim: "Dems have removed any mention of ‘God’ from their Platform."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate as stated. Democratic Party platforms historically and in recent cycles have included references to faith or God in various planks, and there has been no single, party-wide action to expunge every mention of the word “God” from their official platform. Without a specific year or draft, the absolute claim that Democrats “have removed any mention of ‘God’” is unsupported.

claim: Tapping the Strategic Petroleum Reserve would immediately lower gasoline prices
rationale: This is false as stated: the Strategic Petroleum Reserve stores crude oil, not finished gasoline, and released crude must be transported and refined before it affects pump prices. While an SPR drawdown or its announcement can quickly influence futures and wholesale crude prices, retail gasoline prices typically adjust with a delay and are also shaped by refining capacity, local taxes, and distribution constraints, so they would not "immediately" fall across the board.

claim: Marco Rubio's "income skyrocketed while his power increased."
rationale: The statement is vague and overstates the evidence: public financial disclosures for Senator Marco Rubio show some years with higher income (e.g., book advances, royalties and investment income) but do not demonstrate a clear, sustained "skyrocketing" rise directly correlated with an increase in his political power. Without a specified timeframe or definition of "power," the claim is unsubstantiated.

claim: "Fluoride in the water, that was originally done by the Nazis!"
rationale: This claim is false. Municipal water fluoridation originated from 1930s–1940s dental research in the United States (notably H. Trendley Dean's work and the 1945 Grand Rapids pilot) as a public‑health measure to reduce cavities. There is no credible historical evidence that the Nazis invented or implemented community water fluoridation; references tying fluoridation to Nazis are conspiracy theories conflating unrelated Nazi chemical abuses with an independent public‑health program.

claim: "Make no mistake -- Sherrod Brown is one of the main D.C. politicians responsible for Ohio jobs moving to China."
rationale: This is false. Sherrod Brown has a long public record as a pro-labor, anti‑outsourcing advocate who opposed many trade liberalization measures and has criticized companies that move jobs overseas, so he is not plausibly a primary D.C. actor responsible for Ohio jobs shifting to China. Job losses to China resulted from a complex mix of corporate decisions, trade policies across administrations, globalization, and technological change rather than the actions of a single senator.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Faso "voted for an age tax on seniors."
rationale: This is FACT. In May 2017 Rep. John Faso voted for the American Health Care Act (AHCA), which included a provision raising the allowable age-rating to 5:1 and was widely described by critics as an "age tax" because it would allow insurers to charge older adults substantially higher premiums. The phrase is political shorthand for that AHCA provision and Faso's recorded yes vote on the bill.

claim: Oregon Health Plan rations "covered procedures under certain circumstances"
rationale: The Oregon Health Plan has long used prioritized/clinical coverage criteria and prior-authorization rules to determine which services it will pay for, and in practice this means some procedures are limited or denied under specified circumstances. Historically the state created a ranked list of services to allocate limited Medicaid resources, and current OHP policies still set clinical conditions and restrictions that can prevent coverage for certain procedures. This fits common usages of the term “ration” as restricting access based on policy-driven criteria.

claim: The coronavirus "was constructed in the Wuhan Institute of Virology."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that SARS-CoV-2 was deliberately constructed at the Wuhan Institute of Virology. Genomic analyses by multiple independent research groups show patterns consistent with natural evolution and lack telltale signatures of laboratory genetic engineering, and international reviews and intelligence assessments have not produced proof that the virus was engineered or intentionally released. Claims that it was 'constructed' conflate unproven lab-leak hypotheses with evidence of intentional design, which is not supported by available data.

claim: Says the Obama administration "didn't lock people up in cages."
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and photographs from the 2014 immigration surge show Border Patrol and CBP facilities using chain-link enclosures to hold migrants, including children, and the Obama administration operated family detention centers (e.g., Karnes, Dilley, Artesia) that detained families. So the categorical claim that the Obama administration “didn’t lock people up in cages” is false — such enclosures and family detention existed, though policies and scale differed from the later 2018 surge.

claim: Says Trump ties are made "in China, not Colorado. Trump suits in Mexico, not Michigan. Trump furniture in Turkey, not Ohio. Trump picture frames in India, not Wisconsin."
rationale: Multiple independent news reports and product label checks found that a range of Trump-branded merchandise was manufactured overseas rather than in the U.S.; for example, many Trump ties were produced in China, some suits and apparel were made in Mexico, Trump Home furniture lines had items made in Turkey, and picture frames and similar goods were sourced from India. While specific factories and sourcing changed over time and some items or limited runs may have been made domestically, the general claim that those product categories were manufactured abroad is supported by contemporaneous reporting.

claim: "They’ve seen employer-supported coverage increase in Massachusetts after this law (Romneycare) was implemented."
rationale: Empirical analyses of Massachusetts’ 2006 health reform show overall insurance coverage rose and the uninsured fell, but employer-sponsored (employer-supported) coverage did not increase; it remained flat or fell slightly in most post‑reform studies and state data. The gains were driven mainly by Medicaid/CHIP expansions and subsidized individual plans rather than a rise in employer coverage.

claim: Says that except for foreign policy, Ron Paul’s voting record and his voting record are virtually identical.
rationale: The statement is overstated and self-contradictory; if it means Ron Paul and Rand Paul are 'virtually identical' outside foreign policy, that is not accurate. They do share many libertarian-leaning positions on economics and civil liberties, but their actual roll-call votes and tactical choices show notable differences on specific domestic issues and legislative behavior. Saying they are virtually identical except for one topic is therefore false.

claim: Millennials are "more pro-life than baby boomers and older Americans."
rationale: Major U.S. public-opinion polling indicates younger cohorts (Millennials and Gen Z) are generally more likely to support legal abortion and identify as pro‑choice than Baby Boomers and older generations, so the statement that Millennials are "more pro‑life" is incorrect. While there is variation by question wording and subgroup, the overall generational pattern over recent years points toward younger Americans being more pro‑choice rather than more pro‑life.

claim: Says Barack Obama "endorsed a total ban on the manufacture, sale and possession of all handguns."
rationale: There is no credible record that Barack Obama endorsed a blanket ban on the manufacture, sale, and possession of all handguns. His stated gun-policy positions focused on measures like reinstating an assault-weapons ban, universal background checks, and limits on high-capacity magazines, not an outright prohibition of all handguns. Major fact-checkers have investigated similar claims and found them to be misstatements or misattributions.

claim: "Twice as much (federal) money is going back to Hawaii, Virginia and Alaska than is coming home to Oregon."
rationale: The claim gives no timeframe or definition of “going back” (gross federal spending, net fiscal balance, or federal dollars per capita), so it cannot be verified as stated. While the combined population and large federal/military spending in Hawaii, Virginia and Alaska make it plausible their total federal receipts could exceed Oregon’s, the specific assertion that it is exactly “twice as much” is unsupported without a cited fiscal-year dataset. Absent a clear metric and year, the statement is not a verifiable fact.

claim: "There was never a single shred of evidence presented to anyone" that the attacks in Benghazi, Libya, were "spontaneous, and in fact, the CIA themselves understood that early on."
rationale: This claim is false because it misstates the record: in the days after the Sept. 11–12, 2012 Benghazi attacks there were official statements and intelligence discussions about demonstrations and about militant involvement, and multiple U.S. investigations (including the Intelligence Community, State Department Accountability Review Board and congressional inquiries) concluded the attacks were a planned terrorist assault rather than merely a spontaneous protest. The CIA and other agencies had evolving assessments in the immediate aftermath, but they did not uniformly conclude the attacks were spontaneous and there was intelligence indicating organized militant involvement relatively early on.

claim: "There are actually only 30 countries that practice birthright citizenship."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While many reports state 'about 30' countries grant unconditional jus soli, the exact count varies by definition (unconditional vs conditional birthright) and by recent legal changes; some lists exceed 30 if conditional forms are included and others are fewer if only pure unconditional jus soli are counted. Thus an absolute statement that there are only 30 countries is not reliably accurate.

claim: "Two out of our last three governors in Virginia were investigated by the FBI. One went to jail and one is running for office again in this election."
rationale: The claim is not supported by public record. Of the recent Virginia governors, only Bob McDonnell was the subject of a high‑profile federal prosecution (he was convicted in 2014 but the conviction was later overturned by the U.S. Supreme Court and he did not serve prison time); other recent governors (e.g., Ralph Northam, Terry McAuliffe, Glenn Youngkin) were not the subject of FBI criminal prosecutions as a group. The statement also mixes timing (saying one “is running for office again in this election”) without specifying which election, which makes the claim misleading.

claim: Poll results from the past 35 years show that State of the Union speeches "do not move" presidential approval numbers.
rationale: The absolute statement that State of the Union speeches "do not move" approval is inaccurate. Empirical analyses across recent decades generally find only modest and often short-lived changes in presidential approval after SOTU addresses (a few percentage points), though some individual speeches or political contexts have produced larger shifts. Saying they categorically "do not move" ratings overstates the consistency of the null effect.

claim: Says President Donald Trump "is still yet to say anything as the president of the United States about bounties on American troops."
rationale: This is false because President Trump did make public remarks about the reporting of alleged bounties on U.S. troops. In the weeks after media reports, he commented publicly—saying he had seen the stories, casting doubt on the reports, and stating that if true it would be unacceptable—so it is incorrect to say he "is still yet to say anything."

claim: Children born today will carry a $30,000 share of the national debt.
rationale: The statement is misleading and unverifiable as written: there is no fixed, inevitable $30,000 obligation that every child born today will inherit. Current U.S. federal debt is in the tens of trillions of dollars and simple per-capita math yields a much higher figure than $30,000, and future tax burdens depend on economic growth, policy choices, and how debt is financed. Additionally, public debt is not a literal per‑child bill to be directly inherited.

claim: Says "Kurt Schrader supports Obama’s sequester … but won’t cut $1.6 million to fund new video games."
rationale: The claim is misleading and not supported by clear public record. There is no verifiable evidence that Rep. Kurt Schrader explicitly endorsed “Obama’s sequester” while simultaneously refusing to cut a specific $1.6 million line-item described as funding “new video games.” Sequestration was an automatic, across‑the‑board process, not a selective decision to spare a single $1.6M item, and the referenced dollar figure and purpose appear to be a mischaracterization or lack necessary context.

claim: Says he "raised graduation rates to nearly 90 percent."
rationale: The claim as presented is unverifiable because it omits who 'he' is, where and when this occurred, and which graduation-rate metric is meant. Graduation-rate figures vary by jurisdiction and by how rates are calculated, and politicians frequently cherry-pick cohorts or years to make gains look larger. Without specific subject, place, timeframe, and metric, the statement cannot be confirmed and is judged false.

claim: "Nearly 200,000 Florida voters may not be citizens."
rationale: This overstates what the underlying data showed. A widely-cited ~173,000 figure came from a flawed DMV-to-voter-roll matching process (including blank or miscoded citizenship fields) and was not evidence of 200,000 confirmed noncitizen voters; state officials and independent fact-checkers found most matches were errors and only a very small number of registrations were ever confirmed and removed as noncitizens.

claim: Says Republican lawmakers delayed COVID-19 testing
rationale: The claim is misleading as stated. Early widespread testing delays in the U.S. were primarily caused by a faulty CDC test rollout and restrictive federal testing regulations (FDA/CDC policies) and technical capacity limits, rather than a single coordinated action by "Republican lawmakers"; while some Republican officials opposed or slowed certain funding or policy measures, attributing the testing delays solely to Republican lawmakers is inaccurate.

claim: The poorest counties in the U.S. are in Appalachia and "happen to be more than 90 percent white."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate as a general claim. While some of the poorest counties are in Appalachia and many Appalachian counties are majority white, the list of counties with the highest poverty or lowest median incomes also includes many non-Appalachian counties (for example in the Mississippi Delta and on Native American reservations) that are majority Black or Native American, so it is incorrect to say the poorest counties are all in Appalachia and over 90% white.

claim: Says Abraham Lincoln said, "America will never be destroyed from the outside. If we lose our freedoms it will be because we have destroyed ourselves from within."
rationale: The line is widely attributed to Abraham Lincoln but cannot be found in his collected speeches, letters, or other primary sources. Quote researchers and fact-checkers trace the wording to much later, 20th-century usages rather than to Lincoln, so the attribution is incorrect.

claim: Says Donald Trump "says organized crime runs wild on reservations."
rationale: There is no verifiable public record of Donald Trump uttering the exact line “organized crime runs wild on reservations.” While Trump has sometimes criticized crime or governance on reservations in broader remarks, the precise quoted wording cannot be substantiated from known speeches, interviews, or tweets. Absent a sourced transcript or recording, treating the claim as false is appropriate.

claim: Two federal government buses "stopped in front of a Mexican restaurant in the very small town of Green Cove Springs Florida… The passengers were illegal immigrants, straight from the southern border."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that two federal government buses carrying migrants from the southern border stopped in front of a Mexican restaurant in Green Cove Springs, Florida. Reporting on migrant transport around that time shows movements organized by state governments, local agencies, or private contractors rather than a federal operation dropping undocumented migrants in small towns, and no reliable news accounts corroborate this specific incident.

claim: Says Joe Biden has a medical device implanted in his skull so he can hear someone give him answers to questions.
rationale: There is no credible evidence, reporting, or medical documentation that President Biden has an implanted device in his skull for someone to feed him answers. Claims of this kind are based on speculation and misinterpretation of normal hearing aids, earpieces, or video edits and are not supported by verifiable proof.

claim: "Clinton's former pastor convicted of child molestation."
rationale: There is no credible evidence or mainstream reporting that a pastor described as "Clinton's former pastor" was convicted of child molestation. High-profile clergy criminal convictions are widely reported, and none of the pastors commonly associated with Bill or Hillary Clinton have been documented as having such convictions. The claim appears unsubstantiated as stated.

claim: Says the Multnomah County Library system "is the second busiest in the nation."
rationale: The claim is misleading because it gives a definitive national ranking without specifying the metric or time period. Nationally, much larger systems (e.g., New York Public Library, Los Angeles Public Library, Chicago Public Library) typically report higher circulation and visitation than Multnomah County; there is no consistent, current ranking that places Multnomah as the second busiest overall. Without a clear metric and date the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: Obama's budget plan would "take national debt up to about 80 percent of gross national product. ... Historically, it's been about 40 percent."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it conflates measures and timeframes. Projections of U.S. debt under Obama-era budgets varied by scenario and by whether one cites gross federal debt or debt held by the public; CBO projections in the early 2010s showed rising debt under some scenarios but not a simple, undisputed jump to exactly 80% of national output, and the historical debt-to-GDP ratio has fluctuated widely (well above 100% in WWII and much lower in peacetime). Thus the blanket numerical claim is not accurate without qualifiers.

claim: "We are poised to get rid of over 1,000 more regulations in 2012."
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and reads like political hyperbole. Eliminating over 1,000 regulations in a single year would require numerous finalized repeals or withdrawals tracked in official records (e.g., agencies' rulemakings and the OMB Unified Agenda), and there is no credible evidence that such a coordinated removal plan or achievement existed for 2012. Regulatory repeal typically proceeds more slowly and in far smaller numbers than the claim implies.

claim: Only 56 coronavirus deaths a day was enough to collapse the world economy, even though thousands of people die daily from tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and other diseases.
rationale: The claim is misleading: attributing global economic collapse to "only 56 coronavirus deaths a day" is inaccurate and lacks context. COVID-19 proved economically disruptive because of rapid global spread, high hospitalization and ICU demand, and policy responses (lockdowns, travel bans) rather than a low daily death count; global COVID deaths were also much higher at many points. Comparing raw daily deaths from endemic diseases (tuberculosis, hepatitis B) ignores differences in transmissibility, acute healthcare burden, and social disruption that drive emergency economic responses.

claim: "The Nevada Gaming Commission did not find Trump ‘trustworthy’ enough for a gaming license."
rationale: In April 2024 Nevada gaming regulators concluded Trump was not suitable for a gaming license, with the Gaming Control Board’s report and the Nevada Gaming Commission’s action citing concerns about his honesty, integrity and trustworthiness. The agencies explicitly said he had not demonstrated the character and trustworthiness required for licensure and moved to deny the application.

claim: "Donald Trump would receive $17 million for three hotels closed for four days under Republican bill! How in the hell is this right?!"
rationale: There is no credible Republican bill that specifically promises Donald Trump a $17 million automatic payment for three hotels being closed for four days. Proposals that would reimburse businesses for losses have been broad, would require documented losses and eligibility criteria, and do not single out Trump; the $17 million number appears to be an extrapolation or misinterpretation rather than a stated statutory payment. Fact checks of similar social-media claims found them misleading.

claim: "Same little boy died of COVID-19 in three different countries. Still don’t believe the media is #fakenews?"
rationale: The claim that the same little boy literally died of COVID-19 in three different countries is implausible and unsupported. What often happens is that a single photograph or story is misattributed, syndicated, or reused across outlets, but reputable fact-checkers have found no credible evidence that one child actually died multiple times in different nations. Reuse or miscaptioning of images does not prove the media fabricated multiple deaths.

claim: Says President Barack Obama has launched "twice as many strikes (on) countries that are predominantly Muslim" than President George W. Bush.
rationale: The statement is misleading and not reliably supported by public data. While President Obama did expand targeted strikes and drone operations into more Muslim-majority countries (e.g., Pakistan, Yemen, Somalia, Libya, Syria) compared with President Bush (whose major campaigns were Afghanistan and Iraq), independent counts depend heavily on how one defines a “strike,” the timeframe, and which incidents are included — and they do not robustly support the neat claim of exactly “twice as many.”

claim: "On 60 Minutes, Joe said he never met with Hunter and the Burisma CEO. Well, here he is with both."
rationale: The claim misrepresents what Biden said on 60 Minutes. In those interviews Biden said he had not spoken to his son about his overseas business dealings, not that he had never met his son or never met a Burisma executive; he has been photographed with Hunter Biden.
