There is no verified evidence that Joe Biden met a Burisma CEO despite circulating images being misidentified or lacking corroborating context.

claim: "Since 2001, higher education in the state has been cut or allowed to erode ... by 35 or 40 percent."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits which state and which specific metric (total appropriations, per‑student funding, faculty positions, program quality, etc.) is being reduced by 35–40%. While many states reduced higher‑education spending after recessions, the size and timing of cuts vary widely and such a precise percentage cannot be confirmed without a defined measure and state. Thus the claim as stated is not supported.

claim: "A couple of debates ago, (Donald Trump) said if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless."
rationale: There is no reliable record or debate transcript showing Donald Trump saying “if you don’t support socialized health care, you’re heartless.” The line contradicts his long-standing opposition to “socialized” health care and would have been widely reported if he had said it, so it appears to be a misattribution or paraphrase of someone else’s words.

claim: "My plan offers three times as much tax relief to the middle class as Senator McCain's."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it lacks key specifics (who “my” refers to, which version of Senator McCain’s plan, the time period, and how “middle class” and “tax relief” are measured). Without a concrete, comparable numerical breakdown of projected or actual tax relief for both plans, the assertion that one offers exactly three times the relief is not substantiated. Such comparisons require detailed distributional analyses and definitions that are not provided here.

claim: "Heidi Cruz, Ted’s wife, is managing director of Goldman Sachs. They oversee the Texas utilities."
rationale: While Heidi Cruz has worked as a managing director at Goldman Sachs in the past, the claim that "they oversee the Texas utilities" is false. Regulation and oversight of Texas utilities are handled by state bodies (not by Heidi Cruz or Senator Ted Cruz), and Goldman Sachs as a bank does not 'oversee' state utility operations. Therefore the combined claim as stated is misleading and incorrect.

claim: John McCain "voted against the tax cuts of 2001 and 2003, wrongly claiming they helped only the rich."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as stated. John McCain did not vote against both the 2001 and 2003 Bush tax bills; he supported key elements of the Bush-era tax cuts, and whether the cuts “helped only the rich” is a contested, technical matter of tax-distribution analysis rather than a straightforward falsehood. Calling his assertion “wrong” overstates the simple factual record about votes and the complex, varied impacts of those laws.

claim: The average Atlanta resident "spends an extra $924 each year in additional gasoline and wasted time."
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as a general fact because congestion-cost estimates for Atlanta differ by source and year, and commonly refer to commuters (drivers) not all residents. Different analyses (e.g., Urban Mobility Report, INRIX) produce varying per-person costs—some higher, some lower—so the blanket claim of an extra $924 per Atlanta resident lacks a cited study, timeframe, and clear methodology. Without that context the number is misleading.

claim: The Department of Homeland Security’s database of legal immigrants has "never" been "bounced against a state’s voter rolls."
rationale: The absolute claim that DHS’s immigration database has "never" been compared to state voter rolls is incorrect. While DHS policies restrict routine bulk sharing, DHS systems (for example the SAVE verification system and other immigration records) have been used by state agencies and third parties to verify registrants’ immigration status and there are documented instances of state queries and matches. Therefore a categorical "never" is not supported.

claim: Says Texas schools have had "massive increases" in class sizes with Rick Perry as governor.
rationale: Statewide data do not show a consistent, statewide ‘‘massive’’ rise in average class sizes during Rick Perry’s time as governor (2000–2015); pupil–teacher ratios and reported average class sizes in Texas were broadly stable or changed only modestly, though some districts experienced increases. The claim overstates a complex, locally variable trend and uses the vague term “massive” without specification.

claim: "We paid down the debt for four years -- paid down $600 billion on the national debt."
rationale: The claim is not accurate as a general statement: in recent administrations the federal debt increased, not fell by $600 billion over four years. Only in the late 1990s (Clinton-era budget surpluses) was the debt reduced slightly, and reductions depend on whether one cites 'debt held by the public' or total debt; neither commonly cited measure supports a clear $600 billion payoff over exactly four years for recent presidents.

claim: "Grandparents must pickup up all their grandchildren every weekend no matter what or they will be fined $5,000."
rationale: There is no general law that obligates all grandparents to pick up their grandchildren every weekend under threat of a $5,000 fine. Family law and custody/visitation obligations vary by jurisdiction, and while courts can issue specific orders or impose penalties for contempt in individual cases, the sweeping universal mandate in the claim is fictional or fabricated.

claim: "Obama held one of the first meetings of his political career in Bill Ayers's home. And they've worked together on various projects in Chicago."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Obama and Bill Ayers were acquaintances who served together on some Chicago education and civic boards in the 1990s, but reputable fact-checking and reporting found no evidence that one of Obama’s first political meetings took place at Ayers’s home and their relationship was limited rather than a long-term political partnership.

claim: On extreme-risk guns laws, "This idea has passed Republican legislatures in other states and has been signed by Republican governors."
rationale: This is accurate: several states with Republican legislative majorities and Republican governors have enacted extreme-risk (so-called "red flag") laws. Notable examples include Florida (2018 law signed by GOP Gov. Rick Scott), Ohio (2019 law signed by GOP Gov. Mike DeWine), and Utah (2020 law signed by GOP Gov. Gary Herbert). While the laws vary in scope, the general claim that Republican legislatures and governors have passed and signed such laws is supported by these instances.

claim: "There hasn't really been a lot of net growth in the federal workforce when you compare it to say, 1990."
rationale: Official counts of the federal civilian workforce (the usual OPM/CBO measure) show only modest net change since 1990 — totals have been relatively flat with at most a few hundred thousand difference, and the federal workforce as a share of the U.S. population or labor force is smaller than in earlier decades. That supports the claim that there hasn’t been a lot of net growth compared with 1990.

claim: A record number of immigrants not from Mexico are "being apprehended at the border."
rationale: U.S. Customs and Border Protection data in recent years (notably FY2022–FY2023) show record-high encounters with non-Mexican nationals at the southern border, driven by large increases from countries such as Venezuela, Cuba, Nicaragua and Haiti. Thus the general claim that a record number of immigrants not from Mexico are being apprehended/encountered at the border is supported by official statistics.

claim: "The pope and Donald Trump and Tammy Baldwin all agree" on eliminating the "carried-interest" tax break.
rationale: While Donald Trump has publicly pledged to eliminate the carried-interest tax preference and Sen. Tammy Baldwin has supported closing carried-interest loopholes, there is no clear evidence that the pope (normally referring to Pope Francis) has endorsed that specific U.S. tax-policy change. The pope has criticized economic inequality and tax avoidance in general, but that is not the same as an explicit policy-level agreement on the carried-interest provision.

claim: "How is a misogynist bigot of epic proportions (like U.S. Rep. Steven Smith) allowed to serve?"
rationale: The statement is a subjective value judgment rather than a verifiable factual claim about actions or official findings. Calling someone a “misogynist bigot of epic proportions” is opinionated rhetoric and cannot be confirmed or refuted without specific, documented evidence of misconduct, statements, or legal/ethics findings that demonstrate such behavior.

claim: Gov. McDonnell's proposed budget "is cutting" public education.
rationale: The claim is too general and lacks a time frame; Gov. Bob McDonnell served 2010–2014 and proposed multiple budgets with different effects on education funding. Some of his budgets included reductions or shifts in state support for K–12 and higher education, while others included protections or re‑allocations, so a blanket present-tense statement that his proposed budget "is cutting" public education cannot be verified without specifying which proposal. Because the claim is ambiguous, it cannot be treated as clearly true.

claim: "Do this research … watch how much crime picks up if you take away [football]."
rationale: The claim presents a strong causal assertion but empirical research on sports and crime is mixed and largely correlational. Some studies find crime temporarily falls during major sporting events while others find spikes (for example after losses or related to alcohol); results depend on context, timing, and other confounding factors. There is no robust causal evidence that simply “taking away football” would universally cause crime to rise as the claim implies.

claim: It's a good sign for Obamacare that in California, "the proportion of kids who are signing up is the proportion of kids in the population."
rationale: I could not find authoritative evidence that in California the share of children enrolling exactly equals their share of the population, and the statement overgeneralizes. Enrollment by age for ACA programs and Medi-Cal/CHIP typically varies by outreach, eligibility and prior coverage, so an exact proportional match is unlikely and would not by itself prove overall success.

claim: "Amazing fact: Senate has already voted on more amendments in 2015 than Reid allowed ALL YEAR last year."
rationale: The claim is unsupported and likely false because it makes a sweeping comparison without defining what counts as an "amendment" or which period in 2015 is meant. Records of Senate roll-call and amendment activity show counts vary by definition (e.g., amendment adoption votes vs. cloture on amendments), and contemporaneous fact-checks found similar one-off claims about early-2015 activity overstated. Without a clear, standardized metric the assertion that 2015 had already exceeded all of Reid's 2014 "allowed" amendment votes is misleading.

claim: President Joe Biden was confused, "turned around and shook hands with thin air" after a speech.
rationale: The claim frames an interpretive conclusion (that Biden was confused and literally shook hands with 'thin air'). Video clips of Biden appearing to reach for a hand after speeches have often lacked context; fact-checkers have shown people or aides were off-camera or moving away, so the description mischaracterizes what occurred. Describing him as 'confused' is a subjective inference not established by the footage alone.

claim: Says Rick Scott's proposed budget "would lay off 20,000 teachers."
rationale: There is no authoritative, uncontested estimate showing Rick Scott’s proposed budget would directly force exactly 20,000 teacher layoffs. Analyses at the time produced a range of estimates and opponents’ figures were contested; layoffs depend on district choices, offsets, and which specific year/budget is referenced. Because the number was a contested projection rather than a demonstrated consequence, the categorical claim is not supported.

claim: "I have had the challenge during this administration to suspend no less than 37 public officials in about 36 months."
rationale: The claim cannot be verified as stated because it does not identify who made the statement, which administration is meant, or provide sources for the count of suspensions. Determining whether 37 public officials were suspended in roughly 36 months requires consulting official personnel or disciplinary records and contemporary reporting; absent that evidence the assertion is unsubstantiated. Therefore I judge the claim false as presented due to lack of verifiable support.

claim: Says rival Jill Karofsky wants "to disarm law abiding citizens."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Jill Karofsky has advocated a policy of disarming law‑abiding citizens. Public record shows she has supported common gun‑safety measures (such as background checks and other restrictions) and has not called for blanket confiscation of firearms from lawful owners; opponents have used rhetorical language to frame her positions as ‘disarming’ people. The claim therefore mischaracterizes her known positions.

claim: Says of MS-13 gang members, "We are getting them out of our country by the thousands."
rationale: Publicly available enforcement and reporting do not support the blanket claim that MS‑13 members are being deported “by the thousands.” Government and independent fact‑checks have found that while some MS‑13 suspects have been arrested or removed, the counts are much lower and often rely on broad or inconsistent gang‑member designations, so the statement overstates verified removals.

claim: "The Texas unemployment rate is now the lowest it’s been in 40 years & Texas led the nation last month in new job creation."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it gives no date or data source and mixes two distinct measures. Texas has had low unemployment at times and often posts large monthly job gains because of its size, but available BLS and state labor reports show monthly rankings and 40-year lows vary by exact month and by whether rates are seasonally adjusted; therefore the blanket statement that the rate is "now" the lowest in 40 years and that Texas led the nation "last month" cannot be confirmed and is likely inaccurate. Without a specific month and consistent metrics the dual assertion is misleading.

claim: The Dow Jones Industrial Average "jumped 1000 points in last 5 weeks, Record fastest 1000 point move in history."
rationale: The claim is too vague and likely incorrect as stated. Whether the Dow 'jumped 1000 points in last 5 weeks' and that this was the 'record fastest 1000 point move' depends on the specific date range and whether one counts intraday or multi‑day moves; multiple 1,000‑point moves and faster single‑day 1,000+ point gains occurred during volatile periods (notably 2020), so the blanket assertion cannot be verified as true without a precise timeframe. Given the ambiguity and changing record history, the statement as presented is not supported.

claim: 47 percent of Americans "can’t pay for an unexpected $400 expense through savings or credit cards, without selling something or borrowing money."
rationale: This matches a widely reported result from the Federal Reserve’s household survey: about 47% of adults said they would need to borrow money or sell something to cover an unexpected $400 expense rather than paying from savings or by charging and paying a credit card. The figure comes from the Fed’s Report on the Economic Well‑Being of U.S. Households (the SHED report) for that survey year.

claim: "Violent crime is up since the last year of Sharpe James’ administration. This year it’s higher. … The unemployment rate is almost 15 percent. The high school dropout rate is over 50 percent."
rationale: The statement bundles three empirical claims without a clear date or geography, making it unverifiable as stated. Sharpe James left office in 2006, and crime trends since then have fluctuated year-to-year rather than showing a simple steady increase; unemployment near 15% would only match brief severe-recession periods and is not a persistent recent condition for Newark; reported high-school dropout/graduation statistics for the city have not supported a consistent >50% dropout rate. Given the missing time frame and the weight of available municipal/state labor and education data, the composite claim is not supported.

claim: "Bryce Reeves chaired a group bankrolled by a New York billionaire who fired hundreds of Virginia workers and sent their jobs to China."
rationale: Available reporting and public records do not support the claim that Sen. Bryce Reeves chaired a group financed by a New York billionaire who fired hundreds of Virginia workers and sent their jobs to China. There are no credible news accounts linking Reeves to a group bankrolled by any specific New York billionaire responsible for mass firings and offshoring of Virginia jobs, so the asserted chain of relationships and actions is unsubstantiated.

claim: Only "18 percent of jobs are accessible by transit for metro Atlanta residents. 33 percent for those living in the city."
rationale: I could not verify these exact figures and similar published estimates vary by data source, year, geographic boundary and the definition of “accessible” (e.g., travel-time threshold). While multiple analyses have found that a relatively small share of jobs in the Atlanta region are reachable by transit and the city of Atlanta has higher access than the wider metro, I cannot confirm the precise 18% (metro) and 33% (city) claim as stated.

claim: "There are at least 23 countries that refuse to take their people back after they’ve been ordered to leave the United States, including large numbers of violent criminals."
rationale: This statement overstates and mischaracterizes the situation. U.S. government data and reporting show that cooperation on removals and issuance of travel documents varies by country and over time, and there is no consistent, verifiable public list showing 'at least 23' countries that categorically refuse to take back their nationals; moreover the claim that these include 'large numbers of violent criminals' is not substantiated by available aggregated data. Because definitions (refuse vs. delay, temporary non‑cooperation, lack of documents) and the timeframe are unspecified, the claim is misleading.

claim: The last three days of early voting "happen to be the most populated days of voting that we have in early voting."
rationale: The claim states a universal pattern but turnout timing during early voting varies by jurisdiction, election, and year. While many places do see heavy traffic in the final days of early voting, other jurisdictions peak on weekends or earlier periods (and mail/drop-box ballots change the distribution), so the statement is not universally true without specifying location and election. Confirming it requires precinct-level early voting data for the specific jurisdiction and cycle.

claim: Dan Patrick "changed his name from Danny Goeb to hide from" his "debts."
rationale: Dan Patrick was born Daniel Goeb and adopted the name 'Dan Patrick' as an on‑air/stage name during his broadcasting career; mainstream biographies and his own accounts describe it as a professional decision rather than an attempt to evade creditors. There is no reliable evidence that he changed his name to hide from debts, so the specific claim is not supported.

claim: "We're spending millions for each individual" held at Guantanamo Bay, Cuba.
rationale: Multiple U.S. government and watchdog estimates have shown that the annual cost of operating Guantanamo divided by the relatively small detainee population equated to millions of dollars per detainee in recent years. Exact figures vary by year and by which budget items (facility upkeep, legal, medical, security, relocation, construction) are included, but the claim that spending reached millions per individual is accurate in commonly cited analyses.

claim: Image of expansive pit shows a lithium mine.
rationale: There is insufficient evidence to identify a particular mineral from an undated image of an open pit. Many open-pit mines (copper, iron, phosphate, kaolin, etc.) and non-mining features can look similar; lithium is commonly produced from brine evaporation ponds (distinct rectangular ponds) or from specific spodumene hard-rock operations, so a generic expansive pit alone does not confirm a lithium mine. Without corroborating location, company, or geochemical context the claim is not supported.

claim: Says Florida Gov. Rick Scott "subtracted $1.3 billion from public schools."
rationale: This claim is misleading. Governor Scott’s first budget proposal in 2011 sought roughly $1.3 billion less for K‑12 categorical programs, but the budget process, federal stimulus funds, and subsequent legislative actions changed the final totals so there was not a simple, one‑time $1.3 billion permanent subtraction from public schools by Scott alone. Fact‑checks have noted the difference between proposed cuts, enacted budgets, and accounting shifts.

claim: "If the shot actually saved lives, they’d be priced so high that you literally could not afford them, you know like insulin."
rationale: The statement asserts a universal pricing rule that life‑saving shots would be unaffordable like insulin; that is incorrect. Drug and vaccine prices vary widely depending on production cost, patents, market structure, and public procurement—many life‑saving vaccines and treatments are low‑cost or subsidized, while some essential medicines (notably insulin in some markets) are unusually expensive due to specific market and regulatory factors.

claim: "(T)he United States government and its Constitution says that people can be put to death."
rationale: The U.S. Constitution and the U.S. government permit capital punishment: the Constitution’s text and amendments (including the Eighth Amendment’s ban on “cruel and unusual punishments”) have been interpreted by the Supreme Court to allow the death penalty under prescribed procedures, and both federal and many state statutes authorize capital sentences. The Court’s jurisprudence (e.g., Gregg v. Georgia and later cases) has upheld that sentencing people to death is constitutionally permissible in certain circumstances.

claim: "This is the first time since Roe was decided in 1973 that a court has granted personhood status to the preborn."
rationale: False. Since Roe v. Wade (1973) numerous state courts have recognized fetuses as legal persons in specific contexts (for example under fetal-homicide statutes and in some wrongful-death or victim-status rulings). Those decisions grant limited, context-dependent protections rather than a blanket constitutional personhood that would directly overturn Roe.

claim: Says Brett Kavanaugh "refused to uphold key patient protections in the past."
rationale: The claim is vague and asserts a categorical past refusal without identifying which "key patient protections" or specific cases. Public records of Kavanaugh’s D.C. Circuit opinions show a mixed record—he has joined rulings that limited regulatory reach in some health-related matters but also upheld regulations in others—so there is not clear, documented evidence that he broadly "refused to uphold" key patient protections. Without a specific protection or ruling, the blanket statement is not supported.

claim: "Thanks to President Trump and Republicans over the past year through July, U.S. manufacturing added 327,000 jobs, the most of any 12-month period since April 1995, when the figure added a healthy 345,000 positions."
rationale: The numeric portion is accurate for the 12 months through July 2018 (BLS showed about +327,000 manufacturing jobs and the last comparable 12‑month gain was about +345,000 in 1995), but the claim’s causal phrasing “Thanks to President Trump and Republicans” is not supported. Determining that elected officials are the direct cause of a one‑year jobs change requires rigorous attribution analysis, and many factors beyond specific party actions affect manufacturing employment.

claim: Says only about 250 Texans have been killed in action since 9/11.
rationale: The claim understates casualties: Department of Defense casualty records and multiple news analyses that compile state-by-state KIA totals show that far more than ~250 service members from Texas have been killed in action in post‑9/11 wars (Iraq, Afghanistan and related operations). Given Texas’ large military population, official state-by-state tallies run into the hundreds or more, not roughly 250.

claim: Says proposed teacher contract "would layer on more restrictive rules."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no context, speaker, jurisdiction, or specific contract language to compare. Determining whether a proposed teacher contract “would layer on more restrictive rules” requires side‑by‑side comparison of the existing rules and the proposed provisions; without that evidence the claim cannot be confirmed. It may be true in some cases but is not provable from the information provided.

claim: "After one year, Tennessee’s students made their biggest single-year jump in achievement ever recorded in the state."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and not supported by clear, comparable statewide records: Tennessee has reported notable year-to-year gains after reforms, but whether any one single-year increase is the largest “ever recorded” depends on which assessment, grade, subject, and scoring baseline are used. Assessment changes (different tests, scoring scales, or cut scores) make many year-to-year comparisons non-comparable, so the blanket claim is misleading without specific qualifiers. Given the ambiguity and lack of a clear authoritative record showing an unequivocal largest single-year jump, the statement is not reliably true.

claim: "We have 25 million Americans out of work."
rationale: The statement is misleading because it gives no timeframe or definition of "out of work." Official BLS data show the number of unemployed peaked at about 23 million in April 2020, and at most times since then the count has been well below 25 million; different measures (people not in the labor force or receiving benefits) produce different totals. Without a clear date and definition, claiming "we have 25 million Americans out of work" is inaccurate as a general present-tense statement.

claim: "Our larger domestic threat is from racial supremacist groups."
rationale: U.S. federal law-enforcement and intelligence assessments in recent years have identified racially or ethnically motivated violent extremists — especially white supremacist groups — as the most persistent and lethal domestic terrorism threat. While other threats (e.g., anti‑government militants, lone actors, cyber threats) also pose dangers, multiple official reports and leaders have singled out racial supremacist violence as the larger domestic terrorist threat in the relevant period.

claim: Says "an unchecked Democratic Majority in Trenton" is responsible for "years of diversions" from the state’s unemployment insurance trust fund.
rationale: The claim overstates responsibility by blaming an “unchecked Democratic Majority” as solely responsible for “years of diversions.” While New Jersey has seen transfers out of its unemployment insurance trust fund, those moves were enacted at different times under both Democratic and Republican officials and reflect a bipartisan pattern of using UI dollars for other budget purposes. The phrase “unchecked” is vague and the claim omits that governors and legislatures of both parties have played roles in past diversions.

claim: Says "Congressman Eric Cantor wants to eliminate Social Security."
rationale: This claim overstates Cantor’s publicly stated positions. Eric Cantor has advocated for restructuring and reforming Social Security (e.g., raising the retirement age, changing benefit formulas, or introducing private account elements) to address solvency, but he did not call for outright elimination of the program. Saying he “wants to eliminate Social Security” is therefore inaccurate.

claim: Says Amazon has removed "an educational game about Gettysburg."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable reporting or authoritative evidence (to June 2024) that Amazon removed an identifiable "educational game about Gettysburg." The claim is underspecified — no game title, date, or storefront is given — and could be confused with removals on other platforms or with different historical games. Without specific details or corroborating sources the assertion is unproven and therefore treated as false.

claim: Says the federal government threatened to impose a no-fly zone in Texas if state legislators bar airport security officials from performing pat-downs.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official statement that the federal government threatened to impose a no-fly zone over Texas in retaliation for state legislators restricting TSA pat-downs. Federal authorities do control national airspace and can take enforcement or preemption actions, but announcing a punitive no-fly zone against a state would be unprecedented and legally dubious. The claim appears to conflate federal enforcement authority with an asserted threat that was not made.

claim: Says President Barack Obama's parents were communists.
rationale: There is no credible evidence that either of Barack Obama’s parents were members of a communist party. Biographical records show his mother worked in international development and academia and his father was a Kenyan economist educated in the United States; neither has documented communist party affiliation. Claims that they 'were communists' are a recurring conspiracy without substantiation.

claim: Says he got "support all over Raleigh"
rationale: The claim as given is unverifiable: it does not identify who said it, when, or what evidence supports the sweepingly broad assertion that they got 'support all over Raleigh.' Without named sources, polling, endorsements, or geographic turnout data, the statement cannot be confirmed. Per instruction to prefer FALSE when uncertain, I mark it false pending supporting evidence.

claim: Coca-Cola, Ben & Jerry’s and other companies support rioting.
rationale: The broad claim is false as stated. While some companies (for example Ben & Jerry's) have publicly supported racial justice movements or made donations to advocacy organizations, there is no credible evidence that Coca‑Cola, Ben & Jerry's, or major mainstream companies intentionally fund or endorse rioting or violent unlawful behavior; most corporate statements explicitly condemn violence and call for peaceful protest. Allegations often arise from misinterpreted donations, statements, or lobbying activity rather than proof of support for rioting.

claim: President Obama has "stopped using the phrase 'war on terror.' "
rationale: Obama and his administration publicly said they would move away from the phrase “war on terror” and shifted official terminology toward phrases like “overseas contingency operations” and “counterterrorism.” However, the claim’s absolute wording that he has “stopped using” the phrase is inaccurate because intent to avoid a term and administrative shifts do not prove he never used the phrase in all contexts or that similar language was never employed.

claim: A person’s immune system "tanks" after their second COVID-19 vaccine dose.
rationale: This is false. COVID-19 vaccines elicit a stronger immune response (antibodies and T cells) after the full vaccination series; common short-term symptoms like fever and fatigue are signs of immune activation, not immune collapse. Large clinical trials and post‑marketing surveillance have not shown the immune system “tanking” after the second dose, although rare adverse events exist.

claim: Says CNN and other news organizations tweeted that a journalist was executed in Kabul by Taliban fighters.
rationale: The claim is too specific and I cannot verify any instance where CNN and multiple other reputable news organizations explicitly tweeted that a journalist was executed in Kabul by Taliban fighters. While there have been reports over time of journalists being killed or threatened in Afghanistan, I find no clear, attributable set of tweets from CNN and others that match this exact claim. Because the statement lacks a date, victim name, or sourcing, it cannot be confirmed as stated.

claim: "I've been outspent by my opponents every time I've run for U.S. Senate."
rationale: The claim is a universal statement about every Senate campaign by an unspecified person and cannot be confirmed without identifying the candidate and checking campaign finance reports from each race. Campaign spending varies by election and opponents, so absent specific FEC/state filing data showing this pattern, the assertion is not verifiable and is unlikely to be true as stated.

claim: Says George Soros’s son is married to Adam Schiff’s sister.
rationale: This claim is false. There is no credible evidence or reporting that any of George Soros’s sons is married to Rep. Adam Schiff’s sister; public biographies and marriage records of the Soros family and Adam Schiff’s family do not support that connection. The allegation appears to have originated on social media and has been debunked by fact-checkers.

claim: "90,000 Californians are unsheltered and homeless."
rationale: Recent official point-in-time counts show California has substantially more than 90,000 unsheltered people; statewide PIT counts in the 2020–2023 period put total homelessness in the hundreds of thousands with the unsheltered subset typically exceeding 100,000. Saying '90,000 Californians are unsheltered and homeless' understates the most recent commonly reported counts and lacks a year or source.

claim: "She’s voted for 60 tax increases, hurting the middle class and small businesses."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as written because it doesn't identify who “She” is, nor give a timeframe or a clear definition of what counts as a ‘tax increase.’ Past fact‑checks show similar claims are often misleading: totals vary widely depending on whether procedural votes, amendments, budget offsets, or bills with mixed tax provisions are counted. Without a named lawmaker and a consistent counting method the claim cannot be confirmed and is therefore judged false.

claim: "U.S. military at the White House arresting Congress."
rationale: This claim is false. There are no credible reports, official statements, or evidence that U.S. military forces were deployed to the White House to arrest members of Congress, and such an action would directly conflict with constitutional separation of powers and normal legal constraints. An event of that magnitude would have been widely documented by major news outlets and government releases, which it was not.

claim: "Hundreds of illegal immigrants subject to detainers were released in the last week since the new sanctuary policy was adopted by the Travis County Sheriff's Office."
rationale: There is no verifiable evidence that the Travis County Sheriff’s Office released “hundreds” of people subject to ICE detainers within a single week as a direct result of a new sanctuary policy. While Travis County has limited cooperation with ICE detainers in some circumstances, detainers are civil requests (not judicial warrants) and releases depend on booking status, charges, and court orders; available reporting and jail data through mid‑2024 do not corroborate a sudden, policy‑driven release of hundreds in one week. The claim therefore overstates and misattributes routine jail release procedures to the policy change.

claim: Says The Washington Times ran a front-page headline that said, "President Gore."
rationale: There is no corroborated evidence in newspaper archives or reputable fact-checks that The Washington Times ran a front-page headline reading “President Gore.” While networks briefly projected Florida for Gore on election night 2000, that temporary call led to some incorrect early reports, but not a documented Washington Times front-page with that exact headline. The claim appears to conflate brief media projections or other papers’ coverage with an actual Times front-page banner.

claim: "Ron Johnson pushed through a special tax loophole that benefited his own family's business … Then he cashed out of the company for $5 million … (he has) doubled his wealth since taking office."
rationale: The claim combines several assertions that are not supported by public records. There is no evidence that Sen. Ron Johnson personally authored or “pushed through” a bespoke tax loophole to benefit his family’s business, and reporting indicates his business interests were largely divested or restructured before or around his time in office; while his financial disclosures show his net worth has increased since taking office, the specific timeline and the abrupt “cashed out for $5 million” sequence are misleading and unsupported as stated. As a packaged allegation it is therefore false.

claim: "For the first time in 35 years, we have more businesses closing than starting."
rationale: The statement is too specific but lacks a place or time and conflicts with known business-formation data. Historical series (e.g., U.S. Business Dynamics/Formation statistics) show years in recessions (such as 2008–09) when exits rose and net closures occurred, and more recently business applications surged during 2020–21; there is no clear, documented nationwide first occurrence exactly “in 35 years.” Because the claim as phrased is unsubstantiated and ambiguous, it is judged false.

claim: Says Cracker Barrel’s name has racist origins and its logo depicts a whip.
rationale: The claim combines two assertions that lack supporting evidence. Cracker Barrel was named for the old country-store practice of people gathering around a barrel of crackers, and the company and historical records do not show the chain was founded with racist intent; while the word “cracker” has other historical uses as a slur, that is not the origin of the restaurant’s name. The logo depicts an older man seated by a barrel holding a walking stick or cane, not a whip or noose.

claim: "Under the ruling of the Supreme Court, any lobbyist could go into any legislator and say, if you don't vote our way on this bill, we're going to run a million-dollar campaign against you in your district."
rationale: Supreme Court rulings such as Citizens United expanded protection for independent political expenditures as speech, but they did not legalize threats, bribery, or extortion of public officials. Federal and state laws (and other court decisions) still prohibit offering money or making coercive threats to obtain official action, and coordination rules limit how outside spending can be tied to a campaign or candidate.

claim: Says Joe Biden said: "If Haiti just quietly sunk into the Caribbean, or rose up 300 feet, it wouldn’t matter a whole lot in terms of our interests."
rationale: I could not find credible primary-source evidence that Joe Biden ever uttered that exact line; major fact-checkers and contemporary reporting do not document Biden saying “If Haiti just quietly sunk into the Caribbean, or rose up 300 feet, it wouldn’t matter a whole lot in terms of our interests.” Viral attributions appear to be paraphrases or fabrications without an audio/video/transcript citation. Because the claim lacks verifiable sourcing, it should be treated as false.

claim: Says there are fewer than 2,000 confirmed COVID-19 hospitalizations in the U.S.
rationale: The statement is false as a general claim because U.S. COVID-19 hospitalizations have routinely exceeded 2,000 during the pandemic and in multiple subsequent waves; national surveillance data have reported tens of thousands at peaks and often several thousand during surges. Because no date or timeframe is given the claim cannot be verified and is misleading as stated.

claim: Patrick Rose "voted to explore a state income tax."
rationale: I cannot find reliable evidence that Patrick Rose cast a vote to enact a state income tax. While Texas lawmakers occasionally vote to create study committees or hold hearings about revenue options, there is no clear record that Rose voted to impose a statewide income tax; assertions that he “voted to explore” it appear to conflate routine procedural votes or statements with enacting or authorizing an income tax. Given the ambiguity and lack of corroborating votes for an income tax, the claim is not supported.

claim: In Arizona, "there are only one and a half (Border Patrol) agents per every 10 square miles."
rationale: Arizona covers about 114,000 square miles, so 1.5 Border Patrol agents per 10 square miles would imply roughly 17,000 agents stationed in the state. Publicly reported Border Patrol staffing for Arizona sectors is only in the low thousands, far below that level, so the stated density is inconsistent with known counts. The claim also mixes a misleading statewide area metric with deployment patterns concentrated along the border.

claim: California’s Prop 55 "prevents $4 billion in new cuts to our schools."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Prop 55 extended higher income tax rates on high earners and was projected by analysts to raise billions that could be used for schools and healthcare, but it did not automatically or legally 'prevent $4 billion in new cuts' — any offset to school cuts would depend on annual budget choices and revenue realizations. The $4 billion figure appears to be a projection or campaign talking point rather than a guaranteed, legally binding prevention of cuts.

claim: "Two million more people just dropped out of Obamacare. It is in a death spiral."
rationale: There is no reliable evidence that 'two million more people just dropped out' of the Affordable Care Act marketplaces in a single recent event. Enrollment figures since the ARPA subsidy expansion have been broadly stable or higher and regulators have taken steps that undercut the textbook 'death spiral' scenario, so the claim conflates rhetoric with absent enrollment data.

claim: In the United Kingdom, "81% of COVID-19 deaths are among the vaccinated."
rationale: The claim is misleading as a blanket statement. UK data on the share of COVID-19 deaths among vaccinated people changed over time and depended on definitions (one dose vs fully/boosted), age groups, and the reporting period; while in some weeks a majority of deaths were among vaccinated people because most vulnerable people were vaccinated, a flat 81% figure is not generally supported without precise timeframe and definitions. Vaccination substantially reduced the individual risk of death, and proportions must be age-standardized to assess vaccine effectiveness.

claim: Says Jacob Blake "declared he had a gun in the car and was going to go get it" and was "brandishing" a knife
rationale: This claim is false as stated. Publicly released body-worn and bystander video of the Kenosha shooting do not show Jacob Blake declaring he had a gun in the car or stating he was going to retrieve one, nor do they show him brandishing a knife; he is seen walking to his vehicle and leaning inside when officers fired. While authorities later reported a small knife was recovered at the scene/vehicle, that is not evidence he was brandishing it or had announced an intent to get a gun.

claim: Says Conor Lamb "ran on a campaign that said very nice things about me."
rationale: The claim is presented without speaker, context, date, or source and no verifiable public record or reputable reporting confirms a campaign message from Conor Lamb containing the quoted line about an unspecified “me.” Because the statement as given cannot be corroborated and is ambiguous about who is being referenced, it should not be treated as a factual assertion without supporting evidence.

claim: Says Ohio Gov. John Kasich "got lucky with a thing called fracking," which "is why Ohio is doing well."
rationale: The claim oversimplifies and attributes Ohio's overall improvement solely to Kasich "getting lucky" with fracking. While the 2010s shale boom (Utica/Marcellus) did boost energy activity and benefited parts of Ohio, statewide economic performance also reflected the national post‑recession recovery, manufacturing trends, fiscal and tax policies, and other factors; the causal attribution to Kasich luck alone is unsubstantiated and misleading.

claim: "I never called for a partition" of Iraq.
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as written because it does not identify who ‘I’ refers to; without a named speaker and timeframe a blanket denial cannot be confirmed. Public record shows that various politicians and commentators have at times advocated partitioning or federalizing Iraq, so an unqualified statement of never calling for partition is unlikely to be reliably true.

claim: Seth Magaziner "plans to spend billions more of your money."
rationale: The statement is a vague partisan claim and is unsupported as written. Public descriptions of Seth Magaziner's platform include increased investments in areas like education, health care, and clean energy, but there is no clear, specific pledge or verifiable plan saying he will unconditionally spend 'billions more of your money' as the claim frames it. Without a cited policy, timeframe, or baseline for comparison, the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Mitt Romney and Paul Ryan would "eliminate the guarantee of Medicare."
rationale: Paul Ryan’s budget and Medicare proposals would replace traditional guaranteed defined-benefit Medicare with a premium-support/voucher-style system for future beneficiaries, and Mitt Romney endorsed Ryan’s approach during the 2012 campaign. That policy would remove the federal guarantee of a defined Medicare benefit for people covered under the new system (though both said current retirees would be protected). Thus the statement that Romney and Ryan would “eliminate the guarantee of Medicare” is accurate in the context of their proposed reforms for future enrollees.

claim: Greg Abbott "has campaigned with a sexual predator who has bragged about having sex with underage girls."
rationale: The claim names no individual and there is no public evidence that Gov. Greg Abbott has campaigned alongside a person who has openly bragged about having sex with underage girls. Abbott’s widely reported campaign partners have been major GOP figures (e.g., Trump, Pence) who are not on record as bragging about sexual activity with minors; while there are separate high‑profile cases of sexual predators (e.g., Jeffrey Epstein, Roy Moore), there is no verified record of Abbott campaigning with those individuals. Because the statement is unsourced and vague, it cannot be substantiated.

claim: A slain Chicago police officer left behind a two-month-old baby.
rationale: The claim lacks identifying details (which officer and when) and I am not aware of any widely reported case of a slain Chicago police officer explicitly described as having left behind a two-month-old baby. Major news and official statements about officers killed in the line of duty typically list survivors and ages; without a specific name or date there is no corroboration for this precise claim.

claim: Says Republican-approved changes to "make it more difficult to participate in Ohio elections include reducing in-person early voting from 35 days to six."
rationale: Ohio Republican-led legislation approved in 2023/2024 cut the period for in-person early (absentee) voting from the prior multi-week window (commonly 35 days) to a much shorter period of six days immediately before the election. Reporting and summaries of the enacted changes described this specific reduction as part of broader voting-rule revisions passed by Republicans.

claim: "Parents in Vail, Arizona just took over the school board — all according to the rules. Voted in a whole new board, and immediately removed the mask mandate."
rationale: I could not find definitive, corroborated evidence that voters in Vail, Arizona recently elected an entirely new school board and that the board immediately removed a mask mandate. While there have been contentious school-board races nationwide (including in Arizona) and some newly-elected trustees have sought to change mask policies, the claim as stated — a wholesale takeover followed by an immediate rescission of a district mask mandate — is not supported by readily verifiable reporting and oversimplifies how mask policies are governed. Mask rules are often subject to county health orders, state guidance, and legal processes that typically prevent an instantaneous, unilateral repeal by a newly seated board.

claim: The mobilization of the military in response to the storms in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands "is the largest ever mobilization of our military in a naval and marine operation" and an Air Force carrier there "was the first-ever as well."
rationale: The statement is inaccurate. Far larger naval and Marine Corps mobilizations have occurred historically (notably in World War II and other major wars) and large domestic responses (e.g., Hurricane Katrina) involved very substantial troop and Guard deployments; moreover the phrase “Air Force carrier” is incorrect—aircraft carriers are Navy vessels—so the claimed “first-ever” carrier presence is misstated or misleading.

claim: Newt Gingrich has been a proponent of selecting a president by popular vote instead of the Electoral College.
rationale: There is not a clear record of Newt Gingrich advocating abolishing the Electoral College in favor of a national popular vote. As a long-time Republican leader he has more commonly defended constitutional institutions like the Electoral College and criticized proposals to eliminate it, though individuals occasionally make nuanced comments. Because the claim asserts he has been a proponent, and reliable evidence of sustained advocacy is lacking, the statement is judged false.

claim: Says Mitt Romney is using "a million of his presidential campaign dollars to finance his Utah Senate race."
rationale: Contemporary reporting and Romney’s campaign filings indicate he loaned his 2018 Senate campaign roughly $1 million of personal funds, not a transfer of 2012 presidential campaign account dollars. While federal rules permit transfers between a candidate’s federal accounts, there is no clear evidence that Romney moved ‘presidential campaign dollars’ into his Utah Senate bid as the claim states.

claim: Ken Mercer "wants Sean Hannity and James Dobson included in social studies texts."
rationale: I could not find definitive evidence that Ken Mercer explicitly demanded that Sean Hannity and James Dobson be named for inclusion in social studies textbooks. While Mercer (as a Texas State Board of Education member) pushed for conservative viewpoints and greater coverage of religion and conservatism in curricula, the specific claim that he wanted those two individuals included is not clearly supported by reliable contemporaneous reporting or official motions. Absent a direct quote or motion naming Hannity and Dobson, the precise assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: " ... following World War II war crime trials were convened. The Japanese were tried and convicted and hung for war crimes committed against American POWs. Among those charges for which they were convicted was waterboarding."
rationale: It is true that many Japanese were tried and some were executed after World War II for war crimes, including abuses of Allied POWs, but there is no clear historical record that defendants were specifically convicted for an act labeled 'waterboarding.' Postwar prosecutions charged murder, torture, mistreatment and other war crimes, and executions at Sugamo/Tokyo did occur, but the specific charge of 'waterboarding' as named in the claim is not supported by standard trial records.

claim: "If a statue of a person in the park on a horse has both front legs in the air, the person died in battle. If the horse has one front leg in the air, the person died as a result of wounds received in battle. If the horse has all four legs on the ground, the person died of natural causes."
rationale: This is a widespread folk lore but not a factual rule. Art historians and museum sources report no universal ‘hoof code’ tying a horse’s pose to how the rider died; sculptors choose poses for aesthetic, structural, or symbolic reasons and many well-known statues contradict the claim. Therefore the statement is false as a general rule.

claim: "Muslims offended that their kids have to recite national anthem."
rationale: The claim is a broad generalization about all Muslims and lacks supporting evidence. Muslim communities are diverse: some individuals or parents in specific places have objected to pledges or anthem recitation for religious or political reasons, but many Muslim children and families participate in national rituals; there is no basis to say "Muslims" (as a whole) are offended. Therefore the blanket statement is false.

claim: One-third of the economic stimulus package was tax cuts.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous because it doesn’t specify which stimulus package. For the major recent U.S. packages commonly referenced (the 2009 ARRA and the 2020 CARES Act), tax cuts and tax-related provisions were substantial but constituted a minority share of total outlays rather than exactly one-third. Without a specific, sourced breakdown this blanket statement is misleading and not supported by standard budgetary analyses.

claim: Says Mitt Romney opposes requiring employers to cover contraception and would eliminate funding for Planned Parenthood.
rationale: Mitt Romney during his 2012 presidential campaign opposed the Obama administration’s contraceptive mandate and supported protections allowing employers (particularly religious employers) to decline to provide contraception coverage. He also publicly said he would work to end federal funding for Planned Parenthood. Both positions were repeatedly stated in his campaign speeches and policy statements, though details and exceptions were debated.

claim: "Sixty percent of New Jersey doctors do not accept Medicaid patients."
rationale: Available national and state-level surveys show a majority of physicians accept Medicaid patients; for example, national KFF/AMA-type data indicate roughly 60–75% of office-based physicians accept Medicaid (so only about 25–40% do not). There is no credible evidence that 60% of New Jersey doctors refuse Medicaid outright, and reported rates vary by specialty and by whether practices accept new Medicaid patients.

claim: Twitter employee named Jackson Mulholland resigned in a tweet after Elon Musk joined the company’s board.
rationale: Contemporary fact-checking and news reporting found no evidence that a person named Jackson Mulholland was a Twitter employee who resigned in a tweet after Elon Musk joined the board. The viral resignation post appears to have come from an account not verifiably linked to Twitter staff and was not corroborated by credible media or Twitter statements.

claim: "The Public Employee Retirement System is making more millionaires than the Oregon state lottery."
rationale: The claim is imprecise and unsupported as stated: it lacks a timeframe and definition of “making millionaires” (e.g., lifetime pension totals, net worth, or annual payouts). While Oregon PERS pays many retirees large lifetime benefits and the Oregon Lottery produces only a few million-dollar jackpot winners annually, there’s no clear public data directly comparing counts under a consistent definition, so the assertion cannot be verified as presented. Given the ambiguity and missing data, the claim is not reliable.

claim: Says Texas high school "graduation rates are at an all-time high—the third-highest in the nation—which represents a significant turnaround from just a few short years ago."
rationale: This mixes a true element (Texas graduation rates have risen) with inaccurate specifics. Texas has reached record highs in some recent years, but it has not consistently been the third-highest state nationally on the common 4‑year adjusted cohort graduation-rate measures—several states have reported higher rates—and the improvement has been a multi-year trend rather than a dramatic turnaround "from just a few short years ago."

claim: About "1 percent of all the gun sellers are responsible for more than half of the guns that are used in crimes."
rationale: This statement matches multiple ATF trace-data analyses and subsequent academic summaries that found roughly 1% of licensed gun dealers (FFLs) were associated with about half (often cited ~50–60%) of firearms traced to crimes. The key caveat is that these findings refer to traced crime guns and licensed dealers, not literally every possible seller or every crime gun.

claim: "$400,000 ... is more money than I’ve ever made" in a year.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as presented because it does not identify who said it or the year referenced. Whether $400,000 is more than someone has ever made in a year depends entirely on that individual’s earnings history, which requires tax returns or payroll records to confirm. Without a named person and documentation the assertion is unsubstantiated.

claim: Says Ted Cruz "has pledged to eliminate" the U.S. Department of Education, which would end federal aid to college students.
rationale: It is true that Ted Cruz has publicly advocated eliminating the U.S. Department of Education, but abolishing the agency would not by itself automatically end federal student aid. Federal grant and loan programs are created and funded by statute, so ending those programs would require separate congressional repeal or reauthorization decisions; the department is the administrator, not the sole legal source of the programs.

claim: "Illegal counterfeiting and piracy costs the U.S. economy $100 billion... every year."
rationale: There is no authoritative, single-year consensus that illegal counterfeiting and piracy cost the U.S. exactly $100 billion annually. Estimates vary widely by source, year and by what is counted (physical counterfeit goods, online piracy, lost sales, taxes, jobs), so the round $100 billion figure is not a reliably supported precise fact.

claim: DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz "denied unemployment went up under Obama."
rationale: Contemporaneous news coverage records that DNC chair Debbie Wasserman Schultz publicly asserted that unemployment rose under George W. Bush rather than under Barack Obama, effectively denying that unemployment went up under Obama. That statement contradicted Bureau of Labor Statistics data showing the unemployment rate rose sharply early in Obama’s presidency (peaking in 2009).

claim: Says Texas routinely gets "a lot more federal spending" than it pays in taxes.
rationale: State-by-state federal fiscal balance reports and Treasury/BEA analyses show Texas is generally not a large, routine net recipient of federal spending relative to taxes paid. While Texas receives substantial federal dollars for defense, disaster relief, and programs, overall it typically pays about as much or more into the federal government than it gets back, so the claim that it 'routinely gets a lot more' is an overstatement.

claim: "Last week Senator Obama's running mate said, get this, 'Raising taxes is patriotic.' "
rationale: There is no credible reporting or contemporaneous record that Obama’s running mate recently said the quoted line. Public transcripts and news coverage of statements by Joe Biden (Obama’s running mate) do not show him saying “Raising taxes is patriotic” last week, so the claim appears to be a misattribution or fabrication. Without corroborating evidence the statement should be treated as false.

claim: "Right now, we are about 4% behind the (census) response rate where we were in 2010. But for Black and Latino and Native American communities, they’re behind by 10%."
rationale: The statement gives precise percentage gaps but provides no date or source and does not match the contemporaneous, publicly released Census Bureau response-rate snapshots which show that overall and subgroup deficits changed over time. While Black, Latino and Native American populations have historically had lower self‑response and were behind at various points, the specific claim of “about 4%” overall and “10%” for those three groups is not corroborated as a stable, documented figure across official releases. Without a clear timeframe or data source the precise numbers are not verifiable and are likely misleading.

claim: "More businesses are closing than opening in Virginia today."
rationale: The claim is presented as a real-time fact but cannot be verified: there is no publicly available, authoritative source that reports business openings vs. closings in Virginia on a single-day basis. State and federal statistics on business births and deaths are published monthly, quarterly, or annually and show net formations vary over time, so asserting more businesses are closing than opening “today” is unsupported without a specific, current data source. Because of this unverifiable, time-specific phrasing, the claim is judged false in the absence of evidence.

claim: Says John F. Kennedy said, "If a Supreme Court Justice died one day before the election, it would be more Constitutional to indefinitely postpone the election than postpone the confirmation a single day."
rationale: There is no credible historical record or citation in John F. Kennedy’s collected speeches or archival materials showing he made this statement; the wording appears in modern social media as a misattribution. The content and phrasing are anachronistic and inconsistent with documented JFK rhetoric and practice regarding elections and judicial confirmations.

claim: "Vern Buchanan. His old business was caught illegally funneling over $60,000 in campaign donations to Buchanan to influence his election."
rationale: Reporting and enforcement actions found that employees/associates connected to Vern Buchanan's businesses participated in a scheme of reimbursed (straw) contributions totaling roughly $60,000–$65,000 to his campaign, and some individuals pleaded guilty or were fined. While Buchanan himself was not criminally charged, the donations were determined to be illegal conduit contributions funneled to his campaign. The claim's core assertion about illegal funneling of roughly $60K by his old business's associates is therefore accurate.

claim: "We need to pass a carbon tax to stop climate change. Break up the Wall Street banks. And stop the government spying on innocent Americans. Cory Booker doesn’t support any of these ideas."
rationale: The claim is incorrect because Cory Booker has not uniformly opposed these ideas. He has publicly supported strong climate action (including market-based pricing approaches and other carbon-reduction policies), has called for reining in and more strictly regulating large Wall Street banks, and has backed limits on bulk government surveillance and voted for surveillance reform measures. Thus it is inaccurate to say he doesn’t support any of the three proposals in the statement.

claim: The U.S. "only ranks 25th worldwide on defense spending as a percentage of GDP."
rationale: This statement is inaccurate as a blanket claim. Reputable datasets (e.g., SIPRI, World Bank) show U.S. military spending around roughly 3.5–4% of GDP in recent years and its rank by percent of GDP varies by year and data source; it is not consistently or reliably “25th” worldwide. Many small states do record higher shares, so the precise rank depends on the year and methodology, making the categorical claim misleading.

claim: It’s warmer on Mars than it is in parts of the United States and Canada during the polar vortex.
rationale: The statement is true in the sense that during extreme polar-vortex outbreaks some locations in the U.S. and Canada reach temperatures colder than typical Mars surface conditions, and parts of Mars (especially daytime equatorial areas) can be warmer than those extreme lows. Mars has a wide temperature range (very cold on average but with daytime highs that can exceed Earth’s extreme cold points), so direct comparisons depend on which Mars location/time and which Earth location/time are being compared.

claim: "Inflation has gone up every month of the Biden presidency and just hit another 40-year high."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. U.S. inflation (CPI) did not rise every month during President Biden's term — monthly CPI readings have both increased and decreased — and the notable ~40-year high in headline CPI (~9.1%) occurred in mid-2022 rather than having 'just' been hit again recently. Since that peak headline inflation has generally moved downward.

claim: Says state Rep. Diana Maldonado of Round Rock uses Craigslist to hire campaign block walkers.
rationale: I found no reliable or public evidence up to mid‑2024 that State Rep. Diana Maldonado used Craigslist to hire campaign block walkers. The claim appears unverified; campaigns more commonly recruit volunteers through party networks or hire canvassing firms, and a specific allegation like this would normally be documented by local reporting or campaign records. Without such corroboration, the statement should be treated as false.

claim: Says Marco Rubio "was for immigration reform and a pathway to citizenship before he was against it."
rationale: Marco Rubio helped craft and supported the 2013 bipartisan 'Gang of Eight' immigration bill that included a path to legal status leading to citizenship, but by his 2016 presidential campaign he publicly rejected a broad pathway to citizenship and opposed similar measures. The claim summarizes that sequence of positions accurately.

claim: Ninety percent of the job growth in Virginia has been in the private sector.
rationale: The statement gives no timeframe or source and thus cannot be verified as an absolute. Labor statistics (BLS and Virginia employment reports) do show that most job growth in many periods has been in the private sector, but the exact share varies by the reporting window and is not reliably 90% without specifying a period. Because the claim is an unqualified numeric assertion with no supporting citation, it is not supported as stated.

claim: President Obama "promised" families making less than $250,000 a year would not see taxes go up, but "Obamacare raises 18 different taxes."
rationale: This is misleading. Obama did pledge that households earning under $250,000 would not have their income taxes raised, and the Affordable Care Act included multiple new revenue provisions, but the commonly cited "18 taxes" list mixes distinct items (e.g., taxes on high earners, employer/insurer fees, limits on deductions, Medicare payment reductions and penalties) rather than 18 direct tax increases on families under $250,000. Most of the ACA provisions targeted higher-income individuals, employers, or insurers, so the claim that Obamacare raised 18 taxes that violated the specific promise is false.

claim: "I am the only (state attorney general) in America fighting to hold the big tech companies accountable for their behavior."
rationale: The claim is incorrect: multiple state attorneys general have investigated, sued, or joined multistate coalitions against large technology companies on antitrust and consumer-protection grounds. No single state AG is uniquely or solely 'fighting' big tech—several have brought parallel or joint actions against companies like Google, Facebook/Meta, Apple, and Amazon in recent years.

claim: Says under Mayor Cory Booker, Newark has seen "violent crime up five years in a row, murder up five years in a row."
rationale: Available year-by-year crime data for Newark during Cory Booker’s mayoralty do not show a consistent five-year straight increase in violent crime or murders. While there were spikes in some years (notably in homicides around 2012–2013), overall violent-crime trends during his term had fluctuations and declines in several years rather than five consecutive annual increases. Fact-checkers and official crime reports do not support the literal wording of "up five years in a row."

claim: Says that when adjusted for inflation and population growth, state general revenue spending has decreased 10.7 percent on his watch.
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it lacks the actor, the state, and the exact time period of "on his watch." Without a defined baseline and end date, one cannot confirm a 10.7% decline after adjusting for inflation and population. Because these adjustments require specific CPI and population data and official state budget figures, the precise percentage cannot be validated from the claim alone. Given the missing context, the claim is treated as false until substantiated by cited budget reports and methodology.

claim: BREAKING: Trump Just Ended Welfare For One HUGE Group For 5 Years!
rationale: The claim is false: there is no credible evidence that President Trump "ended welfare" for a large group for five years in one action. While his administration tightened immigration 'public charge' rules and proposed restrictions on immigrants' use of certain benefits, that is not the same as a blanket five-year termination of welfare for a huge group. The headline is vague and sensational and does not match documented policy actions.

claim: "Republicans control the U.S. Senate with 54 seats, but those 54 senators were elected by only two-thirds the number of voters who elected the Democrats. In the Senate, the majority party represents a minority of the people."
rationale: The specific numeric claim is not supported: I cannot verify that Republicans hold 54 Senate seats or that those 54 senators were elected with only two‑thirds of the votes that elected Democratic senators. While it is true that Senate apportionment (two senators per state) can produce a majority of seats that represent fewer total voters than the minority party in some election cycles, the asserted 54‑seat/2‑to‑1 vote gap is an overstatement and depends entirely on which races and years are aggregated.

claim: A bill to advance the Keystone XL Pipeline "is an earmark" under House rules.
rationale: Under House rules an "earmark" refers to a congressional directive that provides targeted spending, tax, or tariff benefits to a specific entity or limited recipient. A standalone bill that authorizes or advances construction of the Keystone XL pipeline as general policy or permitting action would not meet that earmark definition unless it explicitly includes directed federal spending or a targeted benefit naming a recipient.

claim: Says Scott Walker "has taken money away from internet expansion in our state."
rationale: The claim as phrased is imprecise and not clearly supported by widely documented, unambiguous evidence. While Governor Scott Walker's budgets and vetoes affected various state programs and funding lines at different times, there is no simple, well-established fact that he singularly "took money away from internet expansion in our state" without specifying which program, year, or state. Because the statement lacks context and is not directly corroborated in a general sense, it cannot be accepted as a clear fact.

claim: "I’m proud to say that under my administration, as you just heard, we will be building the first new heavy icebreakers the United States has seen in over 40 years."
rationale: The last new U.S. heavy icebreakers (USCGC Polar Star and Polar Sea) were commissioned in the mid-1970s, so the U.S. had not built new heavy icebreakers for over 40 years. The Coast Guard’s Polar Security Cutter (heavy icebreaker) program, begun in recent years, is intended to produce new heavy icebreakers under the current administration, making the statement accurate in substance.

claim: "We’re the seventh highest taxed state in America. And that’s not just state, it’s local as well."
rationale: The claim is not verifiable as stated because it omits which state, which year, and which tax metric is being used. Rankings of "highest taxed" states vary widely depending on whether you measure total state taxes, combined state and local taxes, taxes per capita, or taxes as a share of income, and different sources (Census, Tax Foundation) produce different lists. While some states have ranked seventh on some measures in some years, the blanket assertion without context cannot be confirmed.

claim: "I've created over 40,000 jobs."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it omits who is claiming it, the time period, and whether the jobs are direct hires, indirect/induced jobs, or claimed via companies they founded. Without payroll records, audited company employment data, or independent economic analysis attributing that many hires to a single person, the claim cannot be substantiated. In absence of supporting evidence, I mark it as false per the instruction to default to FALSE when uncertain.

claim: Barack Obama "is the first ex-president to ever speak against his successor."
rationale: The claim is false: earlier ex-presidents have publicly spoken against their successors. For example, Theodore Roosevelt openly denounced William Howard Taft’s policies and even ran against him in 1912, and there are other historical instances of former presidents criticizing successors.

claim: Says "47 additional counties used the same software that caused a ‘glitch’ in Antrim County (that switched 6,000 votes from Trump to Biden in that county)" and votes in the state are "potentially fraudulent."
rationale: The claim conflates vendor use with an identical software bug and misstates the nature of the Antrim error. Antrim’s discrepancy resulted from a reporting/configuration error that was corrected and confirmed by hand and machine audits; independent reviews and state officials found no evidence that machines ‘switched’ votes or that widespread fraud occurred. While many Michigan counties used voting equipment from the same vendors, they did not experience the same reporting error and versions/configurations differ, so the assertion that 47 other counties’ votes are ‘potentially fraudulent’ is unsupported.

claim: Says rejecting federal aid to expand Medicaid in Texas will "send $9 billion in federal taxes paid by Texans to other states to insure their working poor."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While rejecting Medicaid expansion means Texas would not receive federal matching dollars that expansion states do receive (and analyses have produced multi‑billion dollar annual estimates), federal tax revenue is pooled nationally and not literally dollars paid by Texans sent directly to other states. The unspecified $9 billion figure lacks a clear timeframe and source, and the characterization that those are "federal taxes paid by Texans" is inaccurate framing.

claim: In Texas, "the No. 1 name for new male babies — many of whom will vote one day — is Jose."
rationale: Recent state-level baby-name data from the U.S. Social Security Administration show names like Liam (and other names) as the top male baby name in Texas in recent years; Jose, while common among Hispanic communities, has not been the No. 1 name statewide. The claim gives no year or source and appears to misstate current SSA rankings.

claim: "If you take into account all the people who are struggling for work, or have just stopped looking, the real unemployment rate is over 15 percent."
rationale: The statement is too general and misleading: whether the “real” rate exceeds 15% depends on the time period and the measure used. The BLS broad measure (U‑6), which includes discouraged and marginally attached workers and those working part‑time for economic reasons, exceeded 15% during deep recessions (e.g., around 2009–2010 and in April 2020) but is well below 15% in many other periods. Without a specified country and date the claim presented as a blanket fact is false.

claim: "This administration is slashing the Navy to pay for more Obamacare."
rationale: There is no evidence that the administration took money out of the Navy and directly used it to 'pay for more Obamacare.' The Affordable Care Act was financed through dedicated revenues and Medicare/Medicaid savings and appropriations for defense are set separately by Congress; while budget caps and sequestration have pressured Navy programs, those savings were not formally reallocated to ACA.

claim: Sweden had few COVID deaths in July, despite low vaccination rates, relaxed lockdown rules and low mask compliance.
rationale: The claim is ambiguous and cannot be verified as stated. Sweden did have relaxed measures and low mask uptake early in the pandemic and experienced lower reported COVID deaths in some summer months (e.g., after the spring 2020 peak), but vaccination availability and coverage, and mortality levels, varied by year; the statement as a general claim about “July” without a year is misleading. Overall excess deaths in 2020 were substantial and vaccination rates were not uniformly low in later summers, so the blanket claim is not reliably true.

claim: "I'll tell you what I can tell this country: If they want a president who doesn't believe in God, there's probably plenty of choices."
rationale: I cannot find a reliable attribution for this exact quotation to any well-documented public political figure or speech. The line reads like a paraphrase or misattribution and is not corroborated by major records of campaign speeches, debates, or media transcripts I know. Without verifiable sourcing, the claim that this was said as quoted is unproven and treated as false.

claim: Says Joe Biden tweeted, "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused."
rationale: There is no record or credible reporting that President Joe Biden posted a tweet saying "the way white people talk leaving minorities confused." Such an explicit, racially phrased tweet would have been widely documented and debunked by fact-checkers; it does not appear in Biden's verified social media history and is inconsistent with his typical public communications. The claim appears to be a fabricated or misattributed quote.

claim: Republican election challengers were unfairly barred from observing absentee ballot processing and counting in Detroit.
rationale: Contemporaneous reporting and court rulings from the relevant Detroit/counting locations indicate Republican challengers were generally allowed to observe absentee processing but were required to stay at specified distances and follow rules; some individuals were temporarily removed for violating rules or causing disruptions. There is no evidence they were systematically or permanently barred from observing the counts, so the claim that they were "unfairly barred" is misleading.

claim: Between 40 and 50 percent of tax filers do not owe any income tax.
rationale: This is generally accurate for recent years: analyses of IRS and tax-policy data show roughly 40–50% of tax units/filing units had zero federal individual income tax liability in several recent years (around mid-40% in many estimates).
