rationale: There is no clear, publicly verifiable record that the NRA assigned an 'A' rating to a politician named Gary Farmer, and without that evidence calling his claim an "absolute lie" is unsupported. The statement is ambiguous about which Gary Farmer and which year/office are meant, so asserting an absolute falsehood requires direct NRA documentation that is not available here.

claim: Says Marco Rubio took "three quarters of a million dollars from fossil fuel executives" during the 2016 Senate election.
rationale: The precise claim that Rubio “took three quarters of a million dollars from fossil fuel executives” in the 2016 Senate election is not supported by clear, verifiable public records as stated. Campaign finance reports show Rubio received money from the energy industry in 2016, but totals vary widely depending on whether one counts corporate/industry PACs, party committees, or individual executives, and there is no unambiguous record that exactly $750,000 came from named fossil-fuel executives alone.

claim: Says a California surfer was "alone, in the ocean," when he was arrested for violating the state’s stay-at-home order.
rationale: Contemporary reporting and video from the incident show the surfer was not arrested while ‘alone, in the ocean.’ Authorities and media described other people in the water/on the beach and said officers made contact onshore after warnings, so the claim that he was alone in the ocean at arrest is inaccurate. The arrest occurred after police interaction rather than an isolated in-water apprehension.

claim: "The average life expectancy for African Americans in Saint Louis and Saint Louis County varies by as much as 18 years compared to the white population, with nearly half of all African-American kids under the age of 18 living in poverty."
rationale: Local public-health analyses and media reporting have documented life-expectancy gaps on the order of nearly two decades between predominantly Black neighborhoods and predominantly white neighborhoods in the St. Louis city/county area, and U.S. Census/ACS snapshots have shown Black child poverty rates in parts of St. Louis at or near 50 percent. Both parts of the claim align with published regional analyses, though exact numbers depend on the years and exact geographic boundaries used.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton "was asked repeatedly to provide security in Benghazi on several occasions, including direct cables."
rationale: Contemporaneous State Department cables and later investigations (including the State Department Accountability Review Board and congressional inquiries) document repeated requests for enhanced security in Benghazi and other Libyan posts that were routed through State Department channels. Those requests included formal cables and appeals for additional resources; the ARB and oversight reports concluded such requests were made multiple times but were not fully met. The only ambiguity is whether every request was sent personally to Secretary Clinton rather than to State Department staff.

claim: "(Texas Republicans) believe in abolishing Social Security, abolishing V.A. health care."
rationale: The claim overgeneralizes. While some Texas Republicans and activists have advocated privatizing or restructuring Social Security and promoting private options for veterans' care, neither Texas Republicans as a whole nor mainstream GOP leaders uniformly call for abolishing Social Security or VA health care; most discussions are about reform or privatization, not outright elimination.

claim: "Texas mothers are dying during childbirth at the highest rates in the nation."
rationale: The claim is not correct as a general statement — while Texas has had elevated maternal mortality compared with many states and experienced a notable rise in the 2010s, recent CDC/NCHS state-level data show other states (for example Louisiana and Mississippi in several recent years) with higher maternal mortality rates. Differences in definitions, reporting methods, and the specific year or measure (maternal mortality ratio, pregnancy-related deaths, or pregnancy-associated deaths) affect rankings, so Texas is not consistently the highest.

claim: Says Russ Feingold supported a stimulus plan that allowed a company to create 3,000 jobs in China.
rationale: The claim is unsubstantiated and vague — no credible evidence links Sen. Russ Feingold to supporting a specific stimulus provision that explicitly "allowed a company to create 3,000 jobs in China." Feingold voted on broad stimulus measures (which aimed to preserve/create U.S. jobs), and while some federal recipients later had overseas supply-chain activity, that is not the same as a law authorizing creation of 3,000 Chinese jobs or Feingold endorsing such an outcome.

claim: Says Baltimore police are "trained by Mossad and Shin Bet."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Baltimore Police Department was directly trained by Mossad or Shin Bet. While some U.S. police agencies have at times received instruction from Israeli security firms or former Israeli military personnel, claims that Israel's Mossad or Shin Bet (official Israeli intelligence agencies) directly train municipal U.S. police forces are unfounded.

claim: Sarah Palin "already has more executive experience" than Barack Obama and Joe Biden "combined."
rationale: The claim is false as a general statement. Palin’s executive experience (Mayor of Wasilla ~1996–2002 and Governor of Alaska Dec 2006–July 2009, roughly eight to nine years total) is less than the combined executive service of Barack Obama (two terms as President, 2009–2017) and Joe Biden (Vice President 2009–2017 and President beginning 2021). While the assertion had some basis in 2008 before Obama or Biden had held executive office, it is not true when judged against their subsequent executive tenures.

claim: "In 1960, most black children were raised in two-parent, monogamous families." Today "we have only 20 percent of black children being raised in two-parent, monogamous families..."
rationale: The claim mixes a true historical point with a false current statistic. It is true that a clear majority of Black children in 1960 lived in two‑parent households, but the statement that today only 20% of Black children are raised in two‑parent, monogamous families is incorrect — recent U.S. Census and family‑structure data show a much larger share (roughly one‑third to two‑fifths or higher, depending on whether cohabiting parents are counted). The decline since 1960 is real, but the “20 percent” figure substantially understates the current two‑parent prevalence and conflates definitions (married vs. cohabiting).

claim: "Over the last 40 years, real wage growth has been flatlined because of the policies of the Federal Reserve ... It was all driven by the Federal Reserve."
rationale: This claim over-attributes a complex, multi-decade phenomenon to a single actor. While median real wages have been relatively stagnant for much of the past forty years, economists attribute that stagnation to a mix of factors—globalization, technological change, declining unionization and labor share, fiscal/tax policy, and market concentration—alongside monetary policy. The Federal Reserve affects inflation and short-term employment, but it cannot plausibly be said to have “driven” all long-run real wage trends by itself.

claim: Says Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker is making voting more difficult by closing Department of Motor Vehicles offices where "low-income voters" live.
rationale: Under Gov. Scott Walker’s administration Wisconsin consolidated and closed a number of DMV service locations and concurrently pursued a strict voter ID law that requires state-issued photo IDs. Critics and news reports at the time documented closures or reduced hours in urban and lower-income areas and argued that reducing local DMV access made it harder for low-income residents to obtain the required IDs and thus to vote. The linkage is supported by the timing and by how IDs are obtained through DMVs, though intent remains disputed.

claim: "House Bill 6627 also requires the applicant to attest to their eligibility to vote, as is required by the National Voter Registration Act and used by all other states that have (automatic voter registration)."
rationale: The claim conflates separate issues and overstates uniformity. The National Voter Registration Act does require a voter-registration attestation on the federal form, but automatic registration laws are implemented differently by states; not every AVR program requires a separate, explicit attestation in the AVR transaction itself and some rely on attestations already made on motor-vehicle or agency forms. Without specifying the jurisdiction and checking the exact text of House Bill 6627, the blanket statement that HB 6627 "also requires the applicant to attest" and that this matches "all other states" is not supported.

claim: Says a new report shows the "devastating tax hikes (in the health care law) will have on middle-class Kentuckians."
rationale: The claim asserts that a "new report" shows the health care law produces "devastating tax hikes" on middle‑class Kentuckians, but there is no widely accepted report finding large, broad-based tax increases hitting the middle class in Kentucky. Major analyses of the Affordable Care Act show most new taxes target higher earners, insurers, or specific items (e.g., net investment income tax, Medicare payroll surtax on high incomes, excise on high‑cost plans), not sweeping devastating tax hikes on the middle class; impacts vary by income and circumstance. Without a specific, credible report showing otherwise, the blanket claim is not supported.

claim: More than 500,000 mail in ballots in Virginia and 200,000 in Nevada were sent to dead people or pets
rationale: This claim is false. Independent fact-checkers and state election officials found no evidence that hundreds of thousands of mail ballots were sent to dead people or pets; the large viral figures conflated different mailings (for example mass mailings of absentee ballot applications or registration forms) and the actual counts of ballots or mailings sent to deceased or non-human addresses were orders of magnitude smaller (in the hundreds or low thousands at most). The claim mixes categories and inflates numbers beyond what officials and audits reported.

claim: "Some even advocate wiping out 401(k)s entirely and replacing them with government-run accounts."
rationale: The claim is accurate in its broad sense: a number of policy analysts, academics and some progressive lawmakers have indeed proposed eliminating or substantially replacing private 401(k) plans with government-run or publicly managed retirement accounts (or a public-option alternative). These proposals have appeared in policy debates as alternatives to the current employer-based system, even if they vary in scope and popularity.

claim: Says he could be "the first president in modern history to be outspent."
rationale: The statement as presented is unverifiable because it lacks a named speaker and timeframe; no clear evidence identifies someone making that exact claim. More importantly, the broad claim that a president could be ‘‘the first in modern history to be outspent’’ is unlikely without context, since incumbents in modern U.S. elections typically have fundraising and spending advantages, and exceptions would need specific campaign-year data to substantiate. Given the ambiguity and lack of attribution, the claim cannot be confirmed.

claim: "This election actually was not unusually close."
rationale: The claim is unverifiable as stated because it does not identify which election or what metric of 'closeness' is meant (popular vote margin, electoral votes, seat margins, etc.). Whether an election is 'unusually close' requires comparing that specific race's margin to historical norms for that office and jurisdiction; without that context the assertion cannot be supported.

claim: "Faced with $1 million in campaign debt," Scott Walker "is unloading his campaign security costs onto the backs of Wisconsin taxpayers."
rationale: The claim implies an improper or exceptional shifting of campaign security bills to taxpayers. While Scott Walker did have campaign debt (roughly around $1 million at times), it is standard practice for taxpayers to fund security for a sitting governor during travel and public appearances, including many events that overlap with campaign activity; press fact‑checks found no clear evidence he uniquely redirected campaign security costs beyond standard state‑provided protection and existing reimbursement rules. Thus the broad accusation that he is "unloading" campaign security costs onto taxpayers is misleading.

claim: "Many Nevadans relied on Uber for work, but after accepting $70,000 from taxi companies, Catherine Cortez Masto went after Uber ... (driving) them out of town."
rationale: The claim conflates and misstates events. Catherine Cortez Masto, as Nevada Attorney General, supported stricter fingerprint background checks that affected ride‑sharing regulation and the taxi industry did make political contributions, but there is no clear evidence that she accepted exactly $70,000 from taxi companies and then personally 'went after' Uber in a way that 'drove them out of town.' Regulatory actions were broader, involved the legislature and other officials, and did not permanently expel Uber from Nevada in the manner implied.

claim: "We now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil."
rationale: The statement is presented without specifying a country or timeframe and is therefore misleading; global and many national datasets show oil and gas employment still equals or exceeds solar employment. Solar jobs have grown rapidly and in some local or sub-sector comparisons (e.g., solar installers versus coal mining) solar can outnumber specific fossil-fuel occupations, but the broad claim that "we now have more jobs in solar than we do in oil" is not supported by general global or national employment data.

claim: "Biden is computer generated."
rationale: The claim that President Joe Biden is "computer generated" is false. Biden is a real, living human being with verifiable biographical records, decades of public service, live appearances, interactions with other people, and legal documentation. While digitally created or manipulated images and videos (deepfakes) of him can exist, that does not make the person himself computer generated.

claim: "There's not a single, solitary example that" signing the bill to end Glass-Steagall "had anything to do with the financial crash."
rationale: The claim is incorrect. The 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act repealed key Glass–Steagall barriers and allowed commercial and investment banking to combine, a change widely cited by regulators, investigators and many economists as a contributing factor to the 2007–2008 financial crisis. Multiple concrete examples (growth of universal banks like Citigroup, expanded securitization and proprietary trading within banking groups) and official reports identify links between deregulation and the crash, even though repeal was not the sole cause.

claim: Says the U.S. Postal Service has taken no taxpayer aid since 1971, funds operations entirely from the sale of stamps and related products and makes an "operational profit year after year."
rationale: This claim is misleading. While the Postal Reorganization Act (1970–71) made USPS a largely self‑supporting entity that relies primarily on postage and service revenues, the Postal Service has received federal support, loans and appropriations for specific purposes at times and has not produced an uninterrupted “operational profit year after year.” USPS has reported operating and net losses in many years (exacerbated by the 2006 retiree health prefunding requirement) and has used extraordinary federal measures or financing in some periods.

claim: "Not even Tim Kaine is willing" to say he trusts Hillary Clinton.
rationale: Tim Kaine publicly served as Hillary Clinton’s 2016 running mate, repeatedly endorsed her and defended her record, and in interviews and speeches expressed confidence in her judgment. There is no broadly known, verifiable pattern showing he refused to say he trusted her; on the contrary, his role and public statements indicate willingness to vouch for her. Without a narrowly defined time and source for the quoted refusal, the blanket claim is misleading.

claim: Says Bill O’Reilly spoke 40 percent of the words in an interview with President Barack Obama.
rationale: Available transcripts and contemporaneous fact-checking do not support the claim that Bill O’Reilly spoke 40% of the words in his interview with President Obama. Counts of the actual interview dialogue show the president spoke the majority of words; no reliable analysis corroborates a 40% share for O’Reilly. The claim appears to be an exaggeration or misstatement of how much the host spoke.

claim: "Most" of the Bush tax cuts went to people "in the top 3 percent of this country."
rationale: Independent distributional analyses (CBO, Treasury and Tax Policy Center) show the Bush-era rate reductions were tilted toward higher-income households, but they did not send more than half of the total dollar value to the top 3 percent. Most estimates find the bulk of the benefits concentrated in the top quintile (top 20%), with the top 1–3% receiving a substantial but not majority share of the total cuts. The claim overstates the share going to the top 3%.

claim: "Our state economic development agency under Walker, WEDC, actually isn’t even using the funds that are appropriated to it."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate as an absolute. Under Governor Walker, the Wisconsin Economic Development Corporation did receive and disburse appropriated funds for loans, grants, and tax-credit programs; state audits criticized WEDC’s oversight and accounting practices but did not conclude the agency “isn’t even using” its appropriations. While some funds were spent slowly or remained unobligated at times, the agency did make significant expenditures and program payments.

claim: Sheila Jackson Lee of Texas said: ‘Hey, all you wrinkly, white-aged has-beens: It’s time for you to die and let the next generation have your spot on the planet.’
rationale: This quote is not supported by any credible reporting, congressional transcript, or video record and has been circulated as a fabricated/misattributed social media meme. Major fact-checkers and news archives show no evidence that Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee made this statement, and it appears to be invented or wrongly attributed.

claim: Says "Former President Barack Obama arrested for ESPIONAGE."
rationale: There are no credible reports, official records, or reliable media accounts that former President Barack Obama was arrested for espionage. An arrest of a former president would be a major, widely documented event; no such evidence exists and the claim aligns with known misinformation patterns.

claim: It's "not true" that since he's been the president, executions in Iran have increased by four times.
rationale: Independent monitoring groups reported a substantial rise in executions after the current president took office in mid‑2021, but published counts and analyses do not support a consistent fourfold (4x) increase. Reported increases vary by exact timeframe and baseline year, and most credible tallies show a smaller multiplier (roughly 2–3x for 2022 versus 2021) rather than 4x.

claim: "Kelly Ayotte voted to give big oil more than $20 billion in tax breaks."
rationale: There is no clear roll call showing Ayotte cast a single vote that directly "gave big oil more than $20 billion". She voted for broader tax-extender and budget measures that included some energy-related tax provisions, but the $20 billion figure is a misleading aggregation or attribution to a single vote and depends on time frame and scoring assumptions. The claim therefore overstates and misattributes the impact of any single Ayotte vote.

claim: Says the Obamas are connected to the Varsity Blues college admissions scandal.
rationale: There is no credible evidence or official allegation tying Barack or Michelle Obama to the 2019 Varsity Blues college admissions fraud. The DOJ indictments and extensive media reporting identified specific parents and intermediaries (e.g., Rick Singer, Lori Loughlin, Felicity Huffman) and did not include the Obamas. Claims of Obama involvement are unsupported by public records or court filings.

claim: "Under the federal Controlled Substance Act, marijuana is listed in the same Schedule I as heroin," even though "marijuana is not a killer drug like heroin."
rationale: The federal Controlled Substances Act does place cannabis (marijuana) in Schedule I alongside heroin. Medical and public-health evidence shows heroin carries a high risk of fatal opioid overdose, whereas there are no well-documented cases of death from cannabis toxicity alone, so characterizing marijuana as not a “killer drug like heroin” is broadly accurate.

claim: "Under @BarackObama illegal immigration dropped to a 50-year low."
rationale: The statement is overly broad and misleading because it does not specify which measure is meant. While some indicators during the Obama years showed big declines (for example net migration from Mexico fell to near zero and certain border apprehensions were at multi-decade lows in the mid-2010s), other measures—such as the total unauthorized immigrant population—remained near its historical highs. Because the claim asserts a blanket “50-year low” without defining the metric or year, it is not supportable as stated.

claim: "This is the slowest job recovery since Hoover."
rationale: The claim overstates the case: while the 2007–2009 recession produced one of the slowest job recoveries in the post–World War II era, it was not as prolonged or deep as the collapse and multi-year slump of the Hoover/Great Depression period. Fact-checks and historical employment data show post-2008 job growth was slower than many postwar recoveries but far faster than the 1930s decline under Hoover. Thus saying it is the slowest 'since Hoover' is inaccurate without heavy qualifiers.

claim: "We had 6,000 oil and gas spills in 2012" with "more oil and gas spreading in the United States than the entire Exxon Valdez spill."
rationale: The statement is misleading and not reliably supported. While federal and state trackers do record thousands of small oil and gas releases in some years, the oft‑quoted “6,000 spills in 2012” lacks a clear, authoritative source and depends on definitions; similarly, aggregating many small incidents to claim a greater total volume than the Exxon Valdez (about 11 million gallons) is not substantiated by publicly available, vetted aggregate-volume data. Different agencies count different types of releases (including produced water, condensate, etc.), so the raw count and any volume comparison are ambiguous and not clearly true as stated.

claim: "One in 19 Americans today get SSDI or SSI. That's one in 19 Americans (who) are disabled."
rationale: The numeric part is roughly plausible—combined SSDI and SSI recipients total on the order of ~17–19 million, which is close to 1 in 19 Americans. However, equating program receipt with being disabled is misleading: SSI includes non-disabled elderly recipients, SSDI/SSI rolls include some dependents, and many people with disabling conditions do not receive these benefits. Thus program enrollment is not the same as the true prevalence of disability.

claim: Says a picture he posted on Facebook of a man posing in front of five decapitated human heads is "one of the subhuman mongrels our president set free."
rationale: I cannot verify this quoted Facebook post from the information given. The claim names no person, date, or source and I have no recollection of a confirmed, attributable post with that exact wording; without corroborating evidence the statement should not be treated as established fact. If specific identifying details or a screenshot are provided it could be re-evaluated.

claim: "Iraq is costing each household about $100 a month."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous and unsupported as written — it does not specify which country’s households, which time period, or what costs are included (direct military spending, reconstruction, veterans’ care, interest). Estimates of the cost of the Iraq War to U.S. households have varied widely depending on methodology and timeframe, and cannot be reduced to a single accurate figure of “about $100 a month” without more context. Because the claim lacks necessary detail and is not universally true, it is assessed as false.

claim: Says Barack Obama "founded ISIS. I would say the co-founder would be crooked Hillary Clinton."
rationale: The claim is false. ISIS traces its origins to al‑Qaeda in Iraq and figures like Abu Musab al‑Zarqawi and later Abu Bakr al‑Baghdadi, arising from the Iraq insurgency and the Syrian civil war—not as an organization founded by Barack Obama or Hillary Clinton. While U.S. and other policies affected regional dynamics, they did not 'found' ISIS or make Hillary Clinton a co‑founder.

claim: Says Republican lieutenants to House Speaker Joe Straus "aired radio ads supporting Democrat(ic state Rep.) Mark Homer... helping the Democrat to a narrow win."
rationale: I find no reliable record that Republican lieutenants allied with House Speaker Joe Straus produced or aired radio ads endorsing Democratic state Rep. Mark Homer that influenced a narrow victory. Major coverage of Texas House factional fights around Speaker Straus documented intra‑Republican battles and occasional cross‑party maneuvering, but this specific claim about radio ads for Homer is unsubstantiated. Given lack of corroborating reporting and the unusual nature of Republicans running ads for a Democrat, the claim is likely false.

claim: "State revenue projections have missed the mark month after month."
rationale: The claim is unqualified and provides no specific state or timeframe, so it cannot be verified as a general fact. While some states and periods have seen systematic forecast shortfalls, that does not justify the blanket statement that "state revenue projections have missed the mark month after month" without additional context or evidence.

claim: "Why was there no news coverage of this raid on the Arizona border? … Seizure was just five days ago. Right on the Arizona border!"
rationale: The statement asserts there was "no news coverage" of a specific border raid five days earlier but provides no verifiable details (date, exact location, agency involved). That broad claim is unlikely: seizures/raids on the U.S.–Mexico border are commonly reported by local media, law enforcement press releases, or national outlets, so a blanket assertion of no coverage cannot be substantiated. Without concrete specifics this is unverified and treated as false.

claim: "In the past year, Floridians, not government, created almost 135,000 new private sector jobs. We netted more than 120,000 total jobs in the first 11 months of 2011; the third most of any state in the nation."
rationale: Contemporary BLS state employment reports and Florida labor data show that Florida posted roughly 134–135 thousand private‑sector job gains on a 12‑month basis around late 2011, and netted just over 120,000 total nonfarm job gains in the first 11 months of 2011. Those totals placed Florida among the top three states in numeric job gains at that time (behind Texas and California). The phrasing emphasizes private‑sector (not government) growth and rounds to close figures reported by official series.

claim: Says Governor Cooper has vetoed "every single teacher pay raise we've ever passed."
rationale: The claim is an absolute statement that Governor Roy Cooper vetoed every teacher pay raise passed by the legislature; that is incorrect. While Cooper has vetoed some budget proposals and clashed with the legislature, he has also signed legislation and budgets that included teacher pay increases, so he did not veto every single raise. The blanket wording “every single” is contradicted by multiple instances where pay increases were enacted with his approval or as part of budgets he signed.

claim: Says Gov. Andrew Cuomo and Democratic lawmakers are "granting free tuition to illegal immigrants while closing Excelsior Scholarship applications to citizen students."
rationale: This claim misstates New York policy. In 2019 New York expanded state financial-aid eligibility (TAP/in-state tuition access) for some undocumented residents, but that did not equate to universal “free tuition” and the Excelsior Scholarship still requires filing the federal FAFSA, which undocumented immigrants generally cannot submit. There was no policy of selectively “closing” Excelsior applications to citizen students while granting tuition to undocumented people; any application windows or eligibility rules apply by program criteria, not by citizen status alone.

claim: "For more than 80 years, there has not been a nomination and confirmation of a Supreme Court Justice in a presidential election year. This is simply not the time to break with decades of bipartisan practice."
rationale: The statement is incorrect: in 2020 President Trump nominated Amy Coney Barrett during the presidential election year and the Senate confirmed her in October 2020. That direct example shows a nomination and confirmation did occur in a presidential election year, contradicting the claim that none had occurred for more than 80 years.

claim: Chris "Sununu supported Obama’s Common Core agenda, taking away local control of our schools."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Common Core standards were developed and adopted by state officials (NGA/CCSSO) and the Obama administration only used federal incentives (e.g., Race to the Top) to encourage adoption; it was not a unilateral Obama ‘agenda’ that took local control. There is no clear evidence that Chris Sununu explicitly supported a federal takeover of schools under Obama’s policies, and as a Republican governor he has publicly opposed federal overreach into education.

claim: "BREAKING: Queen Elizabeth II Dead At 94"
rationale: Queen Elizabeth II did die, but not at 94. Reliable, widely reported sources show she died on 8 September 2022 at age 96, so the claim’s stated age is incorrect (and the “BREAKING” framing is misleading given the event occurred in 2022).

claim: "You can’t get on an airplane, but more than 2,000 people on that list have been able to buy a gun."
rationale: Reliable reporting and government data have shown that being on the terrorism watch/no‑fly list can prevent airline travel but does not automatically block firearm purchases; a 2015 AP analysis of federal records found more than 2,000 people on a terrorism watchlist were able to buy guns. The claim accurately summarizes that discrepancy between travel restrictions and gun‑purchase screening.

claim: Photos show "Ukrainian Christians pray outdoors, in the snow, for their country in this phase of war danger."
rationale: There are no specific images or provenance provided to verify the claim. While genuine news photos have shown Ukrainians praying outdoors (including in winter), many circulated images are miscaptioned or from other times/places, so the generic assertion that "photos show" this cannot be confirmed and is treated as false without source-level verification.

claim: Says "New Jersey’s $1 billion horse racing industry … employs 13,000 individuals and ensures the preservation of 176,000 acres of horse farmland."
rationale: The stated figures are not supported by authoritative state data and appear exaggerated. New Jersey’s total acreage and typical agriculture statistics make preservation of 176,000 acres specifically for horse farmland unlikely, and employment of 13,000 directly attributable to the state’s horse racing industry is much higher than commonly reported sector employment; these numbers appear to originate from industry advocacy materials that conflate broader equine activities or regional totals rather than New Jersey racing alone.

claim: Says Mitt Romney flip-flopped on abortion.
rationale: Mitt Romney publicly supported abortion rights earlier in his career (he identified as pro-choice in the 1990s and while governor of Massachusetts) and later adopted a pro-life stance during his presidential campaigns, advocating greater restrictions. This clear change in his stated positions over time is commonly described as a flip-flop.

claim: Says Mike DeWine "flip-flopped on the gun issue and has earned an F from the NRA."
rationale: The statement bundles two claims that lack clear public support: NRA grades are publicly reported and there is no consistent evidence that Mike DeWine was given an overall “F” by the NRA, and the charge that he “flip-flopped” is subjective and depends on specific policy positions and timing. Without a cited timeframe or documented examples of a reversal, the allegation is unsubstantiated. Therefore the combined claim is not supported as stated.

claim: The Republican replacement for Obamacare does not give massive tax cuts to wealthy Americans.
rationale: Major Republican replacement proposals (notably the 2017 AHCA/related Senate bills) repealed or scaled back several taxes in the ACA that primarily affected high earners (for example the 3.8% net investment income tax and the 0.9% Medicare surtax) and shifted benefits in ways analyses showed disproportionately favored higher-income households. Independent analyses (CBO, Tax Policy Center and others) concluded the net effect was tax relief concentrated among wealthier Americans rather than an absence of such cuts.

claim: Says Republican U.S. Rep. Bob Dold "continues to side with his Republican leadership and the NRA in blocking consideration of a bill that would keep firearms out of the hands of people on the terrorist watch list."
rationale: There is no clear evidence that Rep. Bob Dold uniquely or explicitly "continues to side" with leadership and the NRA to block consideration of a specific "no fly, no buy" bill. While House Republican leadership generally resisted Democratic gun-control measures after high-profile attacks, and some procedural votes prevented floor consideration, I could not find a definitive record tying Dold to a specific action that blocked that exact bill. The claim appears to conflate broader party actions with an individual endorsement without clear documentary support.

claim: Hillary Clinton "starts off with 47 percent of the country against her."
rationale: The statement is presented as a precise, timeless fact but lacks context (which campaign or poll). Public-opinion polls around Hillary Clinton's 2015–2016 campaign did show unfavorable ratings often in the high 30s to mid-40s, so some surveys were near 47%, but there is no consistent, context-free fact that she “starts off” with exactly 47% of the country against her. Because polling varies by date and methodology, the unqualified claim is misleading and cannot be verified as stated.

claim: "Mass media destroyed! Blackout for mass arrests event!"
rationale: The statement asserts that mass media has been 'destroyed' and that there is a 'blackout for mass arrests,' but there is no credible evidence that major news organizations have been dismantled or that a coordinated media blackout and mass-arrest operation has occurred. Such large-scale events would be widely reported and verifiable by multiple independent outlets and official sources; no reliable reports corroborate this claim. The phrasing appears sensational or conspiratorial rather than factual.

claim: "Over 65% of the country believes that (the) 2020 election was fraudulent. That number was around 35% a year ago."
rationale: This is false as stated. Multiple national polls did not find that over 65% of all U.S. adults believed the 2020 election was fraudulent; while large majorities of Republicans often said it was stolen, overall national estimates across reputable polls typically ranged much lower (roughly 30–50% depending on timing and question wording). The claim also conflates partisan subgroups with the entire country and gives an imprecise timeline for the "around 35%" figure.

claim: "Mayor Bloomberg was busy blaming African Americans and Latinos for the housing crisis in 2008."
rationale: There is no clear contemporaneous evidence that Mayor Michael Bloomberg publicly blamed African Americans and Latinos for the 2008 housing crash. Public record and media coverage show Bloomberg and most officials pointed to predatory lending, mortgage-backed securities, lax regulation and Wall Street practices as primary causes rather than assigning blame to racial or ethnic groups. The claim appears to conflate criticism of subprime lending to lower-income borrowers with an assertion that Bloomberg explicitly blamed racial groups, which is not supported by mainstream reporting.

claim: Says science shows the physiological effects of wearing masks include hypoxemia, hypercapnia, shortness of breath, toxicity and increased muscle tension.
rationale: The claim is incorrect as a general statement. Numerous studies and public-health agencies find that commonly worn masks (cloth, surgical, N95) do not cause clinically significant hypoxemia or hypercapnia in healthy people; while masks can cause subjective discomfort, shortness of breath sensations, or headaches for some users, there is no credible evidence that mask use produces systemic “toxicity” or reliably increases muscle tension in the general population. Rare exceptions may occur in people with severe respiratory impairment or during extreme exertion, but that does not validate the broad claim.

claim: Say Bernie Sanders "won Nevada after all."
rationale: The statement is ambiguous as written and cannot be accepted as universally true. Bernie Sanders did not win Nevada in 2016 (Hillary Clinton won the Nevada Democratic contest), though Sanders did win the Nevada caucus in 2020. Without a specified year, the claim is misleading and therefore judged false.

claim: "The violent crime rate has risen, and the homicide rate has risen by more than 20 percent in just two years, really after 30 years of decline in violent crime."
rationale: For the United States the broad claim is accurate: violent crime declined for roughly 20–25+ years after the early‑1990s peak, then began rising again in the late 2010s. National data show a large one‑year jump in homicides in 2020 (around +25–30% versus 2019), and multi‑year comparisons (e.g., 2019 to 2021) show increases in excess of 20 percent. However the exact percentages and years depend on the specific two‑year window and data source.

claim: The "state bureaucracy" Jane Norton managed "grew by $43 million in just three years."
rationale: I could not find verifiable evidence that a state agency under Jane Norton’s supervision increased its budget by $43 million in a three‑year period. Norton served as Colorado’s lieutenant governor and oversaw a relatively small set of offices; such a large, isolated $43 million increase would normally be documented in state budget records and contemporary reporting but isn’t corroborated by available summaries. Without a clear identified agency, timeframe, or source, the claim appears unsubstantiated.

claim: A Mack Trucks employee told Joe Biden, "You can’t drive anything besides the country into the ground."
rationale: I cannot find corroborating contemporaneous reporting or verified video showing a Mack Trucks employee telling Joe Biden the exact line quoted. Major news outlets and fact-checkers covering Biden’s visits to Mack Trucks plants reported different exchanges and no authoritative source records that phrasing. Given the lack of reliable evidence, the claim appears to be a misquote or misattribution.

claim: Says U.S. Sen. Ron Johnson "opposes faster broadband internet in small towns" and "got nearly $90,000 in campaign contributions from the telecom special interests."
rationale: The claim conflates and overstates things: Johnson has opposed certain federal broadband subsidy proposals and emphasized market-based solutions, but that is not equivalent to a categorical opposition to faster broadband in small towns. The stated contribution figure (“nearly $90,000”) is a specific number presented without a timeframe and is misleading — Johnson has received contributions from telecom industry PACs, but reported totals vary by election cycle and reporting period and are not unambiguously described by that single figure.

claim: Quotes Albert Einstein as saying "I fear the day technology will surpass human interaction. The world will have a generation of idiots."
rationale: There is no credible primary source in Einstein's writings, speeches, or biographies that contains this wording; the line first appears in modern internet memes and quotation collections without documentary evidence. Quotation researchers and historians consider it apocryphal and misattributed to Einstein. The phrasing and origin are inconsistent with verified Einstein material.

claim: "In 2011, (Debbie) Wasserman Schultz missed 62 congressional votes — one of the worst records of any member of Congress."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Debbie Wasserman Schultz did miss votes in 2011 (reports put the total near the low dozens), dozens of members missed more votes that year and several missed far more due to long absences, so 62 missed votes was not clearly “one of the worst” records in Congress. The phrase “one of the worst” is subjective and depends on the comparison set and counting method for missed votes.

claim: The employer mandate "affects only 5 percent of businesses in this country."
rationale: The statement is misleading and lacks context. For example in the U.S. the Affordable Care Act employer mandate applies to employers with 50+ full-time-equivalent employees, and while only a small share of firms by count exceed that threshold (commonly cited as roughly 4–6%), the mandate covers a much larger share of workers and can have broader indirect effects—so a blanket claim that it “affects only 5 percent of businesses” is unsupported without definition of “affects” or the jurisdiction.

claim: The Biden administration’s American Jobs Plan will be "the biggest non-defense investment in research and development in the history of our country."
rationale: The American Jobs Plan proposed roughly $180 billion for R&D-related priorities, but that amount is not clearly the largest non-defense R&D investment in U.S. history once you consider past major civilian programs and how ‘‘investment’’ is defined and inflation-adjusted. Historical peaks such as the Apollo-era civilian space program and large NIH/health research funding increases (and the fact the plan was a proposal, not enacted funding) make the Biden claim an overstatement.

claim: Charlie Crist stopped "layoffs of some 20,000 school teachers during the global economic meltdown."
rationale: The claim overstates the evidence. While Crist’s administration participated in using federal stimulus and state budget actions during the Great Recession that helped reduce teacher layoffs, there is no clear, attributable record that he personally “stopped” roughly 20,000 teacher layoffs; numbers differ by source and causation was shared among federal funds, state budgeting and local districts.

claim: "Newgard owed more than $13,000 for unpaid taxes on his $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex."
rationale: I cannot find verifiable evidence that a person named Newgard owed more than $13,000 in unpaid taxes on a $1 million Milwaukie apartment complex. The claim cites a specific dollar amount and property value that would normally be documented in local tax records or contemporaneous news reporting, but I am not aware of such documentation. Without corroborating public records or credible reporting, the claim is not substantiated.

claim: "Supreme Court issues its first bench warrant ever."
rationale: This is incorrect as an absolute statement. Courts routinely issue bench warrants and the Supreme Court (and its predecessors) have had the authority to issue arrest orders or contempt-related warrants in the past, so saying it was the "first ever" is misleading without a narrow, well-defined context. If the claim refers to a particular recent action, it may be novel in some procedural sense but not the Court's first-ever use of such power.

claim: Says Beto O’Rourke is "the only candidate to the U.S. Senate to call for" impeaching President Donald Trump.
rationale: This is false: Beto O’Rourke was not uniquely the only U.S. Senate candidate to call for impeaching President Trump. During 2017–2019 multiple Democratic Senate candidates and other contenders publicly supported impeachment or congressional action against Trump, so the exclusivity claim is incorrect.

claim: Says new figures he released showing Wisconsin job gains for 2011 are "the final job numbers."
rationale: I cannot verify that any named official actually said the released 2011 Wisconsin job figures were "the final job numbers." Official employment statistics are typically subject to revision by state and federal agencies, so a blanket statement calling them final would be unlikely without a direct, citable quote. Because the claim lacks a specific speaker, date, or source, it cannot be confirmed.

claim: Says Bruce Poliquin "voted to strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance."
rationale: Poliquin did vote for House Republican health-care legislation in 2017 that independent analysts said would lead to tens of thousands of Mainers losing coverage, but the specific claim that he “voted to strip 117,000 Mainers of their insurance” is not a firmly established, direct fact. State-level loss estimates vary by model, year, and policy details, and the exact figure 117,000 is not uniquely attributable to a single, indisputable source tied to his vote. Thus the wording is misleading or unverified as a precise factual statement.

claim: A 13-year-old girl "is now in critical care in the hospital here in Halifax because her heart stopped right after she had a vaccine."
rationale: There are no credible public reports or official statements confirming that a 13-year-old in Halifax is in critical care because her heart stopped immediately after a vaccine. The claim appears anecdotal and unverified; temporal proximity alone does not establish causation and a severe event like this would likely be documented by local hospitals or media if confirmed.

claim: Says Hillary Clinton's Iran nuclear deal "lined the pockets of the world's number one state sponsor of terrorism with your money."
rationale: This statement is misleading. The 2015 Iran nuclear agreement (JCPOA) eased sanctions and allowed Iran access to assets held abroad that belonged to Iran (estimates often cited around tens of billions), but it did not involve sending U.S. taxpayer money to Iran. A separate, much-debated settlement and cash transfer occurred around the same time, but that was a legal settlement and not a direct taxpayer giveaway under the nuclear deal.

claim: Says "Obama’s deadliest cover-up (in an explosion that killed 29 miners) has been uncovered" by internal government documents.
rationale: The claim is false. The explosion that killed 29 miners most likely refers to the 2010 Upper Big Branch mine disaster, which multiple official investigations (MSHA and independent probes) attributed to operator negligence and unsafe practices rather than an executive-branch "cover-up." DOJ and other agencies investigated and pursued legal action against company officials; there is no credible evidence that internal government documents reveal an Obama-era cover-up of that event.

claim: "Never mind that no red light camera, no speed camera, nor any radar gun has ever stopped one accident from occurring."
rationale: The claim asserts an absolute that no red light camera, speed camera, or radar gun has ever prevented a single accident, but numerous peer‑reviewed studies and government/road‑safety agency evaluations show these tools reduce speeds and lower crash and injury rates in many settings. While effects vary by context and some implementations can shift crash types (e.g., more rear‑end collisions), the blanket statement that they never stopped any accidents is contradicted by empirical evidence.

claim: Says Missouri Democratic Senate candidate Jason Kander is "attending fancy dinners all over the country."
rationale: The statement asserts a broad, verifiable pattern (Kander attending “fancy dinners all over the country”) but provides no timeframe or sourcing and I find no specific public reporting documenting that he repeatedly attended such events nationwide. While political candidates often travel to donor events, there is no clear evidence that Jason Kander engaged in the extensive, nationwide pattern described. Therefore the claim as stated is not supported by available information.

claim: Says a car driving former University of Missouri System President Tim Wolfe "ran through the students, hit one of them" at the MU Homecoming Parade.
rationale: The claim is false: contemporary news reports, police statements, video footage and subsequent fact-checks showed that Tim Wolfe was not driving the vehicle that moved into the crowd at the MU homecoming parade. The incident involved a vehicle striking a protester, but the driver was a parade participant/spectator and not the former University of Missouri System President.

claim: Graduation rates of players at major football colleges "are still twenty points below their male campus peers and worsened in the past three years."
rationale: Publicly reported NCAA graduation measures (using GSR and related campus comparisons) do not support a consistent, 20-point deficit for players at 'major' football schools nor a recent three‑year worsening. In recent years the gap between football players and their male campus peers has generally narrowed and in many Power Five programs football players graduate at rates similar to or higher than male non‑athletes; trends in the last several reporting cycles were generally flat or improving rather than uniformly worse.

claim: The federal government "reviewed and verified" his administration’s numbers showing Wisconsin added 23,608 jobs in 2011.
rationale: Federal labor agencies do not 'review and verify' a state administration's press-release job tally in the manner claimed. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (and related federal programs) produce their own employment estimates using standard surveys and models and did not certify an administration's specific headline number of 23,608 jobs for Wisconsin in 2011. Prior independent fact-checks found no federal sign-off of that precise figure.

claim: "I got a letter from 20 people who said they wanted their money back, 14 never gave me a penny."
rationale: This is an unverifiable personal anecdote with no provided evidence (the letter or transaction records) to confirm the counts. Without independent documentation or corroboration, the specific numeric claim (20-letter writers and 14 who never paid) cannot be established as factual. Because the statement is narrowly empirical and unsupported, it is judged false for fact-checking purposes.

claim: "Congressman Cicilline, when he was the mayor of Providence, espoused a sanctuary city."
rationale: Available public records and contemporary reporting do not show that Mayor David Cicilline formally declared or explicitly campaigned for Providence to be a "sanctuary city" while he was mayor. He did pursue immigrant-friendly local policies and spoke in favor of protecting immigrant communities, but there is no clear evidence he officially espoused or instituted a formal sanctuary-city designation during his Providence tenure. Given imprecise uses of the term "espoused" and "sanctuary city," the specific claim overstates the historical record.

claim: "Scott Walker has a plan to privatize state lands" and "wants to sell our deer to the highest bidder."
rationale: This claim is false or greatly misleading. While Walker supported selling or transferring certain surplus state-owned properties and favored private management in limited cases, he never advanced a credible plan to wholesale privatize all state lands, nor proposed literally "selling our deer to the highest bidder." The latter phrase is a hyperbolic characterization not reflected in his policy proposals or budgets.

claim: "Johns Hopkins University confirms: You can be vaccinated with a PCR test, even without knowing"
rationale: This claim is false. PCR tests are diagnostic swabs that collect material to detect viral RNA and do not contain vaccines or immunizing agents, and there is no credible evidence Johns Hopkins University has confirmed that a PCR test can vaccinate someone without their knowledge. There is no plausible biological mechanism for a diagnostic swab to induce protective immunity.

claim: "The CDC director just said that 75% of ‘Covid deaths’ occurred in people with at least four comorbidities."
rationale: This claim is not supported by public statements or CDC summaries — the CDC director did not recently say that 75% of COVID deaths occurred in people with at least four comorbidities. While many death certificates list multiple contributing conditions, CDC reporting and independent fact-checkers show the counts and proportions vary by dataset and age group and do not support the blanket 75% assertion as quoted. The claim appears to be a misquotation or misinterpretation of complex mortality-data tables.

claim: Says 13 Texas universities "have announced or implemented a $10,000 degree."
rationale: I could not verify that exactly 13 Texas universities have formally announced or implemented a $10,000 bachelor’s degree program. Media reports and official statements indicate several Texas public universities and systems have proposed or piloted $10K-degree initiatives, but the precise count varies by source and many announcements were exploratory rather than fully implemented. Given the variability and lack of a reliable list confirming 13 completed commitments, the specific numeric claim is not supported.

claim: "Kyle Rittenhouse files $400 million suit against CNN!"
rationale: There is no reliable reporting or public court filing that Kyle Rittenhouse has filed a $400 million lawsuit specifically against CNN. While Rittenhouse has threatened or pursued various legal actions and made defamation claims against media and individuals after his trial, none documented by major outlets or court records match the $400 million figure against CNN. The claim appears to be a misstatement or conflation of other legal threats or suits he has been involved in.

claim: "There is nothing in the current state public records law that prohibits sensitive or confidential business information from being just that, confidential."
rationale: The claim is too broad and inaccurate: most U.S. state public records/FOIA laws include explicit exemptions for trade secrets, proprietary or confidential commercial information, or allow agencies to withhold or redact such material. Whether particular business information must be disclosed or can be kept confidential varies by statute and facts, so it is incorrect to say there is ‘nothing’ in state law that allows or governs confidentiality of sensitive business information.

claim: "I, all the way back in January, warned (President Trump that) this pandemic was coming. I talked about what we needed to do."
rationale: The claim as stated is unverifiable because it does not identify who made the assertion and there is no publicly available corroboration that a specific individual personally warned President Trump in January and outlined concrete actions. Public records show some intelligence and public-health briefings in January 2020 flagged COVID-19 risks to the administration, but many public figures who later claimed early warnings do not have documented private January meetings or advice to the President. Without named, independently corroborated evidence, the blanket statement is unsupported.

claim: "If Rhode Island does a hybrid [retirement] plan we’ll be the first state in the nation to do this.’’
rationale: The claim is incorrect: several U.S. states had already adopted hybrid retirement plans (combining defined‑benefit and defined‑contribution features) during pension reform efforts in the 2000s–2010s. Because hybrid DB/DC models were implemented in multiple states for at least some employee groups before Rhode Island’s proposals, Rhode Island would not be the first state to do this.

claim: "Woman set to testify against Clintons blown up in home explosion."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that a woman who was scheduled to testify against Bill or Hillary Clinton was killed in a house explosion. Multiple reputable fact-checkers and mainstream news outlets investigated the viral posts and found they mischaracterized or conflated unrelated incidents; no court records, prosecutors, or credible reporters corroborate the alleged scheduled testimony or the claimed connection to the Clintons.

claim: "In Rick Perry's Texas, the governor threatens to leave, to secede from the greatest country in the" world.
rationale: This is false: while secessionist sentiment has appeared in Texas politics and Rick Perry has sometimes used strong rhetoric, as governor he did not credibly threaten to have Texas secede from the United States. Perry repeatedly affirmed Texas was part of the U.S. and never issued an official or actionable secession threat while in office.

claim: "Hidden" in the healthcare.gov code is language that means users "waive any reasonable right to privacy of your personal information."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Healthcare.gov contains a hidden code clause that makes users “waive any reasonable right to privacy.” U.S. government sites publish privacy notices and terms publicly and are subject to legal constraints; an HTML comment or hidden field would not create a broad legal waiver of privacy. The claim appears to be a misreading or exaggeration of a comment or policy phrase rather than an enforceable hidden waiver.

claim: The Republicans' alternative health care plan "will still let insurers raise premiums four times faster than wages."
rationale: The statement is an imprecise, predictive claim that names no specific GOP bill or timeframe and is not supported by a single policy text that explicitly allows insurers to raise premiums "four times faster than wages." Premium growth relative to wages is driven by health-care cost trends and state regulatory frameworks, and Republican proposals typically change rules around subsidies, Medicaid, and market regulations rather than setting a fixed multiple for premium increases. Without a cited law or numeric projection tying a particular GOP alternative plan to a 4x wage multiple, the claim is unsupported.

claim: "We know mask mandates work. There’s enough evidence out there between counties that have done it and counties that haven’t."
rationale: Multiple peer‑reviewed observational and quasi‑experimental studies comparing counties, states, and time periods, together with laboratory data on mask filtration and public‑health meta‑analyses, consistently show mask mandates are associated with reduced SARS‑CoV‑2 transmission, hospitalizations, and deaths. While perfect causality is hard to prove because of confounders and concurrent policies, the preponderance of evidence supports that mandates reduce spread when implemented and followed.

claim: Says Alex Sink "failed Florida homeowners by using predatory lending practices."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Alex Sink personally engaged in or implemented predatory lending practices that ‘failed Florida homeowners.’ She served as Florida’s Chief Financial Officer and previously held banking-executive roles, but public records and reporting do not document her running predatory-lending programs; accusations of ties to banks were campaign rhetoric by opponents rather than proven misconduct. The claim therefore overstates and misattributes responsibility without substantiation.

claim: "One of the reasons that Social Security is in so much trouble is that the only funding stream comes from people who get a wage. The people who get wages is declining dramatically."
rationale: The statement is incorrect in two ways. Social Security’s primary revenue is payroll taxes on wages and self-employment earnings, but it also receives interest on trust fund assets and some revenue from taxation of benefits — so payrolls are not its only possible income. Also, the number of wage earners in the U.S. has not been collapsing dramatically; what has shifted more slowly is the ratio of workers per beneficiary due to population aging and slower workforce growth, not a sudden large drop in wage earners.

claim: "A law enforcement officer is more likely to commit a crime than a CWP (concealed weapons permit) holder."
rationale: The claim is an unsupported broad generalization. There is no reliable, comprehensive nationwide data directly comparing criminal offending rates of law enforcement officers to concealed carry permit (CWP) holders, and rates vary by jurisdiction, time period, and crime type. While many studies find CWP holders have low criminal-conviction rates relative to the general population, law enforcement misconduct and criminality are measured differently (internal discipline, arrests, convictions) making a simple across-the-board comparison invalid.

claim: "Over-vaccination causes faster mutation of the (COVID-19) virus, which causes a super virus we may not have the ability to fight off."
rationale: The claim is false. Vaccination reduces viral replication and transmission, which lowers the total number of mutations that can arise; while immune pressure can select for escape mutations in some cases, the evidence shows vaccines overall reduce variant emergence rather than causing a faster mutation rate that produces an inevitable 'super virus.' There is no credible evidence that routine vaccination programs produce untreatable superviruses.

claim: Most voters prefer zombies to the current U.S. Congress.
rationale: There is no credible empirical evidence or reputable public-opinion poll showing a majority of U.S. voters would prefer literal zombies to the current U.S. Congress. While congressional approval is often low and critics use ‘zombies’ as rhetorical hyperbole, that rhetorical use does not constitute a factual majority preference. The claim appears to be figurative rather than an empirically supported statement.

claim: "74 percent of Republicans support the Affordable Care Act."
rationale: Major, reputable polls over the past decade show Republican support for the Affordable Care Act as a whole is substantially lower than 74% (commonly in the ~20–40% range depending on timing and poll). Numbers near 74% typically refer to support for specific provisions (e.g., protections for pre-existing conditions or allowing children to stay on parents' plans), not overall support for the law itself.

claim: "Reporters rehearse questions with White House press (secretary)."
rationale: The claim as a general statement is false: reporters do not routinely rehearse questions with the White House press secretary. White House briefings are live Q&A and journalists adhere to independent questioning; while there are occasional off‑the‑record background briefings or friendly reporters may get advance access, that is not the same as routine rehearsing with the press secretary. Communications staff internally rehearse spokespeople, but journalists normally do not practice questions with the administration they cover.

claim: Says House Democrats leading the impeachment inquiry are "denying President Trump basic fairness and due process accorded every American."
rationale: The claim frames a normative judgment as an objective fact. Impeachment is a constitutional, political process with different procedures than criminal trials; House Democrats conducted committee depositions and public hearings and provided avenues for evidence and responses, while opponents disputed the sufficiency of those procedures. Whether those steps amount to a denial of “basic fairness and due process” is a contested legal and political judgment, not an established factual finding.

claim: "In New Jersey, Gov. Christie vetoed legislation to extend early voting."
rationale: I cannot confirm a specific, widely reported instance in which Gov. Chris Christie vetoed legislation to extend early voting in New Jersey. Major expansions of in-person early voting in New Jersey were enacted after Christie left office, and most well-known Christie vetoes involved other election or budgetary items. Because I lack clear corroboration for the claim as stated, I judge it unlikely to be accurate without more detail (bill number or year).

claim: The polls "show over half of Americans identify themselves as being pro-life."
rationale: Major national polls through mid-2024 (e.g., Gallup, Pew) generally show either a pro-choice plurality or that fewer than 50% of Americans self-identify as strictly "pro-life." While some surveys or specific question wordings can produce a pro-life majority, the broad claim that polls show over half identify as pro-life is not supported without that qualifying context.

claim: "[O]ver 200,000 ordinary citizens were given the opportunity to identify projects they preferred."
rationale: The statement is unverifiable as presented because it gives no context (which program, jurisdiction, or time period) and no source to confirm the number. Without those specifics, I cannot confirm that “over 200,000 ordinary citizens” were given that opportunity; similar-sounding claims may be true for particular initiatives but are not provable from the standalone sentence.

claim: Sotomayor "ruled against the white firefighter — Ricci and other white firefighters — just on the basis that she thought women and minorities should be given a preference because of their skin color and because of the history of discrimination in the past. The law was totally disregarded."
rationale: The claim attributes a simplistic racial‑preference motive and legal disregard to Sotomayor that is not supported by the record. The dispute in Ricci v. DeStefano involved complex Title VII disparate‑impact and disparate‑treatment questions; Sotomayor was on a Second Circuit panel that sided with the city’s concerns about disparate impact, and the Supreme Court later reversed that decision in 2009. There is no reliable evidence she ‘ruled…just on the basis’ of wanting to prefer women or minorities or that she wholly disregarded the law — the outcome reflected differing legal interpretations, not demonstrated personal racial bias.

claim: Wisconsin is "clearly seeing a decline in COVID infections"
rationale: The statement is not verifiable as presented because it gives no timeframe or metric and COVID-19 trends change over time. Whether Wisconsin is ‘‘clearly seeing a decline’’ depends on recent case counts, test positivity, and hospitalizations; some short periods may show declines while others show increases, so the claim is unsupported without current data.

claim: "Matt Rosendale supports plans that don’t have to cover (pre-existing conditions)."
rationale: The claim is misleading. Rosendale has publicly said he supports protecting people with pre-existing conditions, but he has also supported repealing/replacing the ACA and backed policies (state waivers, short‑term or association plans) that could allow plans to limit or exclude coverage for pre‑existing conditions. Without specifying which proposals or time period, the blanket statement is inaccurate.

claim: "It was under Barack Obama and Hillary Clinton that changed the rules of engagement that probably cost (Capt. Humayun Khan’s) life."
rationale: Capt. Humayun Khan was killed in Iraq in July 2004, during the George W. Bush administration. Barack Obama did not become president until 2009 and Hillary Clinton served as Secretary of State beginning in 2009, so they were not in positions to change the rules of engagement that led to a 2004 death; attributing his death to Obama/Clinton is chronologically incorrect.

claim: The newly created state Immigration Enforcement Review Board "can actually prosecute, and get them [violators] into jail, if we bring in the attorney general."
rationale: Administrative review boards generally do not have criminal prosecutorial power; they can investigate, recommend sanctions, or refer matters but cannot themselves bring criminal charges or incarcerate people. Criminal prosecution and jailing require a prosecutor (state AG or local prosecutor) to file charges and a court to convict, and immigration enforcement largely remains a federal responsibility so state remedies are limited. Thus the board itself cannot 'actually prosecute and get them into jail' simply by involving the attorney general.

claim: Congressman Robert Hurt has a plan to cut education by 40 percent.
rationale: There is no credible record that Rep. Robert Hurt authored or formally proposed a plan to cut education funding by 40%. While Hurt supported conservative budgets and measures to reduce federal discretionary spending and to devolve some education programs to states, opponents' claims of a specific 40% cut appear to be political exaggeration rather than a documented policy proposal.

claim: Says U.S. Rep. John Carter "hasn’t held a town hall in five years."
rationale: Public records, constituent newsletters and media reports show Rep. John Carter held constituent meetings and town-hall–style events (including virtual sessions during the COVID period and district meetings afterward) within the last five years, so the categorical claim that he “hasn’t held a town hall in five years” is incorrect. The statement appears to conflate a period without large in-person forums with a complete absence of town-hall–style outreach.

claim: "Breaking: Trump fires deputy attorney general Rod Rosenstein, raising questions over Mueller’s fate."
rationale: This claim is inaccurate: Rod Rosenstein was not fired by President Trump. Public reports indicate Rosenstein submitted a resignation that became effective in May 2019 rather than being abruptly dismissed; although removal of the deputy AG would raise questions about oversight of Special Counsel Mueller, the asserted firing did not occur as stated.

claim: Says Democratic opponents Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith support sanctuary policies.
rationale: Labeling both Cal Cunningham and Erica Smith as supporters of “sanctuary policies” is misleading. Public records show Cunningham backed DACA and comprehensive immigration reform but did not explicitly endorse creating sanctuary cities, and Erica Smith has advocated immigrant protections (e.g., access to driver’s licenses) rather than a clear blanket endorsement of formal sanctuary-city policies. Saying simply that they “support sanctuary policies” overgeneralizes and misstates their documented positions.

claim: Map shows that wildfires stop at the US.-Canada border.
rationale: Wildfires are driven by weather, fuel, and topography, not political boundaries, and have historically crossed the US–Canada border. A map that appears to show fires stopping at the border is almost certainly showing a data artifact (different data sources, reporting times, detection thresholds, or map styling) rather than a physical barrier to fire spread.

claim: Says Jim Renacci has "consistently voted" for loopholes that "encourage outsourcing of our jobs."
rationale: The claim is a broad, unsupported assertion about a consistent pattern of votes; public records do not show a clear, unambiguous series of votes labeled as 'loopholes that encourage outsourcing' attributable to Renacci across his tenure. Without specifying which bills or provisions are meant, the statement is too general to verify and appears to be a partisan characterization rather than a documented voting pattern.

claim: If women seeking an abortion see their ultrasound, "the odds are pretty high they're going to keep the baby."
rationale: Empirical research on mandatory or offered ultrasound viewing for people seeking abortion generally finds little or no large causal effect on whether they continue the pregnancy. Many studies and evaluations of state laws show most people have already decided before the ultrasound and that viewing alone rarely changes the outcome, though small effects in subgroups have been reported. The blanket statement that "the odds are pretty high" that viewing will lead to keeping the baby therefore overstates the evidence.

claim: Says "for the first time ever," Texas lawmakers are not funding student population growth.
rationale: The absolute claim that this is happening "for the first time ever" is unlikely to be true. Texas budget history includes prior sessions where legislatures did not fully fund projected student enrollment growth or froze/cut education funding during revenue shortfalls, so failing to fund growth is not uniquely new. Without a specific year and program (K–12 vs higher education) the blanket "first time ever" statement is unsupported.

claim: Says Donald Trump "has said he wants to be neutral on Israel and the Palestinians"
rationale: This is false as stated. Donald Trump did not publicly declare an intent to be neutral between Israel and the Palestinians; throughout his presidency he repeatedly expressed overtly pro‑Israel positions and enacted policies favoring Israel (recognizing Jerusalem as Israel’s capital, moving the US embassy, recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, and championing the Abraham Accords). Those actions and many public statements (e.g., “I am with Israel 100%”) are inconsistent with a claimed stance of neutrality.

claim: "Japan drops vax rollout"
rationale: The claim is false — Japan did not abandon its COVID-19 vaccination rollout. After an initially slow start, Japan authorized multiple vaccines and carried out nationwide primary series and booster campaigns rather than dropping vaccination efforts; isolated temporary pauses or supply issues do not amount to abandoning the program.

claim: Twitter removed this tweet from Donald Trump: "My blood IS the vaccine!!!!!"
rationale: There is no evidence that Donald Trump ever posted the tweet “My blood IS the vaccine!!!!!” on his official Twitter account, and major fact-checkers and archives do not show such a tweet. The claim appears to stem from a fabricated or doctored screenshot; Twitter did suspend/permanently ban Trump’s account in January 2021 but not for removing a tweet with that wording.

claim: "Farouk is on fire."
rationale: The statement asserts a literal physical event (someone named Farouk is on fire) but provides no evidence, context, or corroborating reports. A real incident of that nature would produce immediate verifiable reports or emergency responses; absent that information the claim cannot be substantiated and is treated as false. If the phrase is intended metaphorically (e.g., doing very well), the meaning would differ and needs context.

claim: "President Trump’s Republican Party will create more debt in one year than was generated in the first 200 years of America’s existence."
rationale: The claim is misleading and depends on ambiguous definitions (which 200‑year span and whether “debt created” means annual deficit or cumulative outstanding debt). The largest single‑year increase under President Trump was the FY2020 deficit (roughly $3 trillion due to COVID relief), which may exceed some narrow 200‑year tallies if you stop early, but does not clearly exceed reasonable measures of the first 200 years of U.S. federal debt (which reach into the low trillions by the late 20th century). Because the statement as written is unqualified and factually unreliable, it is judged false.

claim: "Studies have shown that voter fraud is non-existent in Texas."
rationale: The claim is inaccurate because no reputable studies show that voter fraud is absolutely non-existent in Texas; research and public records find that voter fraud is very rare but not zero. There have been documented prosecutions and validated instances of fraud in Texas, and academic and journalistic analyses characterize its incidence as minimal rather than nonexistent.

claim: Polling shows that nearly 74 percent of National Rifle Association members "support requiring background checks for all gun sales."
rationale: I could not verify a widely cited poll that specifically found "nearly 74%" of NRA members support requiring background checks for all gun sales. While many national polls show very high support for universal background checks among the general public and large majorities among gun owners, figures for self-identified NRA members vary by poll and question wording and do not consistently match the precise 74% claim. Without a clear citation, the claim appears to overstate or misattribute the statistic.

claim: Says Texas has so few gas-pump inspectors in the field, "the HEBs of this state, the Brookshires of this state, they're calibrating their own gas pumps. The (Texas Department of Agriculture) just sends them the stickers and they calibrate them."
rationale: The claim is misleading. While Texas has publicly noted strains in the Department of Agriculture’s weights-and-measures staffing and retailers routinely maintain and have private service technicians calibrate pumps, the state does not simply mail “stickers” and allow grocery chains to unilaterally certify their own pumps without oversight. Official calibration/sealing requires licensed service agents or inspections under the state weights-and-measures program, and seals are tied to inspection/certification procedures rather than unchecked self-certification by stores.

claim: A state senate bill would "criminalize a father teaching his own son how to use a hunting rifle."
rationale: The claim is a broad and misleading summary not supported by standard legislative language. Most state bills that limit minors' access to firearms include explicit exemptions for parental supervision, hunting, or instruction, and I am not aware of any enacted or widely reported state senate bill that plainly makes it a crime for a father to teach his son to use a hunting rifle. Without a specific bill citation, the allegation overstates and mischaracterizes typical firearm-safety or age-restriction proposals.

claim: "Colorado school forces students to wear hijabs."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that any Colorado public school is forcing students to wear hijabs. U.S. public schools are barred by the Constitution from compelling students to adopt religious dress, and reports that circulate about mandates typically misrepresent voluntary programs, private religious-school rules, or isolated classroom activities. Without a specific school and verifiable documentation, the broad claim of a statewide or public-school requirement is unsupported.

claim: Obama would "experiment with socialism."
rationale: There is no credible evidence that Barack Obama said he would “experiment with socialism” or announced a plan to do so; his public statements and policy record emphasize mixed-market approaches and reforms (e.g., the Affordable Care Act, stimulus measures) rather than endorsing socialism.
